abstract: We present a number of Time-Delay Neural Network (TDNN) based architectures for multi-speaker phoneme recognition (/b,d,g/ task). We use speech of two females and four males to compare the performance of the various architectures against a baseline recognition rate of 95.9% for a single IDNN on the six-speaker /b,d,g/ task. This series of modu(cid:173) lar designs leads to a highly modular multi-network architecture capable of performing the six-speaker recognition task at the speaker dependent rate of 98.4%. In addition to its high recognition rate, the so-called "Meta-Pi" architecture learns - without direct supervision - ognize the speech of one particular male speaker using internal models of other male speakers exclusively.

We use speech of two females and four males to compare the performance of the various architectures against a baseline recognition rate of 95.9% for a single IDNN on the six-speaker /b,d,g/ task. This series of modu(cid:173) lar designs leads to a highly modular multi-network architecture capable of performing the six-speaker recognition task at the speaker dependent rate of 98.4%. In addition to its high recognition rate, the so-called "Meta-Pi" architecture learns - without direct supervision - ognize the speech of one particular male speaker using internal models of other male speakers exclusively.

paragraphs: This paper examines neural architectures for distinguishing the phonemes /b/, /d/, and /g/ across multiple speakers. The study uses speech from two women and four men. Its central question is how a modular arrangement of time-delay neural networks can improve recognition when the same sound categories appear in different voices.

The authors compare a series of designs with a single-network baseline that achieves 95.9% recognition on the six-speaker task. Their progression toward greater modularity produces the Meta-Pi architecture, which reaches 98.4%. The abstract identifies this as matching the speaker-dependent recognition rate, giving a concrete reference for the performance of the multi-speaker system.

Meta-Pi also learns, without direct supervision, to recognize one male speaker using internal models of other male speakers exclusively. This finding concerns how the architecture uses its internal speaker models, beyond its overall recognition rate. Together, the results support modular organization as a way to combine strong phoneme recognition with useful relationships among representations of different speakers.
summary.tldr: The modular Meta-Pi architecture improves six-speaker phoneme recognition from 95.9% to 98.4% and learns to reuse other speakers' internal models.

title: Connectionist Architectures for Multi-Speaker Phoneme Recognition

abstract: We built a high-speed, digital mean-field Boltzmann chip and SBus board for general problems in constraint satjsfaction and learning. Each chip has 32 neural processors and 4 weight update processors, supporting an arbitrary topology of up to 160 functional neurons. On-chip learning is at a theoretical maximum rate of 3.5 x 108 con(cid:173) nection updates/sec; recall is 12000 patterns/sec for typical condi(cid:173) tions. The chip's high speed is due to parallel computation of inner products, limited (but adequate) precision for weights and activa(cid:173) tions (5 bits), fast clock (125 MHz), and several design insights.

paragraphs: The authors built a digital mean-field Boltzmann chip and an accompanying SBus board for constraint satisfaction and learning. The work translates a neural computation method into dedicated hardware. Its design addresses both the computation of network activity and the updating of learned connections, making learning itself part of the chip's functionality.

Each chip contains 32 neural processors and four weight-update processors, supporting arbitrary connection arrangements with up to 160 functional neurons. Speed comes from several combined choices: parallel inner-product computation, five-bit precision for weights and activations, a 125 MHz clock, and additional design insights. The abstract describes the limited precision as adequate for the intended computation.

The theoretical maximum learning rate is 350 million connection updates per second. Recall operates at 12,000 patterns per second under typical conditions. These figures characterize different aspects of operation, with the learning figure explicitly representing a theoretical ceiling. The contribution is a built hardware platform showing how parallel arithmetic and compact numerical representations can support fast Boltzmann-network computation.
summary.tldr: A built digital Boltzmann chip combines parallel computation and five-bit precision to accelerate learning and constraint satisfaction.

title: Digital Boltzmann VLSI for constraint satisfaction and learning

abstract: This paper describes the MM32k, a massively-parallel SIMD com(cid:173) puter which is easy to program, high in performance, low in cost and effective for implementing highly parallel neural network ar(cid:173) chitectures. The MM32k has 32768 bit serial processing elements, each of which has 512 bits of memory, and all of which are inter(cid:173) connected by a switching network. The entire system resides on a single PC-AT compatible card. It is programmed from the host computer using a C++ language class library which abstracts the parallel processor in terms of fast arithmetic operators for vectors of variable precision integers.

The MM32k has 32768 bit serial processing elements, each of which has 512 bits of memory, and all of which are inter(cid:173) connected by a switching network. The entire system resides on a single PC-AT compatible card. It is programmed from the host computer using a C++ language class library which abstracts the parallel processor in terms of fast arithmetic operators for vectors of variable precision integers.

paragraphs: The paper presents the MM32k, a computer designed to run many small computations in parallel for neural networks and machine vision. Its SIMD organization lets many processing elements execute a shared instruction on different data. This makes the architecture relevant to neural computations that repeat similar operations across large collections of values.

The hardware contains 32,768 processing elements, each with 512 bits of memory, connected through a switching network. These elements process numbers a bit at a time. The entire machine fits on one PC-AT compatible card, packaging a large amount of parallel processing into a system controlled by a host computer.

Programming uses a C++ class library that presents the hardware as arithmetic operations on vectors of integers with adjustable precision. This interface connects the underlying parallel architecture to familiar numerical operations. The authors describe the resulting system as fast, inexpensive, and easy to program, making both hardware organization and programmer access central to its contribution.
summary.tldr: The MM32k packs 32,768 parallel processing elements onto a PC card and exposes them through a C++ vector-arithmetic interface.

title: A Massively-Parallel SIMD Processor for Neural Network and Machine Vision Applications

The result(cid:173) ing algorithm is applicable t.o a wide range of supervised as well as unsupervised learning problems. Result.s from a classification benchmark-t.he iris data set-are presented.

paragraphs: This paper presents a framework for learning from high-dimensional datasets with arbitrary patterns of missing values. Its starting point is maximum-likelihood density estimation: learning a probabilistic description of the data from the observations that are available. Mixture models supply that description by combining multiple component distributions within one model.

The learning algorithm uses the Expectation-Maximization principle in two distinct roles. One role is estimating the mixture components; the other is handling missing data. Bringing both into the same derivation connects uncertainty about the mixture representation with uncertainty caused by unobserved entries, making incomplete records part of the estimation problem itself.

The authors describe the resulting algorithm as applicable to a broad range of supervised and unsupervised tasks and present classification results on the iris dataset. The main methodological contribution is this unified treatment of mixture estimation and missing values. It provides a probabilistic route from incomplete observations to a learned model that can support classification as well as learning without supplied labels.
summary.tldr: A mixture-model framework uses EM both to estimate components and to learn from arbitrarily missing data.

title: Supervised learning from incomplete data via an EM approach

abstract: Many different discrete-time recurrent neural network architec(cid:173) tures have been proposed. However, there has been virtually no effort to compare these arch:tectures experimentally. In this paper we review and categorize many of these architectures and compare how they perform on various classes of simple problems including grammatical inference and nonlinear system identification.
originalAbstract: Many different discrete-time recurrent neural network architec(cid:173) tures have been proposed. However, there has been virtually no effort to compare these arch:tectures experimentally. In this paper we review and categorize many of these architectures and compare how they perform on various classes of simple problems including grammatical inference and nonlinear system identification.

paragraphs: The paper addresses a comparison problem in recurrent neural network research: many discrete-time architectures had been proposed, but little experimental work had examined them together. The authors review and categorize these architectures before comparing their performance. This gives the study both an organizing role and an empirical one.

The experiments cover several classes of simple problems, including grammatical inference and nonlinear system identification. These represent different kinds of sequential learning: discovering structure in sequences and learning the behavior of a changing system. Including both makes the comparison relevant to more than a single use of recurrence.

The approach matters because proposing a recurrent architecture and understanding how it behaves across tasks are separate contributions. Categorization provides a framework for relating design alternatives, while experiments connect those alternatives to actual learning problems. The abstract presents the scope and purpose of this comparison without naming a winning architecture. Its central contribution is therefore a systematic empirical examination of recurrent designs across different problem classes.
summary.tldr: The paper organizes recurrent network architectures and experimentally compares them on simple sequence-learning and system-identification problems.

title: An experimental comparison of recurrent neural networks

abstract: We present a study which is concerned with word recognition rates for heavily degraded documents. We compare human with machine read(cid:173) ing capabilities in a series of experiments, which explores the interaction of word/non-word recognition, word frequency and legality of non-words with degradation level. We also study the influence of character segmen(cid:173) tation, and compare human performance with that of our artificial neural network model for reading. We found that the proposed computer model uses word context as efficiently as humans, but performs slightly worse on the pure character recognition task.
originalAbstract: We present a study which is concerned with word recognition rates for heavily degraded documents. We compare human with machine read(cid:173) ing capabilities in a series of experiments, which explores the interaction of word/non-word recognition, word frequency and legality of non-words with degradation level. We also study the influence of character segmen(cid:173) tation, and compare human performance with that of our artificial neural network model for reading. We found that the proposed computer model uses word context as efficiently as humans, but performs slightly worse on the pure character recognition task.

paragraphs: Reading a badly degraded document involves both identifying individual characters and using the surrounding word to interpret uncertain letters. This paper compares human readers with a neural-network reading model to examine those contributions. The experiments vary document degradation while also considering whether the presented strings are words or non-words.

The study examines word frequency and the legality of non-words alongside degradation level. These factors help distinguish recognition of familiar words from responses to other letter combinations. It also considers character segmentation, the separation of a written string into individual characters, as another influence on reading performance.

The main finding separates two abilities that an overall reading score could combine. The computer model uses word context as efficiently as human readers, but is slightly worse at recognizing characters on their own. Thus, the reported difference does not arise from a general failure to benefit from word context. The comparison helps locate the remaining performance gap in the character-recognition component of the task.
summary.tldr: A neural reading model benefits from word context as efficiently as humans but performs slightly worse at recognizing individual characters.

title: Comparison of Human and Machine Word Recognition

abstract: We present a probabilistic latent-variable framework for data visu(cid:173) alisation, a key feature of which is its applicability to binary and categorical data types for which few established methods exist. A variational approximation to the likelihood is exploited to derive a fast algorithm for determining the model parameters. Illustrations of application to real and synthetic binary data sets are given.
originalAbstract: We present a probabilistic latent-variable framework for data visu(cid:173) alisation, a key feature of which is its applicability to binary and categorical data types for which few established methods exist. A variational approximation to the likelihood is exploited to derive a fast algorithm for determining the model parameters. Illustrations of application to real and synthetic binary data sets are given.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a probabilistic framework for visualizing high-dimensional data, with particular attention to binary and categorical observations. These data types are a central motivation because few established visualization methods were available for them in the setting described. The framework uses latent variables to support the visualization within a probabilistic model.

The authors derive a fast procedure for determining the model parameters by using a variational approximation to the likelihood. Parameter fitting is therefore tied to an approximation of the model's probabilistic objective. This is the main computational ingredient identified in the abstract and explains how the proposed framework is made practical to fit.

Applications to both real and synthetic binary datasets illustrate the method. These examples demonstrate its use on binary observations, while the framework itself is described as applicable to categorical data as well. The contribution combines a visualization model suited to these discrete data types with a fast parameter-estimation procedure, bringing the representation and its fitting method into one probabilistic approach.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic latent-variable framework visualizes binary and categorical data using a fast fitting algorithm derived from a variational likelihood approximation.

title: Probabilistic Visualisation of High-Dimensional Binary Data

abstract: Recent interpretations of the Adaboost algorithm view it as per(cid:173) forming a gradient descent on a potential function. Simply chang(cid:173) ing the potential function allows one to create new algorithms re(cid:173) lated to AdaBoost. However, these new algorithms are generally not known to have the formal boosting property. This paper ex(cid:173) amines the question of which potential functions lead to new al(cid:173) gorithms that are boosters. The two main results are general sets of conditions on the potential; one set implies that the resulting algorithm is a booster, while the other implies that the algorithm is not. These conditions are applied to previously studied potential functions , such as those used by LogitBoost and Doom II.

Simply chang(cid:173) ing the potential function allows one to create new algorithms re(cid:173) lated to AdaBoost. This paper ex(cid:173) amines the question of which potential functions lead to new al(cid:173) gorithms that are boosters. paragraphs: One interpretation of AdaBoost views it as gradient descent on a potential function. Changing that function creates related learning algorithms, but the resulting resemblance to AdaBoost does not itself establish the formal boosting property. This paper asks which choices of potential function actually support that property.

The authors provide two general sets of conditions. Satisfying one set implies that the resulting algorithm is a booster; satisfying the other implies that it is not. These are distinct sufficient criteria for positive and negative conclusions. The abstract does not describe them as a complete classification of every possible potential function.

The conditions are applied to previously studied potentials, including those associated with LogitBoost and Doom II. Their value is to connect a mathematical design choice—the potential being optimized—to a formal property of the resulting algorithm. This gives the analysis a role beyond proposing another objective: it provides ways to establish when modifying AdaBoost's potential preserves boosting and when it fails to do so.
summary.tldr: The paper gives sufficient conditions showing when potential-based variants of AdaBoost are boosters and when they are not.

title: Potential Boosters?

abstract: Although connectionist models have provided insights into the nature of perception and motor control, connectionist accounts of higher cognition seldom go beyond an implementation of traditional symbol-processing theories. We describe a connectionist constraint satisfaction model of how people solve anagram problems. The model exploits statistics of English orthography, but also addresses the interplay of sub symbolic and symbolic computation by a mechanism that extracts approximate symbolic representations (partial orderings of letters) from sub symbolic structures and injects the extracted representation back into the model to assist in the solution of the anagram. We show the computational benefit of this extraction-injection process and discuss its relationship to conscious mental processes and working memory. We also account for experimental data concerning the difficulty of anagram solution based on the orthographic structure of the anagram string and the target word.
originalAbstract: Although connectionist models have provided insights into the nature of perception and motor control, connectionist accounts of higher cognition seldom go beyond an implementation of traditional symbol-processing theories. We describe a connectionist constraint satisfaction model of how people solve anagram problems. The model exploits statistics of English orthography, but also addresses the interplay of sub symbolic and symbolic computation by a mechanism that extracts approximate symbolic representations (partial orderings of letters) from sub symbolic structures and injects the extracted representation back into the model to assist in the solution of the anagram. We show the computational benefit of this extraction-injection process and discuss its relationship to conscious mental processes and working memory. We also account for experimental data concerning the difficulty of anagram solution based on the orthographic structure of the anagram string and the target word.

paragraphs: The paper models how people solve anagrams using a connectionist constraint-satisfaction system. The model draws on statistical patterns in English spelling to help arrange letters into a solution. Its broader aim is to explain how distributed, subsymbolic processing can interact with more explicit symbolic representations during a task associated with higher cognition.

The key mechanism extracts an approximate symbolic representation from the network's subsymbolic state. That representation consists of partial orderings of letters, capturing some information about their arrangement without requiring a complete solution. The extracted information is then injected back into the model to assist further processing. Symbolic structure therefore becomes an intermediate resource within the ongoing solution process.

The authors demonstrate a computational benefit from this extraction-and-reinjection mechanism. They also account for experimental findings about anagram difficulty associated with the spelling structure of both the scrambled string and the target word. Discussion connects the mechanism to conscious mental processing and working memory, giving the computational model a proposed relationship to psychological processes involved in solving anagrams.
summary.tldr: An anagram-solving network benefits from extracting partial symbolic letter orderings and feeding them back into its distributed computation.

title: The Interplay of Symbolic and Subsymbolic Processes in Anagram Problem Solving

abstract: Prior knowledge about video structure can be used both as a means to improve the peiformance of content analysis and to extract features that allow semantic classification. We introduce statistical models for two important components of this structure, shot duration and activity, and demonstrate the usefulness of these models by introducing a Bayesian formulation for the shot segmentation problem. The new formulations is shown to extend standard thresholding methods in an adaptive and intuitive way, leading to improved segmentation accuracy.
originalAbstract: Prior knowledge about video structure can be used both as a means to improve the peiformance of content analysis and to extract features that allow semantic classification. We introduce statistical models for two important components of this structure, shot duration and activity, and demonstrate the usefulness of these models by introducing a Bayesian formulation for the shot segmentation problem. The new formulations is shown to extend standard thresholding methods in an adaptive and intuitive way, leading to improved segmentation accuracy.

paragraphs: The paper examines how knowledge of video structure can improve the division of a video into shots. It focuses on two structural properties: how long shots last and how much activity they contain. The authors introduce statistical models for these properties so that they can inform decisions about shot boundaries.

These models become part of a Bayesian formulation of shot segmentation. This provides a way to combine evidence about a boundary with prior knowledge of video structure. The authors show that their formulation extends standard thresholding methods in an adaptive, intuitive manner. The decision process therefore incorporates modeled structural information when deciding where one shot ends and another begins.

The reported result is improved segmentation accuracy. The paper also motivates structural modeling as useful for content analysis and for extracting features that support semantic classification. Its demonstrated contribution is the segmentation formulation: shot duration and activity become explicit sources of information for improving the separation of video into meaningful temporal units.
summary.tldr: Statistical models of shot duration and activity support a Bayesian extension of threshold-based video segmentation that improves accuracy.

title: Bayesian Video Shot Segmentation

abstract: Theories of object recognition often assume that only one representa(cid:173) tion scheme is used within one visual-processing pathway. Versatility of the visual system comes from having multiple visual-processing pathways, each specialized in a different category of objects. We propose a theoretically simpler alternative, capable of explaining the same set of data and more. A single primary visual-processing pathway, loosely modular, is assumed. Memory modules are attached to sites along this pathway. Object-identity decision is made independently at each site. A site's response time is a monotonic-decreasing function of its confidence regarding its decision. An observer's response is the first-arriving response from any site. The effective representation(s) of such a system, determined empirically, can appear to be specialized for different tasks and stimuli, consistent with recent clinical and functional-imaging findings. This, however, merely reflects a decision being made at its appropriate level of abstraction. The system itself is intrinsically flexible and adaptive.

paragraphs: The paper proposes an account of object recognition in which a single primary visual pathway can support apparently specialized representations. It challenges theories that explain visual versatility through separate pathways devoted to different object categories. The alternative assumes a loosely modular pathway with memory modules attached at several stages.

Each memory site independently decides an object's identity. A key assumption links confidence to timing: greater confidence produces a faster response. The observer's answer is whichever site's response arrives first. Consequently, different tasks and stimuli can lead different stages of the same pathway to determine the final decision.

This mechanism can make the system appear specialized when studied experimentally, because the winning decision comes from an appropriate level of abstraction. The authors argue that this account can explain the data addressed by competing theories and additional observations, while remaining consistent with clinical and functional-imaging findings. Its significance is a proposed explanation of flexible recognition through distributed memory and decision timing within one pathway.
summary.tldr: A visual pathway with competing memory sites could produce apparently specialized recognition through confidence-dependent response times.

title: Adaptive Object Representation with Hierarchically-Distributed Memory Sites

abstract: Nearest neighbor classification assumes locally constant class con(cid:173) ditional probabilities. This assumption becomes invalid in high dimensions with finite samples due to the curse of dimensionality. Severe bias can be introduced under these conditions when using the nearest neighbor rule. We propose a locally adaptive nearest neighbor classification method to try to minimize bias. We use a Chi-squared distance analysis to compute a flexible metric for pro(cid:173) ducing neighborhoods that are elongated along less relevant feature dimensions and constricted along most influential ones. As a result, the class conditional probabilities tend to be smoother in the mod(cid:173) ified neighborhoods, whereby better classification performance can be achieved. The efficacy of our method is validated and compared against other techniques using a variety of real world data.
originalAbstract: Nearest neighbor classification assumes locally constant class con(cid:173) ditional probabilities. This assumption becomes invalid in high dimensions with finite samples due to the curse of dimensionality. Severe bias can be introduced under these conditions when using the nearest neighbor rule. We propose a locally adaptive nearest neighbor classification method to try to minimize bias. We use a Chi-squared distance analysis to compute a flexible metric for pro(cid:173) ducing neighborhoods that are elongated along less relevant feature dimensions and constricted along most influential ones. As a result, the class conditional probabilities tend to be smoother in the mod(cid:173) ified neighborhoods, whereby better classification performance can be achieved. The efficacy of our method is validated and compared against other techniques using a variety of real world data.

paragraphs: Nearest-neighbor classification relies on nearby examples having roughly stable class probabilities. With many input dimensions and only finitely many examples, that assumption can fail: points treated as neighbors may span regions where the class probabilities change substantially. The paper identifies the resulting bias as a reason to reconsider how neighborhoods are defined.

The proposed method adapts the distance measure locally using a chi-squared distance analysis. It stretches neighborhoods along feature dimensions that matter less for classification and narrows them along dimensions that matter more. This gives different directions different influence over which examples count as nearby, tailoring neighborhood shape to the local classification problem.

Within these reshaped neighborhoods, class probabilities tend to vary more smoothly, which can improve classification. The authors evaluate the method against other techniques on several real-world datasets and report evidence of its efficacy. The central claim is qualified: adapting distance is intended to reduce bias and can improve performance, rather than guaranteeing that every high-dimensional nearest-neighbor problem becomes easy.
summary.tldr: A locally adaptive distance measure reshapes nearest-neighbor neighborhoods to reduce bias and potentially improve classification.

title: An Adaptive Metric Machine for Pattern Classification

abstract: We describe an analogy between psychophysically measured effects in contrast masking, and the behavior of a simple integrate-and(cid:173) fire neuron that receives time-modulated inhibition. In the psy(cid:173) chophysical experiments, we tested observers ability to discriminate contrasts of peripheral Gabor patches in the presence of collinear Gabor flankers. The data reveal a complex interaction pattern that we account for by assuming that flankers provide divisive inhibi(cid:173) tion to the target unit for low target contrasts, but provide sub(cid:173) tractive inhibition to the target unit for higher target contrasts. A similar switch from divisive to subtractive inhibition is observed in an integrate-and-fire unit that receives inhibition modulated in time such that the cell spends part of the time in a high-inhibition state and part of the time in a low-inhibition state. The simi(cid:173) larity between the effects suggests that one may cause the other. The biophysical model makes testable predictions for physiological single-cell recordings.

A similar switch from divisive to subtractive inhibition is observed in an integrate-and-fire unit that receives inhibition modulated in time such that the cell spends part of the time in a high-inhibition state and part of the time in a low-inhibition state. paragraphs: The paper connects a pattern in human contrast perception with the behavior of a simple spiking neuron. Observers judged differences in the contrast of peripheral Gabor patches while other, collinear Gabor patches appeared nearby. These flankers produced an interaction that changed with the target's contrast.

To explain the behavioral measurements, the authors assume that flankers divide down the target unit's response at low target contrasts but subtract from it at higher contrasts. These descriptions capture different ways inhibition can alter a response: changing its scale or reducing it by an offset.

A similar transition appears in an integrate-and-fire model when inhibition varies over time, alternating between relatively high and low states. The correspondence matters because one temporal inhibition mechanism can produce both response patterns. The authors suggest that this neuronal behavior may cause the perceptual effect, while keeping that causal link tentative. The model also produces predictions that could be tested through recordings from individual neurons.
summary.tldr: Time-varying inhibition in a spiking neuron reproduces a contrast-dependent switch resembling measured visual masking effects.

title: Divisive and Subtractive Mask Effects: Linking Psychophysics and Biophysics

abstract: We develop an intuitive geometric framework for support vector regression (SVR). By examining when (cid:15)-tubes exist, we show that SVR can be regarded as a classi(cid:12)cation problem in the dual space. Hard and soft (cid:15)-tubes are constructed by separating the convex or reduced convex hulls respectively of the training data with the response variable shifted up and down by (cid:15). A novel SVR model is proposed based on choosing the max-margin plane between the two shifted datasets. Maximizing the margin corresponds to shrinking the e(cid:11)ective (cid:15)-tube. In the proposed approach the e(cid:11)ects of the choices of all parameters become clear geometrically.

paragraphs: Support vector regression uses an epsilon-tube to express a band of tolerated prediction error. This paper develops a geometric account of when such tubes exist. The authors show that the regression problem can be understood as a classification problem in a dual space, connecting the construction of a regression band to the separation of geometric sets.

The construction shifts the training responses upward and downward by epsilon, producing two versions of the data. Hard tubes correspond to separating their convex hulls, while soft tubes use reduced convex hulls. This gives a geometric interpretation to both forms of the regression problem and makes the role of the shifted responses explicit.

The authors then propose a new SVR model that chooses the maximum-margin plane between the shifted datasets. Increasing this margin corresponds to reducing the effective tube width. The stated benefit is interpretability: the effects of parameter choices become visible through the geometry, providing a unified way to understand the proposed model's behavior.
summary.tldr: A geometric reformulation connects support vector regression to dual-space classification and motivates a maximum-margin regression model.

title: Duality, Geometry, and Support Vector Regression

abstract: We propose the following general method for scaling learning algorithms to arbitrarily large data sets. Consider the model Mii learned by the algorithm using ni examples in step i (ii = (nl , ... ,nm )) , and the model Moo that would be learned using infinite examples. Upper-bound the loss L(Mii' M oo ) between them as a function of ii, and then minimize the algorithm's time complexity f(ii) subject to the constraint that L(Moo , M ii ) be at most f with probability at most 8. We apply this method to the EM algorithm for mixtures of Gaussians. Preliminary experiments on a series of large data sets provide evidence of the potential of this approach.

Consider the model Mii learned by the algorithm using ni examples in step i (ii = (nl , ... ,nm )) , and the model Moo that would be learned using infinite examples. Upper-bound the loss L(Mii' M oo ) between them as a function of ii, and then minimize the algorithm's time complexity f(ii) subject to the constraint that L(Moo , M ii ) be at most f with probability at most 8. We apply this method to the EM algorithm for mixtures of Gaussians. Preliminary experiments on a series of large data sets provide evidence of the potential of this approach.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a general strategy for scaling learning algorithms to arbitrarily large datasets. Its reference point is the model an algorithm would learn from infinitely many examples. The practical question is how much data to use at each step while controlling the difference between a finite-data model and that idealized reference.

The strategy first upper-bounds that difference as a function of the numbers of examples used across learning steps. It then chooses those sample amounts by minimizing computational time subject to a probabilistic loss constraint. This makes data allocation part of the optimization problem: computational effort is chosen in relation to an explicit bound on model discrepancy.

The authors apply the framework to EM for Gaussian mixture models. Preliminary experiments on a series of large datasets provide evidence of its potential. The title thus refers to approximating an infinite-data learning outcome with finite computation, with the method's usefulness tied to obtaining a suitable loss bound and using it to guide the allocation of examples.
summary.tldr: The paper allocates training examples across learning steps to minimize runtime under a bound on discrepancy from an infinite-data model.

title: Learning from Infinite Data in Finite Time

abstract: The mutual information of two random variables z and J with joint probabilities {7rij} is commonly used in learning Bayesian nets as well as in many other fields. The chances 7rij are usually estimated by the empirical sampling frequency nij In leading to a point es(cid:173) timate J(nij In) for the mutual information. To answer questions like "is J (nij In) consistent with zero?" or "what is the probability that the true mutual information is much larger than the point es(cid:173) timate?" one has to go beyond the point estimate. In the Bayesian framework one can answer these questions by utilizing a (second order) prior distribution p( 7r) comprising prior information about 7r. From the prior p(7r) one can compute the posterior p(7rln), from which the distribution p(Iln) of the mutual information can be cal(cid:173) culated. We derive reliable and quickly computable approximations for p(Iln). We concentrate on the mean, variance, skewness, and kurtosis, and non-informative priors. For the mean we also give an exact expression. Numerical issues and the range of validity are discussed.

paragraphs: Mutual information measures statistical dependence between variables, but a value calculated from observed frequencies is only a point estimate. It does not by itself express uncertainty about the underlying dependence. This paper asks how to assess questions such as whether an estimate is compatible with zero or whether the true value could be substantially larger.

The authors use a Bayesian treatment of the unknown joint probabilities. A prior over those probabilities is updated using observed counts, producing a posterior. That posterior then induces a distribution over mutual information. The resulting object describes uncertainty about dependence itself, rather than reporting just the dependence measured in the sample.

The paper derives approximations described as reliable and quick to compute, focusing on the distribution's mean, variance, skewness, and kurtosis with non-informative priors. It also provides an exact expression for the mean and discusses numerical behavior and validity ranges. These results make uncertainty-aware use of mutual information more accessible, including in applications such as learning Bayesian networks.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian analysis provides efficient approximations to the uncertainty distribution of mutual information, including an exact expression for its mean.

title: Distribution of Mutual Information

abstract: We explore approximate policy iteration, replacing the usual cost- function learning step with a learning step in policy space. We give policy-language biases that enable solution of very large relational Markov decision processes (MDPs) that no previous technique can solve. In particular, we induce high-quality domain-speciﬁc planners for clas- sical planning domains (both deterministic and stochastic variants) by solving such domains as extremely large MDPs.
originalAbstract: We explore approximate policy iteration, replacing the usual cost- function learning step with a learning step in policy space. We give policy-language biases that enable solution of very large relational Markov decision processes (MDPs) that no previous technique can solve. paragraphs: The paper explores a change to approximate policy iteration, a method for improving decision-making policies. Instead of using the usual learning step for a cost function, it places the learning step directly in policy space. The object being learned is therefore the policy itself, bringing the representation of decision rules to the center of the approach.

The authors introduce policy-language biases: choices about the form in which policies can be expressed. These choices guide learning toward policies suited to very large relational Markov decision processes. The reported contribution is that suitable policy languages make it possible to solve problems beyond the reach of previous techniques considered in the work.

The application is learning high-quality planners tailored to particular classical planning domains. The authors treat these domains as extremely large MDPs and handle both deterministic and stochastic variants. The result connects policy representation to planning scalability: directing learning through an appropriate policy language can make these large decision problems manageable and produce useful domain-specific planners.
summary.tldr: Learning directly in suitably restricted policy languages enables high-quality planners for extremely large relational MDPs.

title: Approximate Policy Iteration with a Policy Language Bias

abstract: Discriminative learning methods for classification perform well when training and test data are drawn from the same distribution. In many situations, though, we have labeled training data for a source domain, and we wish to learn a classifier which performs well on a target domain with a different distribution. Under what conditions can we adapt a classifier trained on the source domain for use in the target domain? Intuitively, a good feature representation is a crucial factor in the success of domain adaptation. We formalize this intuition theoretically with a generalization bound for domain adaption. Our theory illustrates the tradeoffs inherent in designing a representation for domain adaptation and gives a new justification for a recently proposed model. It also points toward a promising new model for domain adaptation: one which explicitly minimizes the difference between the source and target domains, while at the same time maximizing the margin of the training set.

paragraphs: A classifier trained on one distribution may need to operate on another. Domain adaptation studies this situation: labeled examples come from a source domain, while useful predictions are needed in a different target domain. The paper asks what makes such transfer possible and focuses on the representation used to describe the data.

The authors formalize the importance of representation through a generalization bound for domain adaptation. The theory exposes tradeoffs in choosing features for transfer, giving a mathematical basis for evaluating a representation beyond its usefulness on source examples alone. It also supplies a new justification for a previously proposed adaptation model.

The analysis points toward another model that simultaneously reduces the difference between source and target domains and increases the training margin. In plain terms, it seeks a representation in which the domains become more alike while the labeled training classes remain well separated. The abstract presents this as a promising direction motivated by the theory, rather than as a reported empirical victory for the proposed model.
summary.tldr: A generalization bound explains representation tradeoffs in transferring classifiers between different data distributions.

title: Analysis of Representations for Domain Adaptation

abstract: We propose a Gaussian process (GP) framework for robust inference in which a GP prior on the mixing weights of a two-component noise model augments the standard process over latent function values. This approach is a generalization of the mixture likelihood used in traditional robust GP regression, and a specialization of the GP mixture models suggested by Tresp (2000) and Rasmussen and Ghahramani (2002). The value of this restriction is in its tractable expectation propagation updates, which allow for faster inference and model selection, and better convergence than the standard mixture. An additional benefit over the latter method lies in our ability to incorporate knowledge of the noise domain to influence predictions, and to recover with the predictive distribution information about the outlier distribution via the gating process. The model has asymptotic complexity equal to that of conventional robust methods, but yields more confident predictions on benchmark problems than classical heavy-tailed models and exhibits improved stability for data with clustered corruptions, for which they fail altogether. We show further how our approach can be used without adjustment for more smoothly heteroscedastic data, and suggest how it could be extended to more general noise models. We also address similarities with the work of Goldberg et al. (1998), and the more recent contributions of Tresp, and Rasmussen and Ghahramani.

paragraphs: Robust regression must distinguish the underlying function from unusual or corrupted observations. This paper uses two Gaussian processes: one models the latent function, and the other controls the mixing weights of a two-component noise model. The second process allows the balance between noise components to vary across the input domain.

This restricted mixture construction gives tractable expectation-propagation updates. The authors report faster inference and model selection, with better convergence than the standard mixture approach. The noise-gating process also lets prior knowledge about the noise domain influence predictions and supplies information about the outlier distribution alongside the predictive distribution.

The model has the same asymptotic computational complexity as conventional robust methods. On benchmarks, it produces more confident predictions than classical heavy-tailed models and improves stability with clustered corruptions, where those models fail in the reported comparison. It also handles smoothly varying noise levels without modification. These findings highlight the benefit of modeling where corruption occurs, while the suggested extensions to more general noise models remain proposals.
summary.tldr: A second Gaussian process models varying noise-mixture weights, improving robust regression stability when corruptions cluster.

title: Robust Regression with Twinned Gaussian Processes

abstract: Offline handwriting recognition---the transcription of images of handwritten text---is an interesting task, in that it combines computer vision with sequence learning. In most systems the two elements are handled separately, with sophisticated preprocessing techniques used to extract the image features and sequential models such as HMMs used to provide the transcriptions. By combining two recent innovations in neural networks---multidimensional recurrent neural networks and connectionist temporal classification---this paper introduces a globally trained offline handwriting recogniser that takes raw pixel data as input. Unlike competing systems, it does not require any alphabet specific preprocessing, and can therefore be used unchanged for any language. Evidence of its generality and power is provided by data from a recent international Arabic recognition competition, where it outperformed all entries (91.4% accuracy compared to 87.2% for the competition winner) despite the fact that neither author understands a word of Arabic.

paragraphs: Recognizing handwriting from an image combines two tasks: interpreting visual structure and producing a sequence of text. Many systems handle these separately, extracting image features through specialized preprocessing before passing them to a sequential model. This paper brings the two parts together in a recognizer trained as a whole.

The system combines multidimensional recurrent neural networks with connectionist temporal classification and accepts raw pixels as input. Its design avoids alphabet-specific preprocessing. That matters because the recognition pipeline need not be redesigned around the visual conventions of each alphabet, and the authors present this as enabling use across languages without changing the approach.

Evaluation on data from an international Arabic recognition competition gives 91.4% accuracy, compared with 87.2% for the competition winner. The system outperforms all competition entries on those data. This result provides concrete evidence for the approach's effectiveness and generality, showing that a unified neural recognition system can perform strongly without manually engineered preprocessing specific to the alphabet.
summary.tldr: A jointly trained neural handwriting recognizer processes raw pixels and exceeds the reported Arabic competition results.

title: Offline Handwriting Recognition with Multidimensional Recurrent Neural Networks

abstract: We present a nonparametric hierarchical Bayesian model of document collections that decouples sparsity and smoothness in the component distributions (i.e., the ``topics). In the sparse topic model (STM), each topic is represented by a bank of selector variables that determine which terms appear in the topic. Thus each topic is associated with a subset of the vocabulary, and topic smoothness is modeled on this subset. We develop an efficient Gibbs sampler for the STM that includes a general-purpose method for sampling from a Dirichlet mixture with a combinatorial number of components. We demonstrate the STM on four real-world datasets. Compared to traditional approaches, the empirical results show that STMs give better predictive performance with simpler inferred models.

In the sparse topic model (STM), each topic is represented by a bank of selector variables that determine which terms appear in the topic. Thus each topic is associated with a subset of the vocabulary, and topic smoothness is modeled on this subset. We develop an efficient Gibbs sampler for the STM that includes a general-purpose method for sampling from a Dirichlet mixture with a combinatorial number of components. We demonstrate the STM on four real-world datasets. Compared to traditional approaches, the empirical results show that STMs give better predictive performance with simpler inferred models.

paragraphs: A topic model describes documents through distributions over vocabulary terms. This paper separates two aspects of those distributions: which terms belong to a topic, and how probability is distributed among the included terms. The proposed sparse topic model places that separation inside a nonparametric hierarchical Bayesian model of document collections.

Each topic has selector variables that identify its subset of the vocabulary. Smoothness is then modeled within that selected subset. This makes vocabulary membership an explicit part of the representation, allowing the model to distinguish topic sparsity from the distribution of probability across the words that remain.

The authors develop an efficient Gibbs sampler, including a general-purpose technique for sampling a Dirichlet mixture with a combinatorial number of components. They evaluate the model on four real-world datasets. Compared with traditional approaches, the reported results combine better predictive performance with simpler inferred models. The findings support explicitly modeling which words a topic can contain as a useful part of learning document representations.
summary.tldr: A sparse topic model separates vocabulary selection from probability smoothing and achieves better prediction with simpler models on four datasets.

title: Decoupling Sparsity and Smoothness in the Discrete Hierarchical Dirichlet Process

abstract: We formulate and address the problem of discovering dynamic malicious regions on the Internet. We model this problem as one of adaptively pruning a known decision tree, but with additional challenges: (1) severe space requirements, since the underlying decision tree has over 4 billion leaves, and (2) a changing target function, since malicious activity on the Internet is dynamic. We present a novel algorithm that addresses this problem, by putting together a number of different ``experts algorithms and online paging algorithms. We prove guarantees on our algorithms performance as a function of the best possible pruning of a similar size, and our experiments show that our algorithm achieves high accuracy on large real-world data sets, with significant improvements over existing approaches.
originalAbstract: We formulate and address the problem of discovering dynamic malicious regions on the Internet. We model this problem as one of adaptively pruning a known decision tree, but with additional challenges: (1) severe space requirements, since the underlying decision tree has over 4 billion leaves, and (2) a changing target function, since malicious activity on the Internet is dynamic. We present a novel algorithm that addresses this problem, by putting together a number of different ``experts algorithms and online paging algorithms. We prove guarantees on our algorithms performance as a function of the best possible pruning of a similar size, and our experiments show that our algorithm achieves high accuracy on large real-world data sets, with significant improvements over existing approaches.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to discover regions of the Internet associated with malicious activity as those regions change over time. The authors formulate the task as adaptive pruning of a known decision tree. Choosing a pruning means selecting a representation at an appropriate level of detail, rather than retaining the full tree.

Two difficulties shape the algorithm: the underlying tree has more than four billion leaves, and the target being tracked changes. The proposed method combines several experts algorithms with online paging algorithms. This combination addresses adaptation and space requirements together, which is essential when a full representation is too large and a fixed summary would become outdated.

The authors prove performance guarantees relative to the best possible pruning of a similar size. That comparison evaluates the method against a representation with a comparable space scale. Experiments on large real-world datasets report high accuracy and significant improvements over existing approaches. The work therefore combines a dynamic detection formulation, a space-conscious online algorithm, and both theoretical and empirical support.
summary.tldr: An adaptive tree-pruning algorithm tracks changing malicious Internet regions with guarantees relative to similarly sized prunings and strong reported accuracy.

title: Tracking Dynamic Sources of Malicious Activity at Internet Scale

abstract: A method for computing the rarity of latent fingerprints represented by minutiae is given. It allows determining the probability of finding a match for an evidence print in a database of n known prints. The probability of random correspondence between evidence and database is determined in three procedural steps. In the registration step the latent print is aligned by finding its core point; which is done using a procedure based on a machine learning approach based on Gaussian processes. In the evidence probability evaluation step a generative model based on Bayesian networks is used to determine the probability of the evidence; it takes into account both the dependency of each minutia on nearby minutiae and the confidence of their presence in the evidence. In the specific probability of random correspondence step the evidence probability is used to determine the probability of match among n for a given tolerance; the last evaluation is similar to the birthday correspondence probability for a specific birthday. The generative model is validated using a goodness-of-fit test evaluated with a standard database of fingerprints. The probability of random correspondence for several latent fingerprints are evaluated for varying numbers of minutiae.

paragraphs: The paper develops a method for estimating the rarity of a latent fingerprint represented by minutiae, the local features used to describe a print. Its target is the probability of a random match between an evidence print and a database containing a specified number of known prints. Database size and the permitted matching tolerance enter this assessment.

The procedure has three stages. First, it aligns the latent print by locating its core point with a Gaussian-process-based learning method. Second, a Bayesian-network generative model evaluates the probability of the evidence. That model accounts for dependencies between nearby minutiae and confidence that each feature is actually present. Third, the evidence probability is converted into a random-correspondence probability for the database and tolerance under consideration.

The authors validate the generative model through a goodness-of-fit test on a standard fingerprint database. They also evaluate random-correspondence probabilities for several latent prints while varying the number of minutiae. The method thus connects local feature uncertainty and dependence with a database-level assessment of how unusual a match would be.
summary.tldr: A three-stage probabilistic method estimates random fingerprint correspondence while accounting for feature dependence, feature confidence, database size, and matching tolerance.

title: Evaluation of Rarity of Fingerprints in Forensics

abstract: For a density f on R^d, a high-density cluster is any connected component of {x: f(x) >= c}, for some c > 0. The set of all high-density clusters form a hierarchy called the cluster tree of f. We present a procedure for estimating the cluster tree given samples from f. We give finite-sample convergence rates for our algorithm, as well as lower bounds on the sample complexity of this estimation problem.
originalAbstract: For a density f on R^d, a high-density cluster is any connected component of {x: f(x) >= c}, for some c > 0. The set of all high-density clusters form a hierarchy called the cluster tree of f. We present a procedure for estimating the cluster tree given samples from f. We give finite-sample convergence rates for our algorithm, as well as lower bounds on the sample complexity of this estimation problem.

paragraphs: A density can define clusters at many different thresholds. At a chosen threshold, a high-density cluster is a connected region where the density stays at or above that level. Considering all such regions across thresholds produces a hierarchy called the cluster tree. The paper studies how to estimate this entire hierarchy from sampled observations.

The authors present an estimation procedure and give finite-sample convergence rates for it. These rates describe how the estimator approaches the target as the amount of observed data increases. Addressing finite samples makes the analysis relevant to the amount of information available in a dataset, beyond simply describing what happens with indefinitely many observations.

The paper also gives lower bounds on the sample complexity of estimating the cluster tree. These characterize data requirements inherent in the estimation problem. Together, the algorithmic convergence results and lower bounds provide two complementary perspectives: how well the proposed procedure learns the hierarchy, and how demanding that learning problem is in terms of samples.
summary.tldr: The paper introduces a cluster-tree estimator with finite-sample convergence rates and lower bounds on the data needed for estimation.

title: Rates of convergence for the cluster tree

abstract: We consider a class of sparsity-inducing regularization terms based on submodular functions. While previous work has focused on non-decreasing functions, we explore symmetric submodular functions and their \lova extensions. We show that the Lovasz extension may be seen as the convex envelope of a function that depends on level sets (i.e., the set of indices whose corresponding components of the underlying predictor are greater than a given constant): this leads to a class of convex structured regularization terms that impose prior knowledge on the level sets, and not only on the supports of the underlying predictors. We provide a unified set of optimization algorithms, such as proximal operators, and theoretical guarantees (allowed level sets and recovery conditions). By selecting specific submodular functions, we give a new interpretation to known norms, such as the total variation; we also define new norms, in particular ones that are based on order statistics with application to clustering and outlier detection, and on noisy cuts in graphs with application to change point detection in the presence of outliers.

We show that the Lovasz extension may be seen as the convex envelope of a function that depends on level sets (i.e., the set of indices whose corresponding components of the underlying predictor are greater than a given constant): this leads to a class of convex structured regularization terms that impose prior knowledge on the level sets, and not only on the supports of the underlying predictors. We provide a unified set of optimization algorithms, such as proximal operators, and theoretical guarantees (allowed level sets and recovery conditions). paragraphs: Sparse regularization often expresses preferences about which predictor components are nonzero. This paper develops penalties that can also express preferences about level sets: collections of components whose values exceed a chosen threshold. That expands the structure a regularizer can encode beyond simply selecting a support.

The authors study symmetric submodular functions and their Lovasz extensions. They show that the extension can be understood as the convex envelope of a function depending on level sets. This establishes a route from structural preferences about those sets to convex regularization terms. They also provide optimization methods, including proximal operators, and guarantees concerning permitted level sets and recovery conditions.

Specific choices of submodular function yield a new interpretation of existing norms such as total variation, as well as new norms. Examples use order statistics for clustering and outlier detection, and noisy graph cuts for change-point detection with outliers. The contribution is a unified way to design and optimize penalties around the structure of predictor values.
summary.tldr: Symmetric submodular functions generate convex regularizers that encode structure in predictor level sets, with algorithms and recovery guarantees.

title: Shaping Level Sets with Submodular Functions

abstract: We derive sublinear regret bounds for undiscounted reinforcement learning in continuous state space. The proposed algorithm combines state aggregation with the use of upper confidence bounds for implementing optimism in the face of uncertainty. Beside the existence of an optimal policy which satisfies the Poisson equation, the only assumptions made are Hoelder continuity of rewards and transition probabilities.
originalAbstract: We derive sublinear regret bounds for undiscounted reinforcement learning in continuous state space. The proposed algorithm combines state aggregation with the use of upper confidence bounds for implementing optimism in the face of uncertainty. Beside the existence of an optimal policy which satisfies the Poisson equation, the only assumptions made are Hoelder continuity of rewards and transition probabilities.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes reinforcement learning when states vary continuously and future rewards are not discounted. Its central question is how much reward a learner loses while it is still learning to act well. The authors establish sublinear regret bounds, meaning that the cumulative performance shortfall grows more slowly than the learning horizon.

The algorithm combines state aggregation with upper confidence bounds. Aggregation groups states so that the learner can work with a simplified representation of a continuous space. Upper confidence bounds implement optimism about uncertain outcomes, giving the learner a reason to investigate possibilities whose rewards may be better than current observations suggest.

The guarantees rely on an optimal policy satisfying the Poisson equation and on Hölder continuity of rewards and transition probabilities. The continuity assumptions constrain how sharply the environment can change between nearby states, supporting aggregation. Under the stated assumptions, sublinear regret implies that the average shortfall per step decreases as learning continues, giving a theoretical justification for the combined strategy.
summary.tldr: State aggregation and optimistic exploration yield sublinear regret for continuous-state, undiscounted reinforcement learning under the stated regularity assumptions.

title: Online Regret Bounds for Undiscounted Continuous Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Stochastic variational inference (SVI) lets us scale up Bayesian computation to massive data. It uses stochastic optimization to fit a variational distribution, following easy-to-compute noisy natural gradients. As with most traditional stochastic optimization methods, SVI takes precautions to use unbiased stochastic gradients whose expectations are equal to the true gradients. In this paper, we explore the idea of following biased stochastic gradients in SVI. Our method replaces the natural gradient with a similarly constructed vector that uses a fixed-window moving average of some of its previous terms. We will demonstrate the many advantages of this technique. First, its computational cost is the same as for SVI and storage requirements only multiply by a constant factor. Second, it enjoys significant variance reduction over the unbiased estimates, smaller bias than averaged gradients, and leads to smaller mean-squared error against the full gradient. We test our method on latent Dirichlet allocation with three large corpora.

It uses stochastic optimization to fit a variational distribution, following easy-to-compute noisy natural gradients. As with most traditional stochastic optimization methods, SVI takes precautions to use unbiased stochastic gradients whose expectations are equal to the true gradients. In this paper, we explore the idea of following biased stochastic gradients in SVI. Our method replaces the natural gradient with a similarly constructed vector that uses a fixed-window moving average of some of its previous terms. We will demonstrate the many advantages of this technique. First, its computational cost is the same as for SVI and storage requirements only multiply by a constant factor. Second, it enjoys significant variance reduction over the unbiased estimates, smaller bias than averaged gradients, and leads to smaller mean-squared error against the full gradient. We test our method on latent Dirichlet allocation with three large corpora.

paragraphs: Stochastic variational inference makes Bayesian computation scalable by fitting an approximate distribution with inexpensive, noisy natural gradients. Standard practice favors unbiased estimates, whose averages equal the full gradient. This paper investigates whether deliberately accepting some bias can yield a more useful direction for optimization by reducing the noise.

The method replaces the natural gradient with a similarly constructed vector that includes a fixed-window moving average of some previous terms. It smooths selected ingredients of the update rather than simply averaging complete gradients. According to the authors, the computation costs the same as ordinary stochastic variational inference, while storage increases only by a constant factor.

The proposed estimates have substantially lower variance than unbiased estimates and less bias than averaged gradients. Together, these properties produce a smaller mean-squared error relative to the full gradient. The authors test the method using latent Dirichlet allocation on three large corpora. The contribution shows how a controlled bias-variance tradeoff can improve gradient estimation without increasing its stated computational cost.
summary.tldr: Smoothing selected gradient terms introduces bias but reduces variance and mean-squared error in stochastic variational inference at the same computational cost.

title: Smoothed Gradients for Stochastic Variational Inference

abstract: Nystr\"{o}m method has been used successfully to improve the computational efficiency of kernel ridge regression (KRR). Recently, theoretical analysis of Nystr\"{o}m KRR, including generalization bound and convergence rate, has been established based on reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) associated with the symmetric positive semi-definite kernel. However, in real world applications, RKHS is not always optimal and kernel function is not necessary to be symmetric or positive semi-definite. In this paper, we consider the generalized Nystr\"{o}m kernel regression (GNKR) with $\ell_2$ coefficient regularization, where the kernel just requires the continuity and boundedness. Error analysis is provided to characterize its generalization performance and the column norm sampling is introduced to construct the refined hypothesis space. In particular, the fast learning rate with polynomial decay is reached for the GNKR. Experimental analysis demonstrates the satisfactory performance of GNKR with the column norm sampling.
originalAbstract: Nystr\"{o}m method has been used successfully to improve the computational efficiency of kernel ridge regression (KRR). Recently, theoretical analysis of Nystr\"{o}m KRR, including generalization bound and convergence rate, has been established based on reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) associated with the symmetric positive semi-definite kernel. However, in real world applications, RKHS is not always optimal and kernel function is not necessary to be symmetric or positive semi-definite. In this paper, we consider the generalized Nystr\"{o}m kernel regression (GNKR) with $\ell_2$ coefficient regularization, where the kernel just requires the continuity and boundedness. Error analysis is provided to characterize its generalization performance and the column norm sampling is introduced to construct the refined hypothesis space. In particular, the fast learning rate with polynomial decay is reached for the GNKR. Experimental analysis demonstrates the satisfactory performance of GNKR with the column norm sampling.

paragraphs: Nyström approximation makes kernel regression more computationally manageable, but its theoretical analysis has commonly relied on symmetric positive semidefinite kernels and their associated reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces. This paper studies a broader regression formulation intended to accommodate kernels outside that conventional setting. The kernel itself is required to be continuous and bounded.

The proposed generalized Nyström kernel regression uses an l2 penalty on its coefficients. The authors provide an error analysis to characterize generalization and introduce column norm sampling to construct a refined hypothesis space. In this approach, choosing the approximation space and controlling the regression coefficients are both parts of the learning procedure.

The analysis establishes a fast learning rate with polynomial decay for the generalized method. Experiments also report satisfactory performance when it is combined with column norm sampling. The main significance is extending both the formulation and its theoretical treatment beyond the usual symmetry and positive-semidefiniteness requirements. The empirical claim is favorable performance, rather than a stated universal advantage over conventional kernel regression.
summary.tldr: Generalized Nyström regression receives error guarantees for continuous, bounded kernels without requiring symmetry or positive semidefiniteness.

title: Error Analysis of Generalized Nyström Kernel Regression

abstract: Nowozin \textit{et al} showed last year how to extend the GAN \textit{principle} to all $f$-divergences. The approach is elegant but falls short of a full description of the supervised game, and says little about the key player, the generator: for example, what does the generator actually converge to if solving the GAN game means convergence in some space of parameters? How does that provide hints on the generator's design and compare to the flourishing but almost exclusively experimental literature on the subject? In this paper, we unveil a broad class of distributions for which such convergence happens --- namely, deformed exponential families, a wide superset of exponential families ---. We show that current deep architectures are able to factorize a very large number of such densities using an especially compact design, hence displaying the power of deep architectures and their concinnity in the $f$-GAN game. This result holds given a sufficient condition on \textit{activation functions} --- which turns out to be satisfied by popular choices. The key to our results is a variational generalization of an old theorem that relates the KL divergence between regular exponential families and divergences between their natural parameters. We complete this picture with additional results and experimental insights on how these results may be used to ground further improvements of GAN architectures, via (i) a principled design of the activation functions in the generator and (ii) an explicit integration of proper composite losses' link function in the discriminator.

paragraphs: The f-GAN framework extends adversarial learning to a family of distribution-comparison objectives called f-divergences. This paper asks what convergence in the generator's parameters means for the distribution it represents, and how that relationship can guide architecture design. It approaches those questions through information geometry.

The authors identify deformed exponential families, a broad extension of exponential families, as a class supporting the convergence relationship they study. They also show that deep architectures can compactly factorize a very large number of these densities. Further results and experiments suggest two directions for architecture improvement: principled generator activations and explicit incorporation of a proper composite loss's link function into the discriminator. These contributions supply theoretical guidance for design choices otherwise explored largely through experiments.
summary.tldr: An information-geometric analysis connects f-GAN convergence and compact density representation to distribution families and activation-function conditions.

title: f-GANs in an Information Geometric Nutshell

abstract: Tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS) is a high-throughput technology used to identify the proteins in a complex biological sample, such as a drop of blood. A collection of spectra is generated at the output of the process, each spectrum of which is representative of a peptide (protein subsequence) present in the original complex sample. In this work, we leverage the log-likelihood gradients of generative models to improve the identification of such spectra. In particular, we show that the gradient of a recently proposed dynamic Bayesian network (DBN) may be naturally employed by a kernel-based discriminative classifier. The resulting Fisher kernel substantially improves upon recent attempts to combine generative and discriminative models for post-processing analysis, outperforming all other methods on the evaluated datasets. We extend the improved accuracy offered by the Fisher kernel framework to other search algorithms by introducing Theseus, a DBN representating a large number of widely used MS/MS scoring functions. Furthermore, with gradient ascent and max-product inference at hand, we use Theseus to learn model parameters without any supervision.

paragraphs: Tandem mass spectrometry helps identify proteins in complex biological samples by producing spectra associated with peptides, which are protein subsequences. The paper improves spectrum identification by combining generative modeling with discriminative classification. Its key idea is to use how a generative model's log-likelihood changes with its parameters as information for a classifier.

The authors show that gradients from a dynamic Bayesian network can be incorporated naturally into a kernel-based discriminative classifier. This produces a Fisher kernel, connecting the generative model's description of spectra to the classification task. On the evaluated datasets, the resulting method outperforms all other compared methods and substantially improves on recent approaches combining generative and discriminative models.

Using gradient ascent together with max-product inference, Theseus can learn model parameters without supervision. The work thus uses a common generative representation to support both improved classification and unsupervised parameter learning.
summary.tldr: Gradients from generative models improve peptide-spectrum classification, while the Theseus model extends the approach to common scoring functions.

title: Gradients of Generative Models for Improved Discriminative Analysis of Tandem Mass Spectra

abstract: Recent advances in recording technologies have allowed neuroscientists to record simultaneous spiking activity from hundreds to thousands of neurons in multiple brain regions. Such large-scale recordings pose a major challenge to existing statistical methods for neural data analysis. Here we develop highly scalable approximate inference methods for Poisson generalized linear models (GLMs) that require only a single pass over the data. Our approach relies on a recently proposed method for obtaining approximate sufficient statistics for GLMs using polynomial approximations [Huggins et al., 2017], which we adapt to the Poisson GLM setting. We focus on inference using quadratic approximations to nonlinear terms in the Poisson GLM log-likelihood with Gaussian priors, for which we derive closed-form solutions to the approximate maximum likelihood and MAP estimates, posterior distribution, and marginal likelihood. We introduce an adaptive procedure to select the polynomial approximation interval and show that the resulting method allows for efficient and accurate inference and regularization of high-dimensional parameters. We use the quadratic estimator to fit a fully-coupled Poisson GLM to spike train data recorded from 831 neurons across five regions of the mouse brain for a duration of 41 minutes, binned at 1 ms resolution. Across all neurons, this model is fit to over 2 billion spike count bins and identifies fine-timescale statistical dependencies between neurons within and across cortical and subcortical areas.
