summary.tldr: Quadratic approximations enable single-pass Poisson GLM inference at the scale of billions of neural spike-count bins.

title: Scaling the Poisson GLM to massive neural datasets through polynomial approximations

abstract: We consider the optimization of cost functionals on manifolds and derive a variational approach to accelerated methods on manifolds. We demonstrate the methodology on the infinite-dimensional manifold of diffeomorphisms, motivated by registration problems in computer vision. We build on the variational approach to accelerated optimization by Wibisono, Wilson and Jordan, which applies in finite dimensions, and generalize that approach to infinite dimensional manifolds. We derive the continuum evolution equations, which are partial differential equations (PDE), and relate them to simple mechanical principles. Our approach can also be viewed as a generalization of the $L^2$ optimal mass transport problem. Our approach evolves an infinite number of particles endowed with mass, represented as a mass density. The density evolves with the optimization variable, and endows the particles with dynamics. This is different than current accelerated methods where only a single particle moves and hence the dynamics does not depend on the mass. We derive the theory, compute the PDEs for acceleration, and illustrate the behavior of this new accelerated optimization scheme.

paragraphs: Optimization on a manifold concerns variables whose possible values have geometric structure. This paper develops a variational approach to accelerated optimization in that setting, extending an existing finite-dimensional formulation to infinite-dimensional manifolds. Its motivating example is the space of diffeomorphisms, used in computer-vision registration problems.

The authors derive partial differential equations describing the continuous evolution of the optimization process and relate them to mechanical principles. Their formulation evolves infinitely many particles represented by a mass density. That density changes alongside the optimization variable and contributes to the particles' dynamics, making the evolving distribution of mass part of the acceleration mechanism.

The approach can also be interpreted as a generalization of the L² optimal mass transport problem. The paper develops the theory, computes the acceleration equations, and illustrates the behavior of the resulting scheme. Its contribution is a formulation of accelerated dynamics for an infinite-dimensional geometric setting. The stated results concern the derivation and illustrated behavior of those dynamics, rather than a quantified performance advantage on registration benchmarks.
summary.tldr: A variational framework derives accelerated optimization PDEs on infinite-dimensional manifolds using evolving mass-density dynamics.

title: Variational PDEs for Acceleration on Manifolds and Application to Diffeomorphisms

abstract: A recent trend of fair machine learning is to define fairness as causality-based notions which concern the causal connection between protected attributes and decisions. However, one common challenge of all causality-based fairness notions is identifiability, i.e., whether they can be uniquely measured from observational data, which is a critical barrier to applying these notions to real-world situations. In this paper, we develop a framework for measuring different causality-based fairness. We propose a unified definition that covers most of previous causality-based fairness notions, namely the path-specific counterfactual fairness (PC fairness). Based on that, we propose a general method in the form of a constrained optimization problem for bounding the path-specific counterfactual fairness under all unidentifiable situations. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show the correctness and effectiveness of our method.

paragraphs: Causal definitions of fairness examine how protected attributes influence decisions. A central difficulty is identifiability: observational data may not uniquely determine the fairness quantity being requested. This creates a practical obstacle because a precise causal definition alone does not ensure that its value can be measured from the available observations.

The paper proposes path-specific counterfactual fairness, or PC fairness, as a unified definition covering most previous causality-based fairness notions. The framework organizes fairness questions around counterfactual effects along particular causal paths. This provides a common basis for analyzing different notions and for addressing their shared measurement problem.

When the fairness quantity cannot be uniquely identified, the authors formulate constrained optimization problems that bound it instead. They present the method as covering all unidentifiable situations within the framework. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets support its correctness and effectiveness. The contribution is therefore a way to quantify a range of possible fairness values when the data do not support one unique answer, rather than claiming to remove the underlying ambiguity.
summary.tldr: PC fairness unifies most causal fairness notions and uses constrained optimization to bound values that observational data cannot uniquely identify.

title: PC-Fairness: A Unified Framework for Measuring Causality-based Fairness

abstract: We introduce a new algorithm for multi-objective reinforcement learning (MORL) with linear preferences, with the goal of enabling few-shot adaptation to new tasks. In MORL, the aim is to learn policies over multiple competing objectives whose relative importance (preferences) is unknown to the agent. While this alleviates dependence on scalar reward design, the expected return of a policy can change significantly with varying preferences, making it challenging to learn a single model to produce optimal policies under different preference conditions. We propose a generalized version of the Bellman equation to learn a single parametric representation for optimal policies over the space of all possible preferences. After an initial learning phase, our agent can execute the optimal policy under any given preference, or automatically infer an underlying preference with very few samples. Experiments across four different domains demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning agent may need to pursue several competing objectives, with their relative importance changing between tasks. A policy that works well for one set of priorities can perform poorly under another. This paper studies how to learn a single model that supports different priorities and can adapt when those priorities are initially unknown.

The approach assumes linear preferences: the objectives are combined according to preference weights. The authors generalize the Bellman equation, which relates decisions to their future returns, so that one parametric representation can describe optimal policies across the preference space. This makes preferences part of the learning problem instead of fixing one reward combination in advance.

After initial training, the agent can execute the optimal policy for a supplied preference or infer an underlying preference from very few samples. Experiments in four domains demonstrate the approach's effectiveness. The contribution connects learning across multiple objectives with rapid adaptation, within the stated setting of linear preferences.
summary.tldr: A generalized Bellman equation lets one model learn policies across linear objective preferences and adapt from very few samples.

title: A Generalized Algorithm for Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning and Policy Adaptation

abstract: Learning to solve complex goal-oriented tasks with sparse terminal-only rewards often requires an enormous number of samples. In such cases, using a set of expert trajectories could help to learn faster. However, Imitation Learning (IL) via supervised pre-training with these trajectories may not perform as well and generally requires additional finetuning with expert-in-the-loop. In this paper, we propose an approach which uses the expert trajectories and learns to decompose the complex main task into smaller sub-goals. We learn a function which partitions the state-space into sub-goals, which can then be used to design an extrinsic reward function. We follow a strategy where the agent first learns from the trajectories using IL and then switches to Reinforcement Learning (RL) using the identified sub-goals, to alleviate the errors in the IL step. To deal with states which are under-represented by the trajectory set, we also learn a function to modulate the sub-goal predictions. We show that our method is able to solve complex goal-oriented tasks, which other RL, IL or their combinations in literature are not able to solve.

paragraphs: Tasks that provide a reward only at completion can demand many learning attempts because the agent receives little guidance along the way. Expert demonstrations can help, but supervised imitation may still leave errors that require further correction. This paper uses expert trajectories both to initialize behavior and to discover intermediate goals.

The method learns a function that partitions the state space into subgoals. Those subgoals support an externally specified reward function for reinforcement learning. Training first follows an imitation learning stage, then switches to reinforcement learning with the discovered subgoals to alleviate imitation errors. A second learned function modulates subgoal predictions for states that are poorly represented in the demonstrations.

The authors report solving complex goal-oriented tasks that other reinforcement learning, imitation learning, and combined approaches in the literature could not solve. The stated finding supports using demonstrations as a source of task structure as well as behavior examples. The additional modulation addresses the specific difficulty of making subgoal predictions beyond well-covered demonstration states.
summary.tldr: The method discovers subgoals from expert trajectories and uses them to guide reinforcement learning after an initial imitation stage.

title: Learning from Trajectories via Subgoal Discovery

abstract: Suppose certain data points are overly contaminated, then the existing principal component analysis (PCA) methods are frequently incapable of filtering out and eliminating the excessively polluted ones, which potentially lead to the functional degeneration of the corresponding models. To tackle the issue, we propose a general framework namely robust weight learning with adaptive neighbors (RWL-AN), via which adaptive weight vector is automatically obtained with both robustness and sparse neighbors. More significantly, the degree of the sparsity is steerable such that only exact k well-fitting samples with least reconstruction errors are activated during the optimization, while the residual samples, i.e., the extreme noised ones are eliminated for the global robustness. Additionally, the framework is further applied to PCA problem to demonstrate the superiority and effectiveness of the proposed RWL-AN model.

paragraphs: Severely contaminated observations can interfere with principal component analysis when the method cannot effectively exclude them. This paper proposes a general weighting framework called robust weight learning with adaptive neighbors, or RWL-AN. Its purpose is to automatically decide which samples remain active in optimization while limiting the influence of observations that fit poorly.

The framework learns an adaptive weight vector with controllable sparsity. In particular, it can activate exactly k samples with the smallest reconstruction errors and eliminate the remaining samples from the active set. Reconstruction error therefore guides sample selection, while the chosen sparsity level controls how many observations contribute. This combines weight learning with an explicit restriction on participation.

The authors apply the framework to PCA and report results supporting its effectiveness and superiority. The approach matters because it makes exclusion of poorly reconstructed samples part of optimization itself. Its robustness mechanism depends on retaining the selected well-fitting observations and suppressing the rest, addressing the stated problem of extreme contamination through adaptive sample weighting.
summary.tldr: RWL-AN improves robustness by learning sparse weights that retain exactly k samples with the lowest reconstruction errors.

title: Robust Principal Component Analysis with Adaptive Neighbors

abstract: Learning discriminative global features plays a vital role in semantic segmentation. And most of the existing methods adopt stacks of local convolutions or non-local blocks to capture long-range context. However, due to the absence of spatial structure preservation, these operators ignore the object details when enlarging receptive fields. In this paper, we propose the learnable tree filter to form a generic tree filtering module that leverages the structural property of minimal spanning tree to model long-range dependencies while preserving the details. Furthermore, we propose a highly efficient linear-time algorithm to reduce resource consumption. Thus, the designed modules can be plugged into existing deep neural networks conveniently. To this end, tree filtering modules are embedded to formulate a unified framework for semantic segmentation. We conduct extensive ablation studies to elaborate on the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed method. Specifically, it attains better performance with much less overhead compared with the classic PSP block and Non-local operation under the same backbone. Our approach is proved to achieve consistent improvements on several benchmarks without bells-and-whistles. Code and models are available at https://github.com/StevenGrove/TreeFilter-Torch.

The paper argues that expanding context through stacked local convolutions or non-local blocks can overlook object details because these operations do not preserve spatial structure. Its goal is to connect distant features while retaining the structure useful for detailed segmentation.

The proposed learnable tree filter uses the structural properties of a minimal spanning tree to model long-range dependencies. The authors embed these modules in a unified semantic segmentation framework.

With the same backbone network, the tree-filter approach achieves better performance with much less overhead than the classic PSP block and non-local operation. The authors also report consistent gains across several benchmarks without additional embellishments. These results support the module as a practical way to improve contextual feature processing while preserving image structure.
summary.tldr: A linear-time learnable tree filter captures long-range image context while preserving detail and improving semantic segmentation.

title: Learnable Tree Filter for Structure-preserving Feature Transform

abstract: We consider the problem of minimizing the sum of submodular set functions assuming minimization oracles of each summand function. Most existing approaches reformulate the problem as the convex minimization of the sum of the corresponding Lov\'asz extensions and the squared Euclidean norm, leading to algorithms requiring total variation oracles of the summand functions; without further assumptions, these more complex oracles require many calls to the simpler minimization oracles often available in practice. In this paper, we consider a modified convex problem requiring constrained version of the total variation oracles that can be solved with significantly fewer calls to the simple minimization oracles. We support our claims by showing results on graph cuts for 2D and 3D graphs.

paragraphs: The paper studies minimizing a sum of submodular set functions when a minimization routine is available for each individual component. These routines are called oracles: the overall algorithm can ask them to solve component problems. The computational question is how to combine their capabilities without making an excessive number of calls.

Existing approaches commonly convert the set problem into convex optimization using Lovász extensions and a squared Euclidean norm. This leads to a need for total variation oracles, which perform a more complex operation than ordinary component minimization. Without additional assumptions, implementing those operations may require many calls to the simpler oracles available in practice.

The authors modify the convex formulation so that it instead requires constrained total variation oracles. These can be solved using significantly fewer calls to the basic minimization routines. Results on graph cuts in two-dimensional and three-dimensional graphs support the claimed advantage. The central contribution is a reformulation that better matches the capabilities of the component solvers, reducing the work needed to use them.
summary.tldr: A modified convex formulation reduces the component-oracle calls needed to minimize sums of submodular functions.

title: Fast Decomposable Submodular Function Minimization using Constrained Total Variation

abstract: The ability for policies to generalize to new environments is key to the broad application of RL agents. A promising approach to prevent an agent’s policy from overfitting to a limited set of training environments is to apply regularization techniques originally developed for supervised learning. However, there are stark differences between supervised learning and RL. We discuss those differences and propose modifications to existing regularization techniques in order to better adapt them to RL. In particular, we focus on regularization techniques relying on the injection of noise into the learned function, a family that includes some of the most widely used approaches such as Dropout and Batch Normalization. To adapt them to RL, we propose Selective Noise Injection (SNI), which maintains the regularizing effect the injected noise has, while mitigating the adverse effects it has on the gradient quality. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the Information Bottleneck (IB) is a particularly well suited regularization technique for RL as it is effective in the low-data regime encountered early on in training RL agents. Combining the IB with SNI, we significantly outperform current state of the art results, including on the recently proposed generalization benchmark Coinrun.

In particular, we focus on regularization techniques relying on the injection of noise into the learned function, a family that includes some of the most widely used approaches such as Dropout and Batch Normalization. To adapt them to RL, we propose Selective Noise Injection (SNI), which maintains the regularizing effect the injected noise has, while mitigating the adverse effects it has on the gradient quality. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the Information Bottleneck (IB) is a particularly well suited regularization technique for RL as it is effective in the low-data regime encountered early on in training RL agents. Combining the IB with SNI, we significantly outperform current state of the art results, including on the recently proposed generalization benchmark Coinrun.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning policy can fit its training environments closely yet perform poorly in new ones. Regularization offers a way to address that problem, but techniques developed for supervised learning do not transfer without complications. This paper examines those differences, focusing on methods that inject noise into the learned function, including dropout and batch normalization.

The authors propose Selective Noise Injection, or SNI, to preserve the regularizing benefits of noise while reducing its harmful effects on gradient quality. The key concern is that a technique intended to improve generalization can also interfere with the signal used to learn a policy. SNI aims to manage both effects within the reinforcement learning setting.

The paper also finds the Information Bottleneck particularly suitable for the low-data conditions encountered early in reinforcement learning. Combining it with SNI significantly outperforms the reported state of the art, including on Coinrun. These results support adapting regularization to the learning process itself, with attention to both limited early experience and the quality of policy updates.
summary.tldr: Selective Noise Injection combined with an Information Bottleneck improves reinforcement learning generalization while mitigating noise-related degradation of gradient quality.

title: Generalization in Reinforcement Learning with Selective Noise Injection and Information Bottleneck

abstract: We consider the evaluation and training of a new policy for the evaluation data by using the historical data obtained from a different policy. The goal of off-policy evaluation (OPE) is to estimate the expected reward of a new policy over the evaluation data, and that of off-policy learning (OPL) is to find a new policy that maximizes the expected reward over the evaluation data. Although the standard OPE and OPL assume the same distribution of covariate between the historical and evaluation data, there often exists a problem of a covariate shift,i.e., the distribution of the covariate of the historical data is different from that of the evaluation data. In this paper, we derive the efficiency bound of OPE under a covariate shift. Then, we propose doubly robust and efficient estimators for OPE and OPL under a covariate shift by using an estimator of the density ratio between the distributions of the historical and evaluation data. We also discuss other possible estimators and compare their theoretical properties. Finally, we confirm the effectiveness of the proposed estimators through experiments.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation estimates how a new decision policy would perform using historical data collected under another policy. Off-policy learning uses such data to select a policy with high expected reward. This paper addresses an additional difference: the covariate distribution in the evaluation data may differ from the historical distribution.

The authors derive an efficiency bound for off-policy evaluation under this covariate shift. They then propose doubly robust, efficient estimators for evaluation and learning that use an estimated density ratio between the historical and evaluation covariate distributions. This ratio provides a way to account for the distribution change when targeting expected reward on the evaluation data.

The paper also examines alternative estimators and compares their theoretical properties, then reports experiments confirming the effectiveness of the proposed methods. The contribution makes the evaluation population explicit: performance is assessed for the data distribution where the new policy is meant to operate, while using experience gathered under both a different policy and a different covariate distribution.
summary.tldr: Density-ratio-based estimators support efficient, doubly robust policy evaluation and learning when historical and evaluation covariate distributions differ.

title: Off-Policy Evaluation and Learning for External Validity under a Covariate Shift

abstract: Temporal point process (TPP) models combined with recurrent neural networks provide a powerful framework for modeling continuous-time event data. While such models are flexible, they are inherently sequential and therefore cannot benefit from the parallelism of modern hardware. By exploiting the recent developments in the field of normalizing flows, we design TriTPP - a new class of non-recurrent TPP models, where both sampling and likelihood computation can be done in parallel. TriTPP matches the flexibility of RNN-based methods but permits several orders of magnitude faster sampling. This enables us to use the new model for variational inference in continuous-time discrete-state systems. We demonstrate the advantages of the proposed framework on synthetic and real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Temporal point processes model events occurring in continuous time. Combining them with recurrent neural networks provides flexibility, but recurrence makes computation inherently sequential. This limits how much such models can benefit from modern parallel hardware, particularly when generating event sequences.

The paper introduces TriTPP, a non-recurrent class of temporal point process models built using developments in normalizing flows. Both sampling and likelihood computation can run in parallel. The authors report that TriTPP matches the flexibility of recurrent approaches while allowing sampling that is several orders of magnitude faster. The architectural change therefore targets the computational organization of event modeling while retaining expressive modeling capabilities.

Fast sampling also enables the authors to use TriTPP for variational inference in systems whose states are discrete but evolve in continuous time. Synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate advantages of the framework. The contribution links parallel event generation to a broader inference application, showing how removing sequential computation can expand the practical uses of a temporal point process model.
summary.tldr: TriTPP uses non-recurrent, flow-based temporal point processes to parallelize likelihood computation and achieve much faster sampling.

title: Fast and Flexible Temporal Point Processes with Triangular Maps

abstract: MR images reconstructed from sub-sampled Cartesian data using deep learning techniques show a characteristic banding (sometimes described as streaking), which is particularly strong in low signal-to-noise regions of the reconstructed image. In this work, we propose the use of an adversarial loss that penalizes banding structures without requiring any human annotation. Our technique greatly reduces the appearance of banding, without requiring any additional computation or post-processing at reconstruction time. We report the results of a blind comparison against a strong baseline by a group of expert evaluators (board-certified radiologists), where our approach is ranked superior at banding removal with no statistically significant loss of detail. A reference implementation of our method is available in the supplementary material.

paragraphs: Deep learning reconstructions of MR images from sub-sampled Cartesian data can contain visible bands or streaks. These artifacts are particularly pronounced in regions with low signal-to-noise ratios. This paper addresses that specific reconstruction problem by changing the training objective so that the learned reconstruction method is penalized for producing banding structures.

The proposed approach uses an adversarial loss and does not require human annotations identifying the unwanted artifacts. Its practical advantage is that the correction is incorporated during training: reconstruction requires no additional computation or subsequent processing. This makes the method a way to improve the reconstructed image within the existing reconstruction-time computational burden.

In a blind comparison against a strong baseline, board-certified radiologists rank the proposed approach as better at removing banding. The evaluation finds no statistically significant loss of image detail, alongside a substantial reduction in visible artifacts. That finding supports the reported improvement in banding removal; the statistical qualification means it should not be read as proof that every detail is always preserved.
summary.tldr: An annotation-free adversarial loss reduces MRI banding without extra reconstruction-time computation or statistically significant detail loss in expert evaluation.

title: MRI Banding Removal via Adversarial Training

abstract: Based on a sample of size $n$, we consider estimating the number of symbols that appear at least $\mu$ times in an independent sample of size $a \cdot n$, where $a$ is a given parameter. This formulation includes, as a special case, the well-known problem of inferring the number of unseen species introduced by [Fisher et al.] in 1943 and considered by many others. Of considerable interest in this line of works is the largest $a$ for which the quantity can be accurately predicted. We completely resolve this problem by determining the limit of estimation to be $a \approx (\log n)/\mu$, with both lower and upper bounds matching up to constant factors. For the particular case of $\mu = 1$, this implies the recent result by [Orlitsky et al.] on the unseen species problem. Experimental evaluations show that the proposed estimator performs exceptionally well in practice. Furthermore, the estimator is a simple linear combination of symbols' empirical counts, and hence linear-time computable.

paragraphs: Given an initial sample of n observations, how far can one predict the variety present in a larger, independent sample? This paper studies the number of distinct symbols that will appear at least μ times in a future sample of size a times n. The familiar unseen-species problem appears as a special case.

The central result identifies the scale of the largest expansion factor that permits accurate estimation: a is approximately log(n) divided by μ. Matching upper and lower bounds establish this limit up to constant factors. Thus, requiring more repeated appearances changes the range over which reliable prediction is possible, and increasing the original sample size expands that range logarithmically.

The authors also provide an estimator that is a simple linear combination of empirical symbol counts and can be computed in linear time. Experiments show strong practical performance. The contribution pairs a computationally simple prediction method with a characterization of the problem's statistical limits, rather than offering an estimator without explaining how far extrapolation can reasonably extend.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes a prediction limit of approximately log(n)/μ for future sample expansion and provides a linear-time estimator.

title: Optimal Prediction of the Number of Unseen Species with Multiplicity

abstract: In machine learning applications such as ranking fairness or fairness over intersectional groups, one often encounters optimization problems with an extremely large number of constraints. In particular, with ranking fairness tasks, there may even be a variable number of constraints, e.g. one for each query in the training set. In these cases, the standard approach of optimizing a Lagrangian while maintaining one Lagrange multiplier per constraint may no longer be practical. Our proposal is to associate a feature vector with each constraint, and to learn a ``multiplier model’’ that maps each such vector to the corresponding Lagrange multiplier. We prove optimality, approximate feasibility and generalization guarantees under assumptions on the flexibility of the multiplier model, and empirically demonstrate that our method is effective on real-world case studies.

paragraphs: Some learning problems must satisfy a very large collection of constraints. Fairness in rankings or across intersecting groups provides examples, and a ranking task may introduce a separate constraint for every training query. Maintaining an independent optimization variable for each requirement can then become impractical.

The paper replaces that collection of separately maintained Lagrange multipliers with a learned multiplier model. Each constraint receives a feature vector, and the model maps those features to its multiplier. In a Lagrangian formulation, these multipliers determine how constraints influence optimization. Predicting them from features creates a shared representation of how different requirements should be weighted.

The authors prove guarantees concerning optimality, approximate satisfaction of constraints, and generalization, subject to assumptions about the multiplier model's flexibility. That qualification matters: the model must be expressive enough for the guarantees to apply. Experiments on real-world case studies show that the approach is effective. The contribution is a way to make heavily constrained learning more manageable while retaining conditional theoretical assurances.
summary.tldr: A learned model predicts constraint multipliers from features, making heavily constrained optimization more manageable with guarantees under expressivity assumptions.

title: Approximate Heavily-Constrained Learning with Lagrange Multiplier Models

abstract: Gaussian latent variable models are a key class of Bayesian hierarchical models with applications in many fields. Performing Bayesian inference on such models can be challenging as Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithms struggle with the geometry of the resulting posterior distribution and can be prohibitively slow. An alternative is to use a Laplace approximation to marginalize out the latent Gaussian variables and then integrate out the remaining hyperparameters using dynamic Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, a gradient-based Markov chain Monte Carlo sampler. To implement this scheme efficiently, we derive a novel adjoint method that propagates the minimal information needed to construct the gradient of the approximate marginal likelihood. This strategy yields a scalable differentiation method that is orders of magnitude faster than state of the art differentiation techniques when the hyperparameters are high dimensional. We prototype the method in the probabilistic programming framework Stan and test the utility of the embedded Laplace approximation on several models, including one where the dimension of the hyperparameter is ∼6,000. Depending on the cases, the benefits can include an alleviation of the geometric pathologies that frustrate Hamiltonian Monte Carlo and a dramatic speed-up.

paragraphs: Bayesian models with latent Gaussian variables can produce posterior distributions whose geometry makes sampling difficult and slow. The paper studies a strategy that first uses a Laplace approximation to marginalize those latent variables. Dynamic Hamiltonian Monte Carlo then handles the remaining hyperparameters, reducing the part of the model that must be sampled directly.

The computational challenge is obtaining gradients of the approximate marginal likelihood efficiently. The authors derive an adjoint differentiation method that passes along only the information needed to construct those gradients. For high-dimensional hyperparameters, this method is reported to be orders of magnitude faster than existing leading differentiation techniques.

The approach is prototyped in Stan and tested on several models, including one with roughly 6,000 hyperparameters. Depending on the model, the embedded Laplace approximation can ease problematic posterior geometry and produce a dramatic speed-up. The contribution combines an approximation to latent-variable integration with a more scalable way to differentiate that approximation. Its benefits are case-dependent, and the resulting marginal likelihood remains an approximation.
summary.tldr: An efficient adjoint method accelerates gradients for Laplace-approximated Bayesian inference, enabling substantial speed-ups in some latent Gaussian models.

title: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo using an adjoint-differentiated Laplace approximation: Bayesian inference for latent Gaussian models and beyond

abstract: We introduce a deep learning model for speech denoising, a long-standing challenge in audio analysis arising in numerous applications. Our approach is based on a key observation about human speech: there is often a short pause between each sentence or word. In a recorded speech signal, those pauses introduce a series of time periods during which only noise is present. We leverage these incidental silent intervals to learn a model for automatic speech denoising given only mono-channel audio. Detected silent intervals over time expose not just pure noise but its time-varying features, allowing the model to learn noise dynamics and suppress it from the speech signal. Experiments on multiple datasets confirm the pivotal role of silent interval detection for speech denoising, and our method outperforms several state-of-the-art denoising methods, including those that accept only audio input (like ours) and those that denoise based on audiovisual input (and hence require more information). We also show that our method enjoys excellent generalization properties, such as denoising spoken languages not seen during training.

paragraphs: Pauses in speech contain useful information for removing background noise. During an interval without speech, the recording exposes noise on its own. This paper builds a deep learning denoising model around those incidental pauses, using only a single audio channel to learn about the interference mixed with the speaker's voice.

The model detects silent intervals across time and uses them to learn noise dynamics. This matters because the noise can change during a recording: multiple pauses reveal its evolving features, rather than just providing one fixed noise example. The learned information is then used to suppress noise in the speech signal.

Experiments on multiple datasets support the importance of detecting these intervals. The method outperforms several state-of-the-art denoisers in the reported comparisons, including systems using audio alone and systems using both audio and visual information. It also generalizes to spoken languages absent from training. These results support treating naturally occurring speech pauses as informative observations that can improve denoising from a single-channel recording.
summary.tldr: A speech denoiser learns changing background noise from pauses in single-channel audio and shows strong performance and cross-language generalization.

title: Listening to Sounds of Silence for Speech Denoising

abstract: Multi-agent active perception is a task where a team of agents cooperatively gathers observations to compute a joint estimate of a hidden variable. The task is decentralized and the joint estimate can only be computed after the task ends by fusing observations of all agents. The objective is to maximize the accuracy of the estimate. The accuracy is quantified by a centralized prediction reward determined by a centralized decision-maker who perceives the observations gathered by all agents after the task ends. In this paper, we model multi-agent active perception as a decentralized partially observable Markov decision process (Dec-POMDP) with a convex centralized prediction reward. We prove that by introducing individual prediction actions for each agent, the problem is converted into a standard Dec-POMDP with a decentralized prediction reward. The loss due to decentralization is bounded, and we give a sufficient condition for when it is zero. Our results allow application of any Dec-POMDP solution algorithm to multi-agent active perception problems, and enable planning to reduce uncertainty without explicit computation of joint estimates. We demonstrate the empirical usefulness of our results by applying a standard Dec-POMDP algorithm to multi-agent active perception problems, showing increased scalability in the planning horizon.

paragraphs: In multi-agent active perception, a team gathers observations to estimate something hidden. Agents act separately, but their observations are combined only after the task ends. This creates a planning difficulty: the quality of the final estimate is judged centrally, even though the information-gathering decisions are decentralized.

The authors model the task as a decentralized partially observable Markov decision process with a convex centralized prediction reward. They introduce an individual prediction action for each agent, converting the problem into a standard form with decentralized prediction rewards. They bound the loss introduced by decentralization and give a sufficient condition under which that loss is zero. The condition guarantees zero loss when it holds; it is not presented as necessary.

This conversion makes standard Dec-POMDP solution algorithms applicable and allows uncertainty-reducing plans without explicitly computing joint estimates during planning. The authors demonstrate the approach using a standard algorithm on active-perception problems and report improved scalability as the planning horizon grows. The result connects a difficult centralized evaluation objective to established decentralized planning machinery while accounting for the possible cost of that conversion.
summary.tldr: Individual prediction actions turn cooperative sensing with a centralized reward into standard decentralized planning, with bounded loss and improved empirical horizon scalability.

title: Multi-agent active perception with prediction rewards

abstract: We study the problem of least squares linear regression where the datapoints are dependent and are sampled from a Markov chain. We establish sharp information theoretic minimax lower bounds for this problem in terms of $\tmix$, the mixing time of the underlying Markov chain, under different noise settings. Our results establish that in general, optimization with Markovian data is strictly harder than optimization with independent data and a trivial algorithm (SGD-DD) that works with only one in every $\tmix$ samples, which are approximately independent, is minimax optimal. In fact, it is strictly better than the popular Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) method with constant step-size which is otherwise minimax optimal in the regression with independent data setting. Beyond a worst case analysis, we investigate whether structured datasets seen in practice such as Gaussian auto-regressive dynamics can admit more efficient optimization schemes. Surprisingly, even in this specific and natural setting, Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) with constant step-size is still no better than SGD-DD. Instead, we propose an algorithm based on experience replay--a popular reinforcement learning technique--that achieves a significantly better error rate. Our improved rate serves as one of the first results where an algorithm outperforms SGD-DD on an interesting Markov chain and also provides one of the first theoretical analyses to support the use of experience replay in practice.

paragraphs: This paper studies least-squares regression when observations come from a Markov chain rather than independent sampling. It establishes sharp minimax lower bounds involving the chain’s mixing time under different noise settings, showing that dependence can make the problem fundamentally harder.

In the worst case, a simple method called SGD-DD, which uses roughly one observation per mixing time, is minimax optimal. Constant-step-size SGD can be strictly worse despite its optimality for independent-data regression. Even for Gaussian autoregressive dynamics, ordinary constant-step-size SGD does no better than SGD-DD.

The authors then introduce an experience-replay-based algorithm with a significantly better error rate for that structured setting. This supplies theoretical support for replay beyond the worst-case subsampling baseline. The improved rate is specific to the analyzed process structure and does not contradict the general minimax lower bound over all relevant Markov chains.
summary.tldr: Markov-dependent regression has stricter limits, while experience replay helps on structured processes.

title: Least Squares Regression with Markovian Data: Fundamental Limits and Algorithms

abstract: We propose to personalize a 2D human pose estimator given a set of test images of a person without using any manual annotations. While there is a significant advancement in human pose estimation, it is still very challenging for a model to generalize to different unknown environments and unseen persons. Instead of using a fixed model for every test case, we adapt our pose estimator during test time to exploit person-specific information. We first train our model on diverse data with both a supervised and a self-supervised pose estimation objectives jointly. We use a Transformer model to build a transformation between the self-supervised keypoints and the supervised keypoints. During test time, we personalize and adapt our model by fine-tuning with the self-supervised objective. The pose is then improved by transforming the updated self-supervised keypoints. We experiment with multiple datasets and show significant improvements on pose estimations with our self-supervised personalization. Project page with code is available at https://liyz15.github.io/TTP/.

paragraphs: A human pose estimator trained on diverse data can still struggle with an unfamiliar person or environment. This paper personalizes a 2D pose estimator using a set of test images of one person, without requiring manual annotations. The aim is to exploit person-specific information available when the model is actually used.

Training combines supervised and self-supervised pose-estimation objectives. A Transformer learns a mapping between the keypoints produced by the self-supervised task and those associated with the supervised task. At test time, the model is fine-tuned through its self-supervised objective. The learned transformation then converts the updated self-supervised keypoints into an improved pose estimate.

This design connects an annotation-free adaptation signal to the supervised pose output through the Transformer mapping. The authors report significant improvements across multiple datasets after self-supervised personalization. Their findings show that a person's test images can provide useful adaptation information, allowing the estimator to respond to the individual case through a training objective that does not need new manual labels.
summary.tldr: A Transformer links self-supervised and supervised keypoints so a pose estimator can personalize itself from unlabeled images of a person.

title: Test-Time Personalization with a Transformer for Human Pose Estimation

abstract: While most classic studies of function in experimental neuroscience have focused on the coding properties of individual neurons, recent developments in recording technologies have resulted in an increasing emphasis on the dynamics of neural populations. This has given rise to a wide variety of models for analyzing population activity in relation to experimental variables, but direct testing of many neural population hypotheses requires intervening in the system based on current neural state, necessitating models capable of inferring neural state online. Existing approaches, primarily based on dynamical systems, require strong parametric assumptions that are easily violated in the noise-dominated regime and do not scale well to the thousands of data channels in modern experiments. To address this problem, we propose a method that combines fast, stable dimensionality reduction with a soft tiling of the resulting neural manifold, allowing dynamics to be approximated as a probability flow between tiles. This method can be fit efficiently using online expectation maximization, scales to tens of thousands of tiles, and outperforms existing methods when dynamics are noise-dominated or feature multi-modal transition probabilities. The resulting model can be trained at kiloHertz data rates, produces accurate approximations of neural dynamics within minutes, and generates predictions on submillisecond time scales. It retains predictive performance throughout many time steps into the future and is fast enough to serve as a component of closed-loop causal experiments.

Bubblewrap addresses this requirement by modeling population dynamics online. The motivation is that existing dynamical-system approaches can rely on restrictive parametric assumptions and struggle with noisy recordings or the large numbers of channels available in modern experiments.

The method first reduces the dimensionality of the activity data, then covers the resulting neural manifold with soft tiles. It represents dynamics as probability flowing between these tiles. This provides a way to describe several possible future transitions, rather than forcing the dynamics into a single narrowly prescribed trajectory. Online expectation maximization fits the model efficiently.

The reported system scales to tens of thousands of tiles, trains at kilohertz data rates, and produces predictions in less than a millisecond. It learns accurate approximations within minutes and retains predictive performance over multiple future steps. Its advantages over existing methods are reported particularly for noisy or multimodal dynamics, supporting its possible role in closed-loop causal experiments.
summary.tldr: Bubblewrap models neural population dynamics as probability flow between regions of a reduced space, enabling rapid online prediction.

title: Bubblewrap: Online tiling and real-time flow prediction on neural manifolds

abstract: We analyze a class of stochastic gradient algorithms with momentum on a high-dimensional random least squares problem. Our framework, inspired by random matrix theory, provides an exact (deterministic) characterization for the sequence of function values produced by these algorithms which is expressed only in terms of the eigenvalues of the Hessian. This leads to simple expressions for nearly-optimal hyperparameters, a description of the limiting neighborhood, and average-case complexity. As a consequence, we show that (small-batch) stochastic heavy-ball momentum with a fixed momentum parameter provides no actual performance improvement over SGD when step sizes are adjusted correctly. For contrast, in the non-strongly convex setting, it is possible to get a large improvement over SGD using momentum. By introducing hyperparameters that depend on the number of samples, we propose a new algorithm sDANA (stochastic dimension adjusted Nesterov acceleration) which obtains an asymptotically optimal average-case complexity while remaining linearly convergent in the strongly convex setting without adjusting parameters.

title: Dynamics of Stochastic Momentum Methods on Large-scale, Quadratic Models

abstract: It has been well established that first order optimization methods can converge to the maximal objective value of concave functions and provide constant factor approximation guarantees for (non-convex/non-concave) continuous submodular functions. In this work, we initiate the study of the maximization of functions of the form $F(x) = G(x) +C(x)$ over a solvable convex body $P$, where $G$ is a smooth DR-submodular function and $C$ is a smooth concave function. This class of functions is a strict extension of both concave and continuous DR-submodular functions for which no theoretical guarantee is known. We provide a suite of Frank-Wolfe style algorithms, which, depending on the nature of the objective function (i.e., if $G$ and $C$ are monotone or not, and non-negative or not) and on the nature of the set $P$ (i.e., whether it is downward closed or not), provide $1-1/e$, $1/e$, or $1/2$ approximation guarantees. We then use our algorithms to get a framework to smoothly interpolate between choosing a diverse set of elements from a given ground set (corresponding to the mode of a determinantal point process) and choosing a clustered set of elements (corresponding to the maxima of a suitable concave function). Additionally, we apply our algorithms to various functions in the above class (DR-submodular + concave) in both constrained and unconstrained settings, and show that our algorithms consistently outperform natural baselines.

paragraphs: Some optimization objectives combine diminishing returns with a concave preference. This paper studies maximizing a sum of a smooth DR-submodular function and a smooth concave function over a solvable convex region. The combined class extends both familiar families, so guarantees for either component alone do not directly settle the combined problem.

The authors develop several Frank-Wolfe-style algorithms with approximation guarantees of 1 − 1/e, 1/e, or 1/2. Which guarantee applies depends on whether the component functions are monotone and nonnegative, and whether the feasible region is downward closed. These are conditional guarantees tied to the structure of the particular optimization problem.

The diversity component corresponds to finding a mode of a determinantal point process, while a suitable concave function encourages clustering. Experiments on multiple objectives, with and without constraints, consistently outperform the natural baselines considered. The work supplies both theoretical guarantees and a way to tune between competing selection preferences.
summary.tldr: Frank-Wolfe-style algorithms provide conditional approximation guarantees for objectives combining diminishing returns and concavity.

title: Submodular + Concave

abstract: We introduce a novel perspective on Bayesian reinforcement learning (RL); whereas existing approaches infer a posterior over the transition distribution or Q-function, we characterise the uncertainty in the Bellman operator. Our Bayesian Bellman operator (BBO) framework is motivated by the insight that when bootstrapping is introduced, model-free approaches actually infer a posterior over Bellman operators, not value functions. In this paper, we use BBO to provide a rigorous theoretical analysis of model-free Bayesian RL to better understand its relationship to established frequentist RL methodologies. We prove that Bayesian solutions are consistent with frequentist RL solutions, even when approximate inference is used, and derive conditions for which convergence properties hold. Empirically, we demonstrate that algorithms derived from the BBO framework have sophisticated deep exploration properties that enable them to solve continuous control tasks at which state-of-the-art regularised actor-critic algorithms fail catastrophically.

paragraphs: Bayesian reinforcement learning represents uncertainty while an agent learns how to act. Existing approaches commonly place that uncertainty over the environment's transitions or its action values. This paper instead studies uncertainty in the Bellman operator, the rule used to update value estimates from rewards and estimates of future value.

The motivating observation concerns bootstrapping: learning updates that depend on other learned estimates. The authors argue that, with bootstrapping, model-free Bayesian methods actually infer a distribution over Bellman operators. Their Bayesian Bellman operator framework makes this interpretation explicit and uses it to analyze how Bayesian methods relate to established frequentist approaches.

The theoretical results establish consistency with frequentist reinforcement learning solutions, including when inference is approximate, and identify conditions supporting convergence. Experiments show that algorithms derived from the framework can explore effectively enough to solve continuous control tasks where the compared regularized actor-critic methods fail severely. These findings connect a revised account of uncertainty to both formal analysis and demonstrated exploration behavior.
summary.tldr: Modeling uncertainty in Bellman operators provides theoretical insight into Bayesian reinforcement learning and yields algorithms with strong demonstrated exploration.

title: Bayesian Bellman Operators

abstract: Certifiable local robustness, which rigorously precludes small-norm adversarial examples, has received significant attention as a means of addressing security concerns in deep learning. However, for some classification problems, local robustness is not a natural objective, even in the presence of adversaries; for example, if an image contains two classes of subjects, the correct label for the image may be considered arbitrary between the two, and thus enforcing strict separation between them is unnecessary. In this work, we introduce two relaxed safety properties for classifiers that address this observation: (1) relaxed top-k robustness, which serves as the analogue of top-k accuracy; and (2) affinity robustness, which specifies which sets of labels must be separated by a robustness margin, and which can be $\epsilon$-close in $\ell_p$ space. We show how to construct models that can be efficiently certified against each relaxed robustness property, and trained with very little overhead relative to standard gradient descent. Finally, we demonstrate experimentally that these relaxed variants of robustness are well-suited to several significant classification problems, leading to lower rejection rates and higher certified accuracies than can be obtained when certifying "standard" local robustness.

paragraphs: Standard certifiable local robustness rules out adversarial changes within a small input neighborhood. The paper argues that strict separation between every pair of labels can be unnecessary for some tasks. If an image contains subjects from two classes, for example, either class might be an acceptable label, making a rigid boundary between them an awkward objective.

The authors introduce two alternatives. Relaxed top-k robustness provides a robustness counterpart to top-k accuracy. Affinity robustness specifies which label sets require a separating robustness margin and which may occur close together in input space. These properties let the safety requirement reflect acceptable relationships among labels while retaining a formal certification objective.

The paper shows how to construct models that can be efficiently certified for these relaxed properties and trained with little overhead beyond standard gradient descent. Experiments on several classification problems report lower rejection rates and higher certified accuracies than standard local robustness certification. These gains concern the newly defined safety properties: relaxing unnecessary label separation changes what is certified, allowing certification to better fit the task.
summary.tldr: Two relaxed robustness properties allow task-appropriate relationships among labels while supporting efficient certification and improved reported certified accuracy.

title: Relaxing Local Robustness

abstract: Recovery of support of a sparse vector from simple measurements is a widely studied problem, considered under the frameworks of compressed sensing, 1-bit compressed sensing, and more general single index models. We consider generalizations of this problem: mixtures of linear regressions, and mixtures of linear classifiers, where the goal is to recover supports of multiple sparse vectors using only a small number of possibly noisy linear, and 1-bit measurements respectively. The key challenge is that the measurements from different vectors are randomly mixed. Both of these problems have also received attention recently. In mixtures of linear classifiers, an observation corresponds to the side of the queried hyperplane a random unknown vector lies in; whereas in mixtures of linear regressions we observe the projection of a random unknown vector on the queried hyperplane. The primary step in recovering the unknown vectors from the mixture is to first identify the support of all the individual component vectors. In this work, we study the number of measurements sufficient for recovering the supports of all the component vectors in a mixture in both these models. We provide algorithms that use a number of measurements polynomial in $k, \log n$ and quasi-polynomial in $\ell$, to recover the support of all the $\ell$ unknown vectors in the mixture with high probability when each individual component is a $k$-sparse $n$-dimensional vector.

paragraphs: Recovering a sparse vector’s support means identifying which of its coordinates are nonzero. This paper considers several unknown sparse vectors whose measurements are randomly mixed together. The learner must identify each vector’s support without knowing which component produced a given observation.

The authors study mixtures of linear regressions and mixtures of linear classifiers. Regression measurements reveal a projection of a randomly selected unknown vector, while classifier measurements reveal which side of a queried hyperplane it lies on. The latter provides only a one-bit observation. The framework considers small numbers of measurements that may also be noisy.

The paper gives algorithms that recover all component supports with high probability. For ℓ vectors, each with at most k nonzero coordinates in n dimensions, the sufficient measurement count is polynomial in k and log n and quasi-polynomial in ℓ. These guarantees identify a way to exploit sparsity despite mixing. They concern support identification, described as a primary step toward recovering the unknown vectors, rather than full recovery of every coordinate value.
summary.tldr: Algorithms recover every sparse component’s support from mixed linear or one-bit measurements with high-probability measurement guarantees.

title: Support Recovery of Sparse Signals from a Mixture of Linear Measurements

abstract: We prove an exponential separation for the sample/query complexity between the standard PAC-learning model and a version of the Equivalence-Query-learning model. In the PAC model all samples are provided at the beginning of the learning process. In the Equivalence-Query model the samples are acquired through an interaction between a teacher and a learner, where the teacher provides counterexamples to hypotheses given by the learner. It is intuitive that in an interactive setting fewer samples are needed. We make this formal and prove that in order to achieve an error $\epsilon$ {\em exponentially} (in $\epsilon$) fewer samples suffice than what the PAC bound requires. It was shown experimentally by Stutz, Hein, and Schiele that adversarial training with on-manifold adversarial examples aids generalization (compared to standard training). If we think of the adversarial examples as counterexamples to the current hypothesis then our result can be thought of as a theoretical confirmation of those findings. We also discuss how our result relates to adversarial robustness. In the standard adversarial model one restricts the adversary by introducing a norm constraint. An alternative was pioneered by Goldwasser et. al. Rather than restricting the adversary the learner is enhanced. We pursue a third path. We require the adversary to return samples according to the Equivalance-Query model and show that this leads to robustness. Even though our model has its limitations it provides a fresh point of view on adversarial robustness.

paragraphs: The paper compares learning from a fixed collection of examples with learning through interaction. In the PAC setting considered here, the learner receives all samples at the beginning. In the equivalence-query setting, it proposes a hypothesis and a teacher responds with counterexamples. The next example can therefore address the learner's current mistakes.

The authors prove an exponential separation in sample or query complexity between PAC learning and a version of equivalence-query learning. For achieving a specified error, exponentially fewer examples suffice in the interactive model than the PAC bound requires. This formalizes a benefit of receiving counterexamples through an interaction rather than relying entirely on examples supplied in advance.

The paper also connects this result to adversarial training and robustness. Interpreting adversarial examples as counterexamples offers a theoretical perspective on previously observed generalization benefits from on-manifold adversarial training. For robustness, the authors require the adversary to return samples according to their equivalence-query model. Their robustness result depends on that restriction and is presented as a limited but fresh perspective on adversarial learning.
summary.tldr: A theoretical separation shows that interactive counterexamples can dramatically reduce sample needs and yield robustness under an equivalence-query adversary.

title: Exponential Separation between Two Learning Models and Adversarial Robustness

abstract: We can compress a rectifier network while exactly preserving its underlying functionality with respect to a given input domain if some of its neurons are stable. However, current approaches to determine the stability of neurons with Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) activations require solving or finding a good approximation to multiple discrete optimization problems. In this work, we introduce an algorithm based on solving a single optimization problem to identify all stable neurons. Our approach is on median 183 times faster than the state-of-art method on CIFAR-10, which allows us to explore exact compression on deeper (5 x 100) and wider (2 x 800) networks within minutes. For classifiers trained under an amount of L1 regularization that does not worsen accuracy, we can remove up to 56% of the connections on the CIFAR-10 dataset. The code is available at the following link, https://github.com/yuxwind/ExactCompression .

paragraphs: A ReLU network can sometimes be compressed without changing its function over a specified input domain. The opportunity comes from stable neurons, whose activation status does not change within that domain. Identifying them has been costly because previous approaches require solving, or adequately approximating, multiple discrete optimization problems.

This paper introduces an algorithm that identifies all stable neurons through a single optimization problem. On CIFAR-10, its median speedup over the state-of-the-art method is 183 times. That improvement makes it possible to investigate exact compression of deeper networks with five layers of 100 neurons and wider networks with two layers of 800 neurons within minutes.

The exactness claim is tied to the specified input domain: within it, the compressed network preserves the original functionality. The contribution makes the search for such removable structure substantially more practical.
summary.tldr: A single optimization problem identifies stable ReLU neurons much faster, enabling compression that exactly preserves network behavior on a specified input domain.

title: Scaling Up Exact Neural Network Compression by ReLU Stability

abstract: Incrementality, which measures the causal effect of showing an ad to a potential customer (e.g. a user in an internet platform) versus not, is a central object for advertisers in online advertising platforms. This paper investigates the problem of how an advertiser can learn to optimize the bidding sequence in an online manner \emph{without} knowing the incrementality parameters in advance. We formulate the offline version of this problem as a specially structured episodic Markov Decision Process (MDP) and then, for its online learning counterpart, propose a novel reinforcement learning (RL) algorithm with regret at most $\widetilde{O}(H^2\sqrt{T})$, which depends on the number of rounds $H$ and number of episodes $T$, but does not depend on the number of actions (i.e., possible bids). A fundamental difference between our learning problem from standard RL problems is that the realized reward feedback from conversion incrementality is \emph{mixed} and \emph{delayed}. To handle this difficulty we propose and analyze a novel pairwise moment-matching algorithm to learn the conversion incrementality, which we believe is of independent interest.

paragraphs: Advertising incrementality measures the causal effect of showing an advertisement compared with not showing it. This paper asks how an advertiser can learn a sequence of bids without knowing those effects beforehand. The learning problem is complicated because feedback about additional conversions arrives late and combines contributions rather than presenting a straightforward immediate reward.

The authors first express the offline problem as an episodic Markov decision process with special structure. They then develop a reinforcement learning algorithm for its online counterpart. To learn conversion incrementality from the mixed and delayed observations, they introduce and analyze a pairwise moment-matching algorithm as a central component.

The resulting regret guarantee is at most O-tilde(H squared times the square root of T), where H counts rounds and T counts episodes. The bound does not depend on the number of possible bids. This theoretical result shows how the problem's structure can support learning despite difficult reward feedback, without adding a dependence on action count to the stated guarantee.
summary.tldr: A reinforcement learning approach learns incrementality-based bidding from mixed, delayed rewards with a regret bound independent of the number of bids.

title: Incrementality Bidding via Reinforcement Learning under Mixed and Delayed Rewards

abstract: We present a PAC-Bayes-style generalization bound which enables the replacement of the KL-divergence with a variety of Integral Probability Metrics (IPM). We provide instances of this bound with the IPM being the total variation metric and the Wasserstein distance. A notable feature of the obtained bounds is that they naturally interpolate between classical uniform convergence bounds in the worst case (when the prior and posterior are far away from each other), and improved bounds in favorable cases (when the posterior and prior are close). This illustrates the possibility of reinforcing classical generalization bounds with algorithm- and data-dependent components, thus making them more suitable to analyze algorithms that use a large hypothesis space.

This illustrates the possibility of reinforcing classical generalization bounds with algorithm- and data-dependent components, thus making them more suitable to analyze algorithms that use a large hypothesis space.

paragraphs: Generalization bounds describe how performance on observed data relates to performance beyond it. PAC-Bayes analyses use a prior and posterior over hypotheses and typically measure their difference through KL divergence. This paper develops a PAC-Bayes-style bound that allows that comparison to use a range of integral probability metrics instead.

The authors give specific versions based on total variation and Wasserstein distance. A central feature is how the resulting guarantees change with the separation between prior and posterior. When they are far apart, the bounds recover the behavior of classical uniform convergence guarantees. When they are close, the bounds can improve.

This creates a connection between worst-case guarantees over a hypothesis space and guarantees sensitive to the algorithm and observed data. The contribution matters particularly for analyzing algorithms that operate in large hypothesis spaces: the bound can incorporate favorable information about the learned posterior rather than depending only on the broad space available. The improvement remains conditional on favorable prior-posterior proximity, not an unconditional tightening for every learning problem.
summary.tldr: PAC-Bayes-style bounds using probability metrics interpolate between uniform convergence guarantees and improvements when prior and posterior are close.

title: Integral Probability Metrics PAC-Bayes Bounds

abstract: Knowledge Distillation (KD) aims at transferring the knowledge of a well-performed neural network (the {\it teacher}) to a weaker one (the {\it student}). A peculiar phenomenon is that a more accurate model doesn't necessarily teach better, and temperature adjustment can neither alleviate the mismatched capacity. To explain this, we decompose the efficacy of KD into three parts: {\it correct guidance}, {\it smooth regularization}, and {\it class discriminability}. The last term describes the distinctness of {\it wrong class probabilities} that the teacher provides in KD. Complex teachers tend to be over-confident and traditional temperature scaling limits the efficacy of {\it class discriminability}, resulting in less discriminative wrong class probabilities. Therefore, we propose {\it Asymmetric Temperature Scaling (ATS)}, which separately applies a higher/lower temperature to the correct/wrong class. ATS enlarges the variance of wrong class probabilities in the teacher's label and makes the students grasp the absolute affinities of wrong classes to the target class as discriminative as possible. Both theoretical analysis and extensive experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of ATS. The demo developed in Mindspore is available at \url{https://gitee.com/lxcnju/ats-mindspore} and will be available at \url{https://gitee.com/mindspore/models/tree/master/research/cv/ats}.
