paragraphs: Knowledge distillation trains a smaller student network using the outputs of a stronger teacher. Surprisingly, a teacher with better prediction accuracy does not necessarily produce a better student. This paper examines why increasing teacher quality can fail to improve teaching, and why conventional temperature adjustment does not resolve the capacity mismatch.

The authors separate distillation's effects into correct guidance, smooth regularization, and class discriminability. The third concerns differences among the probabilities assigned to incorrect classes. Those differences communicate how strongly each alternative relates to the target. Complex teachers tend to be overconfident, while conventional temperature scaling limits how distinctly these alternatives can be represented.

Asymmetric Temperature Scaling applies a higher temperature to the correct class and a lower temperature to incorrect classes. This increases variation among the incorrect-class probabilities, giving the student more differentiated information about alternatives. The paper supports the method with theoretical analysis and extensive experiments. Its central contribution is a targeted adjustment to the teaching signal, motivated by information that ordinary scaling can obscure.
summary.tldr: Applying different temperatures to correct and incorrect classes helps stronger teachers provide more informative knowledge-distillation targets.

title: Asymmetric Temperature Scaling Makes Larger Networks Teach Well Again

abstract: Due to the drastic gap in complexity between sequential and batch statistical learning, recent work has studied a smoothed sequential learning setting, where Nature is constrained to select contexts with density bounded by $1/\sigma$ with respect to a known measure $\mu$. Unfortunately, for some function classes, there is an exponential gap between the statistically optimal regret and that which can be achieved efficiently. In this paper, we give a computationally efficient algorithm that is the first to enjoy the statistically optimal $\log(T/\sigma)$ regret for realizable $K$-wise linear classification. We extend our results to settings where the true classifier is linear in an over-parameterized polynomial featurization of the contexts, as well as to a realizable piecewise-regression setting assuming access to an appropriate ERM oracle. Somewhat surprisingly, standard disagreement-based analyses are insufficient to achieve regret logarithmic in $1/\sigma$. Instead, we develop a novel characterization of the geometry of the disagreement region induced by generalized linear classifiers. Along the way, we develop numerous technical tools of independent interest, including a general anti-concentration bound for the determinant of certain matrix averages.
originalAbstract: Due to the drastic gap in complexity between sequential and batch statistical learning, recent work has studied a smoothed sequential learning setting, where Nature is constrained to select contexts with density bounded by $1/\sigma$ with respect to a known measure $\mu$. Unfortunately, for some function classes, there is an exponential gap between the statistically optimal regret and that which can be achieved efficiently. In this paper, we give a computationally efficient algorithm that is the first to enjoy the statistically optimal $\log(T/\sigma)$ regret for realizable $K$-wise linear classification. We extend our results to settings where the true classifier is linear in an over-parameterized polynomial featurization of the contexts, as well as to a realizable piecewise-regression setting assuming access to an appropriate ERM oracle. Somewhat surprisingly, standard disagreement-based analyses are insufficient to achieve regret logarithmic in $1/\sigma$. Instead, we develop a novel characterization of the geometry of the disagreement region induced by generalized linear classifiers. Along the way, we develop numerous technical tools of independent interest, including a general anti-concentration bound for the determinant of certain matrix averages.

paragraphs: Online learning processes examples sequentially, and computational efficiency can prevent an algorithm from achieving the best statistically possible regret. This paper studies a smoothed setting: Nature may choose incoming contexts, but their density relative to a known reference measure is bounded by 1/σ. That restriction is part of the setting supporting the results.

For realizable K-wise linear classification, the authors give a computationally efficient algorithm attaining the statistically optimal log(T/σ) regret dependence. Realizability means the setting assumes a true classifier within the relevant class. The results also extend to classifiers linear in an over-parameterized polynomial feature representation, and to realizable piecewise regression when an appropriate empirical risk minimization oracle is available.

The analysis requires more than standard arguments based on regions where candidate classifiers disagree. The authors develop a new geometric characterization of those regions for generalized linear classifiers, along with technical tools including a determinant anti-concentration bound. The contribution connects computational efficiency with optimal statistical behavior under the stated smoothing and realizability conditions.
summary.tldr: Under smoothing and realizability assumptions, an efficient online classification algorithm attains statistically optimal logarithmic regret.

title: Efficient and Near-Optimal Smoothed Online Learning for Generalized Linear Functions

abstract: Visual search is an essential part of almost any everyday human interaction with the visual environment. Nowadays, several algorithms are able to predict gaze positions during simple observation, but few models attempt to simulate human behavior during visual search in natural scenes. Furthermore, these models vary widely in their design and exhibit differences in the datasets and metrics with which they were evaluated. Thus, there is a need for a reference point, on which each model can be tested and from where potential improvements can be derived. In this study, we select publicly available state-of-the-art visual search models and datasets in natural scenes, and provide a common framework for their evaluation. To this end, we apply a unified format and criteria, bridging the gaps between them, and we estimate the models’ efficiency and similarity with humans using a specific set of metrics. This integration has allowed us to enhance the Ideal Bayesian Searcher by combining it with a neural network-based visual search model, which enables it to generalize to other datasets. The present work sheds light on the limitations of current models and how integrating different approaches with a unified criteria can lead to better algorithms. Moreover, it moves forward on bringing forth a solution for the urgent need for benchmarking data and metrics to support the development of more general human visual search computational models. All of the code used here, including metrics, plots, and visual search models, alongside the preprocessed datasets, are available at $\url{https://github.com/FerminT/VisualSearchBenchmark}$.

Existing visual-search models differ in their designs, datasets, and evaluation measures, making comparisons difficult. ViSioNS brings publicly available models and natural-scene datasets into a shared evaluation framework.

The benchmark unifies data formats and evaluation criteria so that the models can be assessed on common terms. Its metrics examine both search efficiency and similarity to human behavior. This provides a reference point for studying where current models succeed or fall short and for identifying opportunities to combine complementary approaches.

The authors use the integration to improve the Ideal Bayesian Searcher by combining it with a neural-network-based visual-search model. The resulting approach can generalize to other datasets. This example shows how a common evaluation framework can support model development as well as comparison. The released code, metrics, plotting tools, models, and preprocessed datasets provide a shared basis for further work on computational models of human visual search.
summary.tldr: ViSioNS standardizes visual-search evaluation and supports a combined Bayesian and neural model that generalizes across datasets.

title: ViSioNS: Visual Search in Natural Scenes Benchmark

abstract: In this paper, we study the problem of fair sequential decision making with biased linear bandit feedback. At each round, a player selects an action described by a covariate and by a sensitive attribute. The perceived reward is a linear combination of the covariates of the chosen action, but the player only observes a biased evaluation of this reward, depending on the sensitive attribute. To characterize the difficulty of this problem, we design a phased elimination algorithm that corrects the unfair evaluations, and establish upper bounds on its regret. We show that the worst-case regret is smaller than $\mathcal{O}(\kappa_* ^{1/3}\log(T)^{1/3}T^{2/3})$, where $\kappa_*$ is an explicit geometrical constant characterizing the difficulty of bias estimation. We prove lower bounds on the worst-case regret for some sets of actions showing that this rate is tight up to a possible sub-logarithmic factor. We also derive gap-dependent upper bounds on the regret, and matching lower bounds for some problem instance. Interestingly, these results reveal a transition between a regime where the problem is as difficult as its unbiased counterpart, and a regime where it can be much harder.

paragraphs: This paper studies sequential decisions when feedback contains bias tied to a sensitive attribute. Each action has ordinary covariates and a sensitive attribute, while its reward follows a linear relationship with the covariates. The learner observes an attribute-dependent biased evaluation, so choosing good actions also requires addressing distorted feedback.

The authors design a phased elimination algorithm that corrects these unfair evaluations and derive bounds on regret. Their worst-case upper bound scales with T to the two-thirds power and the cube roots of log T and a geometric constant, kappa-star. That constant characterizes the difficulty of estimating the bias, tying the cost of learning to the geometry of the available actions.

Lower bounds for some action sets show that this rate is tight up to a possible sub-logarithmic factor. The paper also gives gap-dependent upper bounds and matching lower bounds for some instances. These results reveal two regimes: bias can leave the problem as difficult as its unbiased counterpart, or make it substantially harder. The analysis characterizes when correcting biased feedback carries an additional learning cost.
summary.tldr: Regret bounds show how the geometry of bias estimation determines whether biased bandit feedback adds little difficulty or makes learning much harder.

title: The price of unfairness in linear bandits with biased feedback

abstract: Neural networks are known to exploit spurious artifacts (or shortcuts) that co-occur with a target label, exhibiting heuristic memorization. On the other hand, networks have been shown to memorize training examples, resulting in example-level memorization. These kinds of memorization impede generalization of networks beyond their training distributions. Detecting such memorization could be challenging, often requiring researchers to curate tailored test sets. In this work, we hypothesize—and subsequently show—that the diversity in the activation patterns of different neurons is reflective of model generalization and memorization. We quantify the diversity in the neural activations through information-theoretic measures and find support for our hypothesis in experiments spanning several natural language and vision tasks. Importantly, we discover that information organization points to the two forms of memorization, even for neural activations computed on unlabeled in-distribution examples. Lastly, we demonstrate the utility of our findings for the problem of model selection.

paragraphs: Neural networks can memorize in different ways: they may exploit shortcut features associated with labels, or memorize individual training examples. Both can undermine generalization beyond the training distribution. Detecting these behaviors often requires specially constructed test data. This paper investigates whether the network's internal activation patterns provide another source of evidence.

The authors hypothesize that diversity across neurons' activation patterns reflects both memorization and generalization. They quantify this diversity using information-theoretic measures and test the relationship across natural-language and vision tasks. The approach examines how information is organized within the network, connecting internal behavior with the kinds of patterns the model has learned.

The experiments support the proposed relationship and show that the information organization can indicate both shortcut-based and example-level memorization. These signals appear even when activations are computed on unlabeled examples from the training distribution. The authors also demonstrate usefulness for model selection. This suggests that internal activation measurements can help assess candidate models without always requiring labels or specially tailored test sets for detecting memorization.
summary.tldr: Information-theoretic measurements of neural activations reveal memorization patterns and help with model selection, even using unlabeled in-distribution examples.

title: Measures of Information Reflect Memorization Patterns

abstract: The training of neural networks by gradient descent methods is a cornerstone of the deep learning revolution. Yet, despite some recent progress, a complete theory explaining its success is still missing. This article presents, for orthogonal input vectors, a precise description of the gradient flow dynamics of training one-hidden layer ReLU neural networks for the mean squared error at small initialisation. In this setting, despite non-convexity, we show that the gradient flow converges to zero loss and characterise its implicit bias towards minimum variation norm. Furthermore, some interesting phenomena are highlighted: a quantitative description of the initial alignment phenomenon and a proof that the process follows a specific saddle to saddle dynamics.

paragraphs: This paper examines how a neural network moves through training, rather than only whether its final predictions are accurate. It studies gradient flow, the continuous-time form of gradient-based optimization, for a ReLU network with one hidden layer. The analysis specifically assumes orthogonal input vectors, squared-error loss, and small initialization.

Within this setting, the authors prove that training reaches zero loss despite the nonconvex optimization problem. They also characterize an implicit preference for solutions with minimum variation norm. This connects successful fitting to the type of solution selected by training: reaching a fit and choosing among possible fits are separate aspects of the dynamics.

The analysis further quantifies an early alignment phenomenon and proves that the trajectory follows a particular sequence of movements from saddle to saddle. These results offer a detailed account of intermediate training behavior, not just an endpoint guarantee. Their explanatory scope is the stated shallow-network setting with orthogonal inputs and small initialization.
summary.tldr: For shallow ReLU networks with orthogonal inputs and small initialization, the paper characterizes zero-loss convergence, implicit bias, and saddle-to-saddle training dynamics.

title: Gradient flow dynamics of shallow ReLU networks for square loss and orthogonal inputs

abstract: We consider a linear stochastic bandit problem involving $M$ agents that can collaborate via a central server to minimize regret. A fraction $\alpha$ of these agents are adversarial and can act arbitrarily, leading to the following tension: while collaboration can potentially reduce regret, it can also disrupt the process of learning due to adversaries. In this work, we provide a fundamental understanding of this tension by designing new algorithms that balance the exploration-exploitation trade-off via carefully constructed robust confidence intervals. We also complement our algorithms with tight analyses. First, we develop a robust collaborative phased elimination algorithm that achieves $\tilde{O}\left(\alpha+ 1/\sqrt{M}\right) \sqrt{dT}$ regret for each good agent; here, $d$ is the model-dimension and $T$ is the horizon. For small $\alpha$, our result thus reveals a clear benefit of collaboration despite adversaries. Using an information-theoretic argument, we then prove a matching lower bound, thereby providing the first set of tight, near-optimal regret bounds for collaborative linear bandits with adversaries. Furthermore, by leveraging recent advances in high-dimensional robust statistics, we significantly extend our algorithmic ideas and results to (i) the generalized linear bandit model that allows for non-linear observation maps; and (ii) the contextual bandit setting that allows for time-varying feature vectors.

paragraphs: In collaborative bandit learning, multiple agents share information through a central server while deciding which actions to try. Sharing can reduce the reward lost while learning, known as regret. But if a fraction of the agents can behave arbitrarily, the same communication can introduce misleading evidence. This paper quantifies that tension for linear stochastic bandits.

The authors construct robust confidence intervals and use them in a phased elimination algorithm. Its regret bound for each trustworthy agent scales, up to logarithmic factors, as the adversarial fraction plus the inverse square root of the number of agents, multiplied by the square root of model dimension times time horizon. When the adversarial fraction is small, the bound demonstrates a benefit from collaboration.

An information-theoretic lower bound matches the result up to the stated qualifications, establishing near-optimal guarantees. The authors also extend their ideas using robust statistics to generalized linear bandits and contextual bandits with changing feature vectors. The results explain both the learning gains available through cooperation and the cost imposed by adversarial participants.
summary.tldr: Robust collaborative bandit algorithms achieve near-optimal regret bounds that quantify when cooperation remains beneficial despite adversarial agents.

title: Collaborative Linear Bandits with Adversarial Agents: Near-Optimal Regret Bounds

abstract: Recent breakthroughs in the development of agents to solve challenging sequential decision making problems such as Go, StarCraft, or DOTA, have relied on both simulated environments and large-scale datasets. However, progress on this research has been hindered by the scarcity of open-sourced datasets and the prohibitive computational cost to work with them. Here we present the NetHack Learning Dataset (NLD), a large and highly-scalable dataset of trajectories from the popular game of NetHack, which is both extremely challenging for current methods and very fast to run. NLD consists of three parts: 10 billion state transitions from 1.5 million human trajectories collected on the NAO public NetHack server from 2009 to 2020; 3 billion state-action-score transitions from 100,000 trajectories collected from the symbolic bot winner of the NetHack Challenge 2021; and, accompanying code for users to record, load and stream any collection of such trajectories in a highly compressed form. We evaluate a wide range of existing algorithms for learning from demonstrations, showing that significant research advances are needed to fully leverage large-scale datasets for challenging sequential decision making tasks.

paragraphs: Learning agents for difficult sequential decisions often depends on both interactive environments and large collections of demonstrations. Access to suitable data and the cost of processing it can constrain research. This paper introduces the NetHack Learning Dataset, using a game that is challenging for current methods while being fast to run.

The dataset brings together human and automated play. Its human portion contains 10 billion state transitions from 1.5 million trajectories collected on the public NAO server between 2009 and 2020. Its bot portion contains 3 billion state-action-score transitions from 100,000 trajectories produced by the symbolic bot that won the NetHack Challenge 2021. Accompanying code supports recording, loading, and streaming trajectories in highly compressed form.

The authors evaluate a broad range of existing demonstration-learning algorithms on this resource. Their results indicate that substantial research advances are still needed to make full use of large datasets for difficult sequential decisions. The contribution therefore combines accessible data and processing tools with evidence of a continuing gap between having demonstrations at scale and learning effectively from them.
summary.tldr: The NetHack Learning Dataset supplies billions of human and bot transitions, exposing challenges in learning effectively from large demonstration datasets.

title: Dungeons and Data: A Large-Scale NetHack Dataset

abstract: We investigate the generalization capabilities of neural signed distance functions (SDFs) for learning 3D object representations for unseen and unlabeled point clouds. Existing methods can fit SDFs to a handful of object classes and boast fine detail or fast inference speeds, but do not generalize well to unseen shapes. We introduce a two-stage semi-supervised meta-learning approach that transfers shape priors from labeled to unlabeled data to reconstruct unseen object categories. The first stage uses an episodic training scheme to simulate training on unlabeled data and meta-learns initial shape priors. The second stage then introduces unlabeled data with disjoint classes in a semi-supervised scheme to diversify these priors and achieve generalization. We assess our method on both synthetic data and real collected point clouds. Experimental results and analysis validate that our approach outperforms existing neural SDF methods and is capable of robust zero-shot inference on 100+ unseen classes. Code can be found at https://github.com/princeton-computational-imaging/gensdf

paragraphs: This paper studies how neural signed distance functions can represent three-dimensional objects from unseen, unlabeled point clouds. The central challenge is transferring learned shape knowledge to new categories. Existing methods can offer detailed reconstructions or fast inference within a small collection of classes, yet struggle to generalize to unfamiliar shapes.

GenSDF addresses this through two stages of semi-supervised meta-learning. The first stage uses training episodes that simulate learning from unlabeled data, developing initial shape priors. The second stage introduces unlabeled examples from disjoint classes, broadening those priors. This arrangement transfers knowledge from labeled examples while exposing the model to additional categories without requiring labels for those examples.

The authors evaluate the approach on synthetic data and real collected point clouds. They report better performance than existing neural signed distance function methods and robust zero-shot inference across more than 100 unseen classes. The stated findings support the value of diversifying learned shape priors: the model can use its training experience to reconstruct categories beyond those for which labeled examples were provided.
summary.tldr: GenSDF combines two stages of semi-supervised meta-learning to reconstruct unfamiliar shapes, reporting robust zero-shot inference on over 100 unseen classes.

title: GenSDF: Two-Stage Learning of Generalizable Signed Distance Functions

abstract: Latent variable discovery is a central problem in data analysis with a broad range of applications in applied science.In this work, we consider data given as an invertible mixture of two statistically independent components, and assume that one of the components is observed while the other is hidden. Our goal is to recover the hidden component.For this purpose, we propose an autoencoder equipped with a discriminator.Unlike the standard nonlinear ICA problem, which was shown to be non-identifiable, in the special case of ICA we consider here, we show that our approach can recover the component of interest up to entropy-preserving transformation.We demonstrate the performance of the proposed approach in several tasks, including image synthesis, voice cloning, and fetal ECG extraction.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to recover a hidden component from data containing a mixture of two components. Its setting makes two central assumptions: the components are statistically independent, and the mixing process is invertible. One component is observed, while the other is hidden. That observed component supplies additional information for the recovery problem.

The authors propose an autoencoder equipped with a discriminator. They show that, in this special case of independent component analysis, their approach can recover the hidden component up to an entropy-preserving transformation. The qualification describes the recovery guarantee: it allows a transformed version of the component, rather than requiring its exact original form.

This result addresses a setting distinct from standard nonlinear independent component analysis, which is non-identifiable. The paper demonstrates the proposed approach on image synthesis, voice cloning, and fetal ECG extraction. Together, the theory and demonstrations show how observing one independent component can make hidden-component discovery possible under the stated mixing assumptions, across several different kinds of data.
summary.tldr: Given an invertible mixture of two independent components with one observed, the method can recover the hidden component up to an entropy-preserving transformation.

title: Discovery of Single Independent Latent Variable

abstract: AI systems are becoming increasingly intertwined with human life. In order to effectively collaborate with humans and ensure safety, AI systems need to be able to understand, interpret and predict human moral judgments and decisions. Human moral judgments are often guided by rules, but not always. A central challenge for AI safety is capturing the flexibility of the human moral mind — the ability to determine when a rule should be broken, especially in novel or unusual situations. In this paper, we present a novel challenge set consisting of moral exception question answering (MoralExceptQA) of cases that involve potentially permissible moral exceptions – inspired by recent moral psychology studies. Using a state-of-the-art large language model (LLM) as a basis, we propose a novel moral chain of thought (MoralCoT) prompting strategy that combines the strengths of LLMs with theories of moral reasoning developed in cognitive science to predict human moral judgments. MoralCoT outperforms seven existing LLMs by 6.2% F1, suggesting that modeling human reasoning might be necessary to capture the flexibility of the human moral mind. We also conduct a detailed error analysis to suggest directions for future work to improve AI safety using MoralExceptQA. Our data is open-sourced at https://huggingface.co/datasets/feradauto/MoralExceptQA and code at https://github.com/feradauto/MoralCoT.

paragraphs: Human moral judgments often follow rules while allowing exceptions in unusual circumstances. Predicting those exceptions is a challenge for systems intended to understand human decisions. This paper introduces MoralExceptQA, a question-answering challenge set inspired by moral psychology and focused on situations involving potentially permissible exceptions.

The authors also propose MoralCoT, a prompting strategy that combines a large language model with theories of moral reasoning from cognitive science. Its purpose is to predict human judgments by incorporating reasoning about moral exceptions into the prompting process. The dataset and method therefore address both how to evaluate this flexibility and how to encourage it in a model.

MoralCoT outperforms seven existing language models by a reported 6.2% F1. The authors interpret this as suggesting that modeling human reasoning might be necessary to capture moral flexibility; the result does not establish that necessity. A detailed error analysis identifies directions for further work. The study concerns predicting human moral judgments, so the measured improvement should be understood as better agreement on that task.
summary.tldr: MoralExceptQA and MoralCoT study moral exceptions, with cognitively informed prompting improving prediction of human judgments.

title: When to Make Exceptions: Exploring Language Models as Accounts of Human Moral Judgment

abstract: Label distribution can provide richer information about label polysemy than logical labels in multi-label learning. There are currently two strategies including LDL (label distribution learning) and LE (label enhancement) to predict label distributions. LDL requires experts to annotate instances with label distributions and learn a predictive mapping on such a training set. LE requires experts to annotate instances with logical labels and generates label distributions from them. However, LDL requires costly annotation, and the performance of the LE is unstable. In this paper, we study the problem of predicting label distribution from multi-label ranking which is a compromise w.r.t. annotation cost but has good guarantees for performance. On the one hand, we theoretically investigate the relation between multi-label ranking and label distribution. We define the notion of EAE (expected approximation error) to quantify the quality of an annotation, give the bounds of EAE for multi-label ranking, and derive the optimal range of label distribution corresponding to a particular multi-label ranking. On the other hand, we propose a framework of label distribution predicting from multi-label ranking via conditional Dirichlet mixtures. This framework integrates the processes of recovering and learning label distributions end-to-end and allows us to easily encode our knowledge about current tasks by a scoring function. Finally, we implement extensive experiments to validate our proposal.

paragraphs: A label distribution describes degrees of relevance across labels, offering richer information than simple yes-or-no assignments. Directly collecting these distributions is costly, while reconstructing them from logical labels can be unstable. This paper investigates ranked labels as an intermediate form of annotation that balances information and annotation effort.

The authors theoretically relate a ranking to the distributions it can represent. They define expected approximation error to measure annotation quality, derive bounds for rankings, and identify an optimal range of distributions corresponding to a given ranking. This analysis characterizes what information ranked annotations can provide about label relevance.

The proposed learning framework uses conditional Dirichlet mixtures to recover distributions from rankings while learning to predict them end to end. A scoring function allows task knowledge to enter the process. Extensive experiments validate the proposal. The contribution brings together a theoretical account of ranking quality and a practical method for turning that form of supervision into distributional predictions.
summary.tldr: The paper uses ranked labels as intermediate supervision for learning label distributions, supported by approximation bounds and an end-to-end mixture model.

title: Predicting Label Distribution from Multi-label Ranking

abstract: Quantization compresses models to low bits for efficient inferences which has received increasing attentions. However, existing approaches focused on balanced datasets, while imbalanced data is pervasive in the real world. Therefore, in this study, we investigate the realistic problem, quantization on class-imbalanced data. We observe from the analytical results that quantizing imbalanced data tends to obtain a large error due to the differences between separate class distributions, which leads to a significant accuracy loss. To address this issue, we propose a novel quantization framework, Class Imbalanced Quantization (ClimbQ) that focuses on diminishing the inter-class heterogeneity for quantization error reduction. ClimbQ first scales the variance of each class distribution and then projects data through the new distributions to the same space for quantization. To guarantee the homogeneity of class variances after the ClimbQ process, we examine the quantized features and derive that the homogeneity satisfies when data size for each class is restricted (bounded). Accordingly, we design a Homogeneous Variance Loss (HomoVar Loss) which reweights the data losses of each class based on the bounded data sizes to satisfy the homogeneity of class variances. Extensive experiments on class-imbalanced and benchmark balanced datasets reveal that ClimbQ outperforms the state-of-the-art quantization techniques, especially on highly imbalanced data.

This paper examines what happens when the training data contains very different numbers of examples from different classes. Its analysis finds that differences between class distributions can produce large quantization errors and substantial accuracy loss in this setting.

title: ClimbQ: Class Imbalanced Quantization Enabling Robustness on Efficient Inferences

abstract: In this paper, we propose an autonomous information seeking visual question answering framework, AVIS. Our method leverages a Large Language Model (LLM) to dynamically strategize the utilization of external tools and to investigate their outputs via tree search, thereby acquiring the indispensable knowledge needed to provide answers to the posed questions. Responding to visual questions that necessitate external knowledge, such as "What event is commemorated by the building depicted in this image?", is a complex task. This task presents a combinatorial search space that demands a sequence of actions, including invoking APIs, analyzing their responses, and making informed decisions. We conduct a user study to collect a variety of instances of human decision-making when faced with this task. This data is then used to design a system comprised of three components: an LLM-powered planner that dynamically determines which tool to use next, an LLM-powered reasoner that analyzes and extracts key information from the tool outputs, and a working memory component that retains the acquired information throughout the process. The collected user behavior serves as a guide for our system in two key ways. First, we create a transition graph by analyzing the sequence of decisions made by users. This graph delineates distinct states and confines the set of actions available at each state. Second, we use examples of user decision-making to provide our LLM-powered planner and reasoner with relevant contextual instances, enhancing their capacity to make informed decisions. We show that AVIS achieves state-of-the-art results on knowledge-based visual question answering benchmarks such as Infoseek and OK-VQA.

AVIS achieves reported state-of-the-art results on knowledge-based visual question answering benchmarks including Infoseek and OK-VQA. These findings support the usefulness of coordinated information seeking for visual questions that require external knowledge.
summary.tldr: AVIS uses human-informed planning, external tools, and working memory to answer visual questions requiring outside knowledge.

title: AVIS: Autonomous Visual Information Seeking with Large Language Model Agent

abstract: Reasoning system dynamics is one of the most important analytical approaches for many scientific studies. With the initial state of a system as input, the recent graph neural networks (GNNs)-based methods are capable of predicting the future state distant in time with high accuracy. Although these methods have diverse designs in modeling the coordinates and interacting forces of the system, we show that they actually share a common paradigm that learns the integration of the velocity over the interval between the initial and terminal coordinates. However, their integrand is constant w.r.t. time. Inspired by this observation, we propose a new approach to predict the integration based on several velocity estimations with Newton–Cotes formulas and prove its effectiveness theoretically. Extensive experiments on several benchmarks empirically demonstrate consistent and significant improvement compared with the state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Predicting a dynamic system's future state requires accounting for how it changes over the intervening time. Graph neural networks have achieved accurate predictions even for distant future states. This paper examines a shared structure beneath otherwise different approaches to modeling system coordinates and interacting forces.

The authors show that these approaches can be viewed as learning an integral of velocity between initial and final coordinates. In the methods they analyze, however, the integrated quantity is constant with respect to time. Their proposed approach instead combines several velocity estimates using Newton–Cotes formulas, allowing the integration calculation to incorporate more than one estimate across the interval.

The paper provides a theoretical argument for the method's effectiveness and reports consistent, significant improvements over state-of-the-art approaches on several benchmarks. The contribution concerns how learned velocity information becomes a prediction of future coordinates. By revisiting that integration step, the authors identify a shared simplification in existing designs and provide a numerically motivated way to improve dynamic prediction.
summary.tldr: Newton–Cotes graph networks improve dynamic-system prediction by integrating several velocity estimates instead of a time-constant integrand.

title: Newton–Cotes Graph Neural Networks: On the Time Evolution of Dynamic Systems

abstract: Conversational generative AI has demonstrated remarkable promise for empowering biomedical practitioners, but current investigations focus on unimodal text. Multimodal conversational AI has seen rapid progress by leveraging billions of image-text pairs from the public web, but such general-domain vision-language models still lack sophistication in understanding and conversing about biomedical images. In this paper, we propose a cost-efficient approach for training a vision-language conversational assistant that can answer open-ended research questions of biomedical images. The key idea is to leverage a large-scale, broad-coverage biomedical figure-caption dataset extracted from PubMed Central, use GPT-4 to self-instruct open-ended instruction-following data from the captions, and then fine-tune a large general-domain vision-language model using a novel curriculum learning method. Specifically, the model first learns to align biomedical vocabulary using the figure-caption pairs as is, then learns to master open-ended conversational semantics using GPT-4 generated instruction-following data, broadly mimicking how a layperson gradually acquires biomedical knowledge. This enables us to train a Large Language and Vision Assistant for BioMedicine (LLaVA-Med) in less than 15 hours (with eight A100s). LLaVA-Med exhibits excellent multimodal conversational capability and can follow open-ended instruction to assist with inquiries about a biomedical image. On three standard biomedical visual question answering datasets, LLaVA-Med outperforms previous supervised state-of-the-art on certain metrics. To facilitate biomedical multimodal research, we will release our instruction-following data and the LLaVA-Med model.

title: LLaVA-Med: Training a Large Language-and-Vision Assistant for Biomedicine in One Day

abstract: Extracting a stable and compact representation of the environment is crucial for efficient reinforcement learning in high-dimensional, noisy, and non-stationary environments. Different categories of information coexist in such environments -- how to effectively extract and disentangle the information remains a challenging problem. In this paper, we propose IFactor, a general framework to model four distinct categories of latent state variables that capture various aspects of information within the RL system, based on their interactions with actions and rewards. Our analysis establishes block-wise identifiability of these latent variables, which not only provides a stable and compact representation but also discloses that all reward-relevant factors are significant for policy learning. We further present a practical approach to learning the world model with identifiable blocks, ensuring the removal of redundancies but retaining minimal and sufficient information for policy optimization. Experiments in synthetic worlds demonstrate that our method accurately identifies the ground-truth latent variables, substantiating our theoretical findings. Moreover, experiments in variants of the DeepMind Control Suite and RoboDesk showcase the superior performance of our approach over baselines.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning agent needs a useful account of its environment, but high-dimensional observations can mix task-relevant information with noise and changing background factors. IFactor organizes the hidden state into four categories according to how its variables interact with actions and rewards. This gives the world model a structured way to separate different kinds of information.

The paper establishes block-wise identifiability for these latent variables. This supports recovering meaningful groups of hidden information rather than relying on an arbitrary undifferentiated representation. The analysis also shows that all reward-relevant factors matter for policy learning. The practical learning approach removes redundancy while retaining minimal, sufficient information for policy optimization.

Together, these results connect representation structure with useful control: separating information according to actions and rewards can support both interpretable latent recovery and stronger learned policies.
summary.tldr: IFactor separates world-model states into identifiable blocks organized by actions and rewards, improving representation recovery and evaluated control performance.

title: Learning World Models with Identifiable Factorization

abstract: Recent advancements in vision foundation models (VFMs) have opened up new possibilities for versatile and efficient visual perception. In this work, we introduce Seal, a novel framework that harnesses VFMs for segmenting diverse automotive point cloud sequences. Seal exhibits three appealing properties: i) Scalability: VFMs are directly distilled into point clouds, obviating the need for annotations in either 2D or 3D during pretraining. ii) Consistency: Spatial and temporal relationships are enforced at both the camera-to-LiDAR and point-to-segment regularization stages, facilitating cross-modal representation learning. iii) Generalizability: Seal enables knowledge transfer in an off-the-shelf manner to downstream tasks involving diverse point clouds, including those from real/synthetic, low/high-resolution, large/small-scale, and clean/corrupted datasets. Extensive experiments conducted on eleven different point cloud datasets showcase the effectiveness and superiority of Seal. Notably, Seal achieves a remarkable 45.0% mIoU on nuScenes after linear probing, surpassing random initialization by 36.9% mIoU and outperforming prior arts by 6.1% mIoU. Moreover, Seal demonstrates significant performance gains over existing methods across 20 different few-shot fine-tuning tasks on all eleven tested point cloud datasets. The code is available at this link.

paragraphs: Seal transfers knowledge from vision foundation models into models for segmenting automotive point-cloud sequences. Its pretraining procedure directly distills visual knowledge into point clouds without requiring either 2D or 3D annotations. This offers a way to obtain useful point-cloud representations from existing visual models.

The framework enforces spatial and temporal relationships at two stages: transferring information from cameras to LiDAR and regularizing relationships between points and segments. These constraints support consistent learning across sensing modalities and across a sequence. The resulting representations can transfer to downstream point clouds spanning real and synthetic data, different resolutions and scales, and clean or corrupted inputs.

Experiments cover eleven point-cloud datasets. With linear probing, Seal reaches 45.0% mIoU on nuScenes, with reported margins of 36.9 over random initialization and 6.1 over prior approaches in mIoU. It also improves results across 20 few-shot fine-tuning tasks on the tested datasets. These findings support the usefulness of the transferred representations both with limited downstream adaptation and when only a small amount of task-specific data is available.
summary.tldr: Seal distills vision foundation models into point-cloud representations without pretraining annotations and improves segmentation across diverse datasets.

title: Segment Any Point Cloud Sequences by Distilling Vision Foundation Models

abstract: Training on large-scale datasets can boost the performance of video instance segmentation while the annotated datasets for VIS are hard to scale up due to the high labor cost. What we possess are numerous isolated filed-specific datasets, thus, it is appealing to jointly train models across the aggregation of datasets to enhance data volume and diversity. However, due to the heterogeneity in category space, as mask precision increase with the data volume, simply utilizing multiple datasets will dilute the attention of models on different taxonomy. Thus, increasing the data scale and enriching taxonomy space while improving classification precision is important. In this work, we analyze that providing extra taxonomy information can help models concentrate on specific taxonomy, and propose our model named Taxonomy-aware Multi-dataset Joint Training for Video Instance Segmentation (TMT-VIS) to address this vital challenge. Specifically, we design a two-stage taxonomy aggregation module that first compiles taxonomy information from input videos and then aggregates these taxonomy priors into instance queries before the transformer decoder. We conduct extensive experimental evaluations on four popular and challenging benchmarks, including YouTube-VIS 2019, YouTube-VIS 2021, OVIS, and UVO. Our model shows significant improvement over the baseline solutions, and sets new state-of-the-art records on all these benchmarks. These appealing and encouraging results demonstrate the effectiveness and generality of our proposed approach. The code and trained models will be publicly available.

paragraphs: Video instance segmentation can benefit from more annotated data, but creating those annotations requires substantial labor. Combining existing datasets offers greater volume and diversity, yet their category systems differ. The paper identifies a tension: additional data can improve object masks while making it harder for a model to focus on the appropriate categories.

TMT-VIS addresses this with explicit taxonomy information. A two-stage module first compiles category-related information from the input video, then incorporates those taxonomy priors into instance queries before the transformer decoder. This gives the model category context at the point where it prepares to produce its instance-level outputs.

The authors evaluate the method on YouTube-VIS 2019, YouTube-VIS 2021, OVIS, and UVO. They report significant improvements over baseline solutions and new state-of-the-art results on all four benchmarks. The findings support taxonomy-aware joint training as a way to benefit from multiple datasets while maintaining attention to their category distinctions, connecting increased training diversity with the classification demands of video instance segmentation.
summary.tldr: TMT-VIS injects taxonomy information into instance queries to improve video instance segmentation when training jointly across datasets.

title: TMT-VIS: Taxonomy-aware Multi-dataset Joint Training for Video Instance Segmentation

abstract: In this paper, we explore the structure of the penultimate Gram matrix in deep neural networks, which contains the pairwise inner products of outputs corresponding to a batch of inputs. In several architectures it has been observed that this Gram matrix becomes degenerate with depth at initialization, which dramatically slows training. Normalization layers, such as batch or layer normalization, play a pivotal role in preventing the rank collapse issue. Despite promising advances, the existing theoretical results do not extend to layer normalization, which is widely used in transformers, and can not quantitatively characterize the role of non-linear activations. To bridge this gap, we prove that layer normalization, in conjunction with activation layers, biases the Gram matrix of a multilayer perceptron towards the identity matrix at an exponential rate with depth at initialization. We quantify this rate using the Hermite expansion of the activation function.

paragraphs: This paper studies the geometry of neural-network representations at initialization through the penultimate Gram matrix. That matrix records pairwise inner products between representations of inputs in a batch. In several architectures, it becomes degenerate as depth increases, a form of rank collapse associated with dramatically slower training.

Normalization can prevent this collapse, but existing theory did not cover layer normalization or quantitatively explain the contribution of nonlinear activations. The authors address both gaps for multilayer perceptrons. They prove that layer normalization combined with activation layers biases the Gram matrix toward the identity at an exponential rate as depth increases.

An identity-like Gram matrix means the batch representations have controlled self-inner-products and small cross-inner-products, giving a concrete geometric interpretation to the result. The authors quantify the rate through the activation function's Hermite expansion. This connects the choice of activation to the strength of the effect, with the stated theorem concerning representation geometry at initialization in the analyzed multilayer perceptron.
summary.tldr: The paper quantifies how layer normalization and activations push a multilayer perceptron's Gram matrix toward identity exponentially with depth at initialization.

title: On the impact of activation and normalization in obtaining isometric embeddings at initialization

abstract: Explicit finite-sample statistical guarantees on model performance are an important ingredient in responsible machine learning. Previous work has focused mainly on bounding either the expected loss of a predictor or the probability that an individual prediction will incur a loss value in a specified range. However, for many high-stakes applications it is crucial to understand and control the \textit{dispersion} of a loss distribution, or the extent to which different members of a population experience unequal effects of algorithmic decisions. We initiate the study of distribution-free control of statistical dispersion measures with societal implications and propose a simple yet flexible framework that allows us to handle a much richer class of statistical functionals beyond previous work. Our methods are verified through experiments in toxic comment detection, medical imaging, and film recommendation.

However, for many high-stakes applications it is crucial to understand and control the \textit{dispersion} of a loss distribution, or the extent to which different members of a population experience unequal effects of algorithmic decisions. We initiate the study of distribution-free control of statistical dispersion measures with societal implications and propose a simple yet flexible framework that allows us to handle a much richer class of statistical functionals beyond previous work. Our methods are verified through experiments in toxic comment detection, medical imaging, and film recommendation.

paragraphs: An average prediction loss describes overall performance but does not reveal how unevenly errors affect a population. This paper focuses on dispersion: the spread of losses experienced by different people. That perspective matters when similar average performance can coexist with different degrees of inequality in the consequences of algorithmic decisions.

The authors initiate a framework for controlling statistical dispersion with distribution-free, finite-sample guarantees. Earlier approaches mainly bounded expected loss or the probability that an individual prediction's loss falls within a specified range. The proposed framework accommodates a richer collection of statistical functionals, extending the kinds of properties of a loss distribution that can be controlled.

Experiments examine the methods in toxic comment detection, medical imaging, and film recommendation. These applications provide empirical verification across different prediction settings. The contribution is a statistical way to reason about unequal effects alongside overall performance: it brings the variability of losses into the set of quantities for which explicit guarantees can be sought.
summary.tldr: The paper introduces a distribution-free framework for controlling loss dispersion, extending statistical guarantees to unequal effects across a population.

title: Distribution-Free Statistical Dispersion Control for Societal Applications

abstract: Permutation matrices play a key role in matching and assignment problems across the fields, especially in computer vision and robotics. However, memory for explicitly representing permutation matrices grows quadratically with the size of the problem, prohibiting large problem instances. In this work, we propose to tackle the curse of dimensionality of large permutation matrices by approximating them using low-rank matrix factorization, followed by a nonlinearity. To this end, we rely on the Kissing number theory to infer the minimal rank required for representing a permutation matrix of a given size, which is significantly smaller than the problem size. This leads to a drastic reduction in computation and memory costs, e.g., up to $3$ orders of magnitude less memory for a problem of size $n=20000$, represented using $8.4\times10^5$ elements in two small matrices instead of using a single huge matrix with $4\times 10^8$ elements. The proposed representation allows for accurate representations of large permutation matrices, which in turn enables handling large problems that would have been infeasible otherwise. We demonstrate the applicability and merits of the proposed approach through a series of experiments on a range of problems that involve predicting permutation matrices, from linear and quadratic assignment to shape matching problems.

paragraphs: Permutation matrices encode one-to-one assignments and appear in matching problems in vision and robotics. Their explicit storage grows quadratically with problem size, making large instances expensive. This paper proposes representing them through two smaller matrices whose low-rank product is followed by a nonlinear transformation.

The authors use kissing number theory to infer the minimum rank needed for a permutation matrix of a given size under this representation. That rank can be much smaller than the assignment problem itself. The nonlinear step is a key part of the proposed construction, connecting compact factors to accurate representations of large permutations.

For a problem of size 20,000, the abstract gives a representation using 840,000 elements instead of 400 million. This illustrates the substantial memory reduction that makes otherwise infeasible instances manageable. Experiments cover linear assignment, quadratic assignment, and shape matching, demonstrating the representation’s applicability to several settings where models must predict large permutation matrices.
summary.tldr: Low-rank factors followed by a nonlinearity compactly represent large permutation matrices, substantially reducing memory and computation.

title: Kissing to Find a Match: Efficient Low-Rank Permutation Representation

abstract: Recently, artificial intelligence for drug discovery has raised increasing interest in both machine learning and chemistry domains. The fundamental building block for drug discovery is molecule geometry and thus, the molecule's geometrical representation is the main bottleneck to better utilize machine learning techniques for drug discovery. In this work, we propose a pretraining method for molecule joint auto-encoding (MoleculeJAE). MoleculeJAE can learn both the 2D bond (topology) and 3D conformation (geometry) information, and a diffusion process model is applied to mimic the augmented trajectories of such two modalities, based on which, MoleculeJAE will learn the inherent chemical structure in a self-supervised manner. Thus, the pretrained geometrical representation in MoleculeJAE is expected to benefit downstream geometry-related tasks. Empirically, MoleculeJAE proves its effectiveness by reaching state-of-the-art performance on 15 out of 20 tasks by comparing it with 12 competitive baselines.

paragraphs: A molecular representation needs to capture both which atoms are bonded and how those atoms are arranged in space. This paper identifies geometric representation as a bottleneck for applying machine learning to drug discovery. Molecule Joint Auto-Encoding, or MoleculeJAE, is a pretraining method designed to learn from both forms of molecular information together.

The method combines two-dimensional bond topology with three-dimensional conformation. It uses a diffusion process to model augmented trajectories of these two modalities and learns from those trajectories in a self-supervised manner. The aim is to capture inherent chemical structure in a representation that can subsequently support tasks where molecular geometry matters.

The authors evaluate MoleculeJAE against 12 competitive baselines across 20 tasks and report state-of-the-art performance on 15. This provides empirical support for the proposed joint pretraining approach across the tested tasks. The broader motivation is to make molecular features more informative by learning connectivity and spatial arrangement together, with the expectation that the resulting representation benefits downstream geometry-related prediction.
summary.tldr: MoleculeJAE jointly pretrains on molecular bonds and three-dimensional conformations through diffusion trajectories, achieving state-of-the-art results on 15 of 20 tasks.

title: Molecule Joint Auto-Encoding: Trajectory Pretraining with 2D and 3D Diffusion

abstract: In many search applications related to passage retrieval, text entailment, and subgraph search, the query and each 'document' is a set of elements, with a document being relevant if it contains the query. These elements are not represented by atomic IDs, but by embedded representations, thereby extending set containment to *soft* set containment. Recent applications address soft set containment by encoding sets into fixed-size vectors and checking for elementwise *vector* *dominance*. This 0/1 property can be relaxed to an asymmetric *hinge* *distance* for scoring and ranking candidate documents. Here we focus on data-sensitive, trainable indices for fast retrieval of relevant documents. Existing LSH methods are designed for mostly symmetric or few simple asymmetric distance functions, which are not suitable for hinge distance. Instead, we transform hinge distance into a proposed *dominance* *similarity* measure, to which we then apply a Fourier transform, thereby expressing dominance similarity as an expectation of inner products of functions in the frequency domain. Next, we approximate the expectation with an importance-sampled estimate. The overall consequence is that now we can use a traditional LSH, but in the frequency domain. To ensure that the LSH uses hash bits efficiently, we learn hash functions that are sensitive to both corpus and query distributions, mapped to the frequency domain. Our experiments show that the proposed asymmetric dominance similarity is critical to the targeted applications, and that our LSH, which we call FourierHashNet, provides a better query time vs. retrieval quality trade-off, compared to several baselines. Both the Fourier transform and the trainable hash codes contribute to performance gains.

paragraphs: Some retrieval tasks ask whether a document contains the information in a query, rather than whether the two are simply similar. When set elements are represented by embeddings, this becomes soft set containment. Its direction matters: a document may contain a query without the query containing the document. Standard hashing methods are poorly suited to the resulting asymmetric hinge distance.

The paper converts hinge distance into a dominance similarity and applies a Fourier transform. This expresses similarity as an expectation of inner products in the frequency domain, which the method approximates using importance sampling. The transformation makes traditional locality-sensitive hashing applicable to this otherwise awkward retrieval objective.

The resulting system, FourierHashNet, learns hash functions using both query and document distributions so that its hash bits are used effectively. Experiments show a better tradeoff between query time and retrieval quality than several baselines. They also indicate that asymmetric dominance similarity matters for the target applications, and that both the Fourier transformation and learned hash codes contribute to the gains.
summary.tldr: FourierHashNet transforms asymmetric soft-containment similarity into a frequency-domain form that supports efficient learned hashing.

title: Locality Sensitive Hashing in Fourier Frequency Domain For Soft Set Containment Search

abstract: We address the challenge of generating fair and unbiased image retrieval results given neutral textual queries (with no explicit gender or race connotations), while maintaining the utility (performance) of the underlying vision-language (VL) model. Previous methods aim to disentangle learned representations of images and text queries from gender and racial characteristics. However, we show these are inadequate at alleviating bias for the desired equal representation result, as there usually exists test-time bias in the target retrieval set. So motivated, we introduce a straightforward technique, Post-hoc Bias Mitigation (PBM), that post-processes the outputs from the pre-trained vision-language model. We evaluate our algorithm on real-world image search datasets, Occupation 1 and 2, as well as two large-scale image-text datasets, MS-COCO and Flickr30k. Our approach achieves the lowest bias, compared with various existing bias-mitigation methods, in text-based image retrieval result while maintaining satisfactory retrieval performance. The source code is publicly available at \url{https://github.com/timqqt/Fair_Text_based_Image_Retrieval}.

The source code is publicly available at \url{https://github.com/timqqt/Fair_Text_based_Image_Retrieval}.

paragraphs: A neutral text query can still return image results with unequal gender or racial representation. This paper studies how to reduce that imbalance while keeping search results useful. Its fairness objective concerns equal representation in the retrieved results, even when the query itself contains no explicit demographic connotations.

Earlier approaches try to remove gender and race information from the image and text representations learned by a vision-language model. The authors show that this can be insufficient because the image collection being searched may itself contain test-time bias. They introduce Post-hoc Bias Mitigation, or PBM, which adjusts the outputs of an already trained vision-language model.

Evaluation uses the Occupation 1 and 2 image-search datasets and the MS-COCO and Flickr30k image-text datasets. PBM achieves the lowest reported bias among the compared mitigation methods while maintaining satisfactory retrieval performance. The findings highlight the target retrieval collection as an important source of unequal representation and support output-level adjustment as a practical way to address it.
summary.tldr: PBM post-processes vision-language search outputs to reduce demographic imbalance caused by test-time retrieval data while maintaining satisfactory search performance.

title: Mitigating Test-Time Bias for Fair Image Retrieval

abstract: Score-based diffusion models (SBDMs) have achieved state-of-the-art results in image generation. In this paper, we propose a Non-isotropic Gaussian Diffusion Model (NGDM) for image editing, which requires editing the source image while preserving the image regions irrelevant to the editing task. We construct NGDM by adding independent Gaussian noises with different variances to different image pixels. Instead of specifically training the NGDM, we rectify the NGDM into an isotropic Gaussian diffusion model with different pixels having different total forward diffusion time. We propose to reverse the diffusion by designing a sampling method that starts at different time for different pixels for denoising to generate images using the pre-trained isotropic Gaussian diffusion model. Experimental results show that NGDM achieves state-of-the-art performance for image editing tasks, considering the trade-off between the fidelity to the source image and alignment with the desired editing target.

We construct NGDM by adding independent Gaussian noises with different variances to different image pixels. Instead of specifically training the NGDM, we rectify the NGDM into an isotropic Gaussian diffusion model with different pixels having different total forward diffusion time. We propose to reverse the diffusion by designing a sampling method that starts at different time for different pixels for denoising to generate images using the pre-trained isotropic Gaussian diffusion model. paragraphs: Image editing must balance two goals: changing the requested content and preserving parts of the source image unrelated to the edit. This paper approaches that balance by varying the amount of Gaussian noise added across pixels. Its non-isotropic diffusion model gives different pixels independent noise with different variances, rather than treating the whole image uniformly.

The central construction avoids training a dedicated model for this unequal-noise process. Instead, the authors reformulate it using an isotropic Gaussian diffusion model in which different pixels have different total forward diffusion times. Their reverse sampling procedure begins denoising different pixels at different times, allowing an already trained isotropic model to generate the edited image.

This matters because spatially varying noise becomes a way to control editing while reusing a pretrained diffusion model. The reported experiments achieve state-of-the-art image-editing performance when judged by the trade-off between resemblance to the source and agreement with the desired edit. That result concerns the balance between these objectives, rather than claiming that every edit preserves all source details perfectly.
summary.tldr: Pixel-specific noise levels and denoising start times let a pretrained diffusion model balance targeted image edits with source-image preservation.

title: Constructing Non-isotropic Gaussian Diffusion Model Using Isotropic Gaussian Diffusion Model for Image Editing

abstract: We consider nonconvex stochastic optimization problems in the asynchronous centralized distributed setup where the communication times from workers to a server can not be ignored, and the computation and communication times are potentially different for all workers. Using an unbiassed compression technique, we develop a new method—Shadowheart SGD—that provably improves the time complexities of all previous centralized methods. Moreover, we show that the time complexity of Shadowheart SGD is optimal in the family of centralized methods with compressed communication. We also consider the bidirectional setup, where broadcasting from the server to the workers is non-negligible, and develop a corresponding method.
originalAbstract: We consider nonconvex stochastic optimization problems in the asynchronous centralized distributed setup where the communication times from workers to a server can not be ignored, and the computation and communication times are potentially different for all workers. Using an unbiassed compression technique, we develop a new method—Shadowheart SGD—that provably improves the time complexities of all previous centralized methods. Moreover, we show that the time complexity of Shadowheart SGD is optimal in the family of centralized methods with compressed communication. We also consider the bidirectional setup, where broadcasting from the server to the workers is non-negligible, and develop a corresponding method.

paragraphs: Distributed optimization depends on how quickly workers compute updates and communicate them to a central server. Shadowheart SGD studies a setting where communication takes meaningful time and each worker may have different computation and communication speeds. The optimization problems are stochastic and nonconvex, and the workers operate asynchronously.

The method uses unbiased compression to reduce communication while retaining correctness in expectation for the compressed quantities. Its analysis explicitly includes both worker computation and communication delays. The authors prove improved time complexity over previous centralized methods, addressing elapsed time in a heterogeneous system rather than treating communication as a negligible part of optimization.

They also prove that Shadowheart SGD’s time complexity is optimal within the family of centralized methods using compressed communication. That family defines the scope of the optimality claim. Finally, they examine bidirectional communication, where the server’s broadcasts to workers also incur substantial delays, and develop a corresponding method. The paper therefore covers both costly worker-to-server updates and a broader setting with costly communication in both directions.
summary.tldr: Shadowheart SGD achieves provably optimal time complexity within centralized methods with compressed communication under heterogeneous worker speeds and communication delays.

title: Shadowheart SGD: Distributed Asynchronous SGD with Optimal Time Complexity Under Arbitrary Computation and Communication Heterogeneity

abstract: We introduce FindingEmo, a new image dataset containing annotations for 25k images, specifically tailored to Emotion Recognition. Contrary to existing datasets, it focuses on complex scenes depicting multiple people in various naturalistic, social settings, with images being annotated as a whole, thereby going beyond the traditional focus on faces or single individuals. Annotated dimensions include Valence, Arousal and Emotion label, with annotations gathered using Prolific. Together with the annotations, we release the list of URLs pointing to the original images, as well as all associated source code.

Contrary to existing datasets, it focuses on complex scenes depicting multiple people in various naturalistic, social settings, with images being annotated as a whole, thereby going beyond the traditional focus on faces or single individuals. Annotated dimensions include Valence, Arousal and Emotion label, with annotations gathered using Prolific. Together with the annotations, we release the list of URLs pointing to the original images, as well as all associated source code.

paragraphs: FindingEmo is a dataset for studying emotion recognition in complex social images. It contains annotations for 25,000 images and focuses on naturalistic settings with multiple people. The main contribution is the choice of what receives an emotion annotation: each image is judged as a whole, extending beyond the familiar focus on individual faces or single people.

The annotations cover three dimensions: valence, arousal, and an emotion label. Valence describes the positive or negative character of an emotional impression, while arousal describes its level of activation. Including these dimensions alongside a categorical label provides several ways to describe the emotional character assigned to an entire scene.

Annotations were gathered through Prolific. The release includes those annotations, URLs pointing to the original images, and the associated source code. This makes the dataset a resource for research that treats emotion recognition as a scene-level task. Its distinctive emphasis is on the overall emotional impression of multi-person social settings, rather than assigning a separate emotional judgment to each depicted individual.
summary.tldr: FindingEmo provides whole-image emotion annotations for 25,000 images featuring complex, naturalistic social scenes.

title: FindingEmo: An Image Dataset for Emotion Recognition in the Wild

abstract: Frequently, the burgeoning field of black-box optimization encounters challenges due to a limited understanding of the mechanisms of the objective function. To address such problems, in this work we focus on the deterministic concept of Order Oracle, which only utilizes order access between function values (possibly with some bounded noise), but without assuming access to their values. As theoretical results, we propose a new approach to create non-accelerated optimization algorithms (obtained by integrating Order Oracle into existing optimization “tools”) in non-convex, convex, and strongly convex settings that are as good as both SOTA coordinate algorithms with first-order oracle and SOTA algorithms with Order Oracle up to logarithm factor. Moreover, using the proposed approach, _we provide the first accelerated optimization algorithm using the Order Oracle_. And also, using an already different approach we provide the asymptotic convergence of _the first algorithm with the stochastic Order Oracle concept_. Finally, our theoretical results demonstrate effectiveness of proposed algorithms through numerical experiments.

As theoretical results, we propose a new approach to create non-accelerated optimization algorithms (obtained by integrating Order Oracle into existing optimization “tools”) in non-convex, convex, and strongly convex settings that are as good as both SOTA coordinate algorithms with first-order oracle and SOTA algorithms with Order Oracle up to logarithm factor. Finally, our theoretical results demonstrate effectiveness of proposed algorithms through numerical experiments.

paragraphs: Black-box optimization can require searching for a good solution without knowing how the objective function works. This paper studies an especially restricted source of feedback: an Order Oracle, which tells an algorithm how two objective values compare without revealing either value. The deterministic formulation also allows some bounded noise in those comparisons.

The authors develop a way to incorporate this comparison feedback into existing optimization tools. They obtain non-accelerated algorithms for non-convex, convex, and strongly convex problems. Their theoretical performance matches state-of-the-art coordinate methods using first-order information and existing Order Oracle methods up to a logarithmic factor. This comparison establishes how competitive optimization can remain despite receiving substantially less direct information about the objective.

The central contribution is what the authors identify as the first accelerated optimization algorithm using an Order Oracle. A separate approach provides an algorithm for stochastic order feedback and establishes its asymptotic convergence. Numerical experiments support the proposed methods. The results distinguish two advances: acceleration with comparison-based feedback, and convergence when the comparison mechanism itself is stochastic.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes accelerated optimization using only comparisons of objective values and separately proves convergence for a stochastic comparison oracle.

title: Acceleration Exists! Optimization Problems When Oracle Can Only Compare Objective Function Values

abstract: Federated learning faces challenges due to the heterogeneity in data volumes and distributions at different clients, which can compromise model generalization ability to various distributions. Existing approaches to address this issue based on group distributionally robust optimization (GDRO) often lead to high communication and sample complexity.To this end, this work introduces algorithms tailored for communication-efficient Federated Group Distributionally Robust Optimization (FGDRO). Our contributions are threefold: Firstly, we introduce the FGDRO-CVaR algorithm, which optimizes the average top-K losses while reducing communication complexity to $O(1/\epsilon^4)$, where $\epsilon$ denotes the desired precision level. Secondly, our FGDRO-KL algorithm is crafted to optimize KL regularized FGDRO, cutting communication complexity to $O(1/\epsilon^3)$. Lastly, we propose FGDRO-KL-Adam to utilize Adam-type local updates in FGDRO-KL, which not only maintains a communication cost of $O(1/\epsilon^3)$ but also shows potential to surpass SGD-type local steps in practical applications.The effectiveness of our algorithms has been demonstrated on a variety of real-world tasks, including natural language processing and computer vision.

Our contributions are threefold: Firstly, we introduce the FGDRO-CVaR algorithm, which optimizes the average top-K losses while reducing communication complexity to $O(1/\epsilon^4)$, where $\epsilon$ denotes the desired precision level.
