paragraphs: MOSAIC studies how a platform can combine advertisers' preferences over language-model responses while also considering user satisfaction. Advertisers may want different outcomes from users and may misrepresent their preferences to gain influence. The paper treats this as a mechanism-design problem, where the rules governing influence and payment must account for strategically self-interested participants.

The proposed auction makes truthful reporting a dominant strategy for advertisers and aligns each advertiser's utility with its contribution to social welfare. It works without fine-tuning the language model or accessing its weights. The authors also prove that its output converges to that of an optimally fine-tuned model as computational resources increase, giving a theoretical relationship between the mechanism and a fine-tuning-based optimum.

Advertiser context can be incorporated to improve social welfare. Experiments with publicly available language models show high advertiser value and platform revenue at low computational cost. Although advertising motivates the work, the proposed mechanism applies more broadly to preference aggregation over generated replies in settings that permit monetary transfers. Its contribution combines strategic truthfulness with a computational approach for influencing language-model outputs.
summary.tldr: MOSAIC uses an auction to truthfully aggregate advertiser preferences over LLM replies without model fine-tuning or weight access.

title: Truthful Aggregation of LLMs with an Application to Online Advertising

abstract: Multi-instance multi-label learning (MIML) is a framework for learning in the presence of label ambiguity. In MIML, experts provide labels for groups of instances (bags), instead of directly providing a label for every instance. When labeling efforts are focused on a set of target classes, instances outside this set will not be appropriately modeled. For example, ornithologists label bird audio recordings with a list of species present. Other additional sound instances, e.g., a rain drop or a moving vehicle sound, are not labeled. The challenge is due to the fact that for a given bag, the presence or absence of novel instances is latent. In this paper, this problem is addressed using a discriminative probabilistic model that accounts for novel instances. We propose an exact and efficient implementation of the maximum likelihood approach to determine the model parameters and consequently learn an instance-level classifier for all classes including the novel class. Experiments on both synthetic and real datasets illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

paragraphs: In multi-instance multi-label learning, experts label a group of instances without identifying the label of every individual instance. A bird recording, for example, may list the species present while also containing rain or vehicle sounds. When annotation focuses on target classes, these additional instances remain unaccounted for, and even their presence within a group is hidden.

The paper introduces a discriminative probabilistic model that explicitly allows novel-class instances. This changes what the learner must explain: a group's contents can include both labeled target categories and an additional novel category. The method therefore addresses ambiguity about individual labels together with uncertainty about whether novel instances occur at all.

The authors provide an exact and efficient implementation of maximum-likelihood estimation for the model parameters. The fitted model yields an instance-level classifier covering the target classes and the novel class. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets illustrate effectiveness. The key contribution is making unannotated, out-of-target content an explicit part of learning from group labels, rather than leaving it outside the model.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic model learns instance-level target and novel classes from ambiguous group-level labels.

title: Multi-instance multi-label learning in the presence of novel class instances

abstract: We consider the problem of maximizing an unknown function f over a compact and convex set using as few observations f(x) as possible. We observe that the optimization of the function f essentially relies on learning the induced bipartite ranking rule of f. Based on this idea, we relate global optimization to bipartite ranking which allows to address problems with high dimensional input space, as well as cases of functions with weak regularity properties. The paper introduces novel meta-algorithms for global optimization which rely on the choice of any bipartite ranking method. Theoretical properties are provided as well as convergence guarantees and equivalences between various optimization methods are obtained as a by-product. Eventually, numerical evidence is given to show that the main algorithm of the paper which adapts empirically to the underlying ranking structure essentially outperforms existing state-of-the-art global optimization algorithms in typical benchmarks.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to maximize an unknown function while observing its value as few times as possible. The search takes place over a compact, convex set. Its central idea is that optimization depends heavily on learning which inputs are better than others, making ranking a useful route to finding good solutions.

The authors connect global optimization to bipartite ranking and introduce general optimization procedures that can use a chosen ranking method. This connection provides a way to address high-dimensional inputs and functions with weak regularity properties. The approach organizes the search around the function’s ordering structure, giving ranking methods a direct role in deciding where to search.

The paper supplies theoretical properties and convergence guarantees, and also derives equivalences between several optimization methods. Its main algorithm adapts empirically to the underlying ranking structure. Numerical results on typical benchmarks indicate that it generally outperforms the existing global optimization algorithms considered, supporting the practical value of the ranking perspective.
summary.tldr: The paper turns global optimization into a ranking problem to guide an observation-efficient search for high-value inputs.

title: A ranking approach to global optimization

abstract: In structured prediction problems where we have indirect supervision of the output, maximum marginal likelihood faces two computational obstacles: non-convexity of the objective and intractability of even a single gradient computation. In this paper, we bypass both obstacles for a class of what we call linear indirectly-supervised problems. Our approach is simple: we solve a linear system to estimate sufficient statistics of the model, which we then use to estimate parameters via convex optimization. We analyze the statistical properties of our approach and show empirically that it is effective in two settings: learning with local privacy constraints and learning from low-cost count-based annotations.
originalAbstract: In structured prediction problems where we have indirect supervision of the output, maximum marginal likelihood faces two computational obstacles: non-convexity of the objective and intractability of even a single gradient computation. In this paper, we bypass both obstacles for a class of what we call linear indirectly-supervised problems. Our approach is simple: we solve a linear system to estimate sufficient statistics of the model, which we then use to estimate parameters via convex optimization. We analyze the statistical properties of our approach and show empirically that it is effective in two settings: learning with local privacy constraints and learning from low-cost count-based annotations.

paragraphs: Structured prediction becomes difficult when training provides indirect information about outputs instead of the outputs themselves. Maximum marginal likelihood then faces two obstacles: its objective can be nonconvex, and even computing one gradient can be intractable. This paper develops an alternative for a particular class of problems whose indirect supervision has a linear structure.

The method separates estimation into two stages. First, it solves a linear system to estimate the model’s sufficient statistics, the quantities used for the subsequent parameter estimation. It then estimates parameters through convex optimization. This sequence bypasses both computational obstacles for the supported class of linear indirectly supervised problems.

The authors analyze the statistical properties of the approach and evaluate it in two settings: learning under local privacy constraints and learning from inexpensive count-based annotations. The empirical results show effectiveness in both. The contribution is a concrete route from indirect observations to model parameters, where the linear relationship makes it possible to replace a difficult marginal-likelihood calculation with more manageable estimation steps.
summary.tldr: For a class of indirectly supervised problems, linear-system estimation followed by convex optimization avoids difficult marginal-likelihood computations.

title: Estimation from Indirect Supervision with Linear Moments

abstract: This paper introduces DeepBach, a graphical model aimed at modeling polyphonic music and specifically hymn-like pieces. We claim that, after being trained on the chorale harmonizations by Johann Sebastian Bach, our model is capable of generating highly convincing chorales in the style of Bach. DeepBach’s strength comes from the use of pseudo-Gibbs sampling coupled with an adapted representation of musical data. This is in contrast with many automatic music composition approaches which tend to compose music sequentially. Our model is also steerable in the sense that a user can constrain the generation by imposing positional constraints such as notes, rhythms or cadences in the generated score. We also provide a plugin on top of the MuseScore music editor making the interaction with DeepBach easy to use.

The combination of the sampling procedure and the representation is identified as the main source of the model’s strength.

Generation can therefore respond to musical choices supplied by a person, rather than requiring the person to accept an entirely unconstrained result. A MuseScore plugin provides an interface for this interaction. Together, the model and interface connect automatic chorale generation with direct control over selected musical details.
summary.tldr: DeepBach combines a musical graphical model with sampling to generate Bach-style chorales under user-specified score constraints.

title: DeepBach: a Steerable Model for Bach Chorales Generation

abstract: Graph convolutional networks (GCNs) are powerful deep neural networks for graph-structured data. However, GCN computes the representation of a node recursively from its neighbors, making the receptive field size grow exponentially with the number of layers. Previous attempts on reducing the receptive field size by subsampling neighbors do not have convergence guarantee, and their receptive field size per node is still in the order of hundreds. In this paper, we develop control variate based algorithms with new theoretical guarantee to converge to a local optimum of GCN regardless of the neighbor sampling size. Empirical results show that our algorithms enjoy similar convergence rate and model quality with the exact algorithm using only two neighbors per node. The running time of our algorithms on a large Reddit dataset is only one seventh of previous neighbor sampling algorithms.

paragraphs: Graph convolutional networks compute a node's representation using its neighbors, whose representations depend on their own neighbors. Across layers, this recursive expansion can make the computation grow exponentially. Sampling fewer neighbors reduces the workload, but the paper notes that earlier sampling approaches lacked convergence guarantees and still involved large receptive fields.

The authors develop algorithms based on control variates to reduce the variance associated with stochastic training. Their theory guarantees convergence to a local optimum regardless of the neighbor sampling size. This directly addresses whether aggressive sampling can remain compatible with a principled training procedure.

In the experiments, using only two neighbors per node yields a convergence rate and model quality similar to the exact algorithm. On a large Reddit dataset, runtime is one seventh that of previous neighbor-sampling methods. These findings show that very small sampled neighborhoods can be effective with the proposed variance reduction, while the theoretical endpoint remains a local optimum rather than a global one.
summary.tldr: Control-variate training lets GCNs use very small neighbor samples with local-convergence guarantees and substantial reported speed gains.

title: Stochastic Training of Graph Convolutional Networks with Variance Reduction

abstract: We propose temporal Poisson square root graphical models (TPSQRs), a generalization of Poisson square root graphical models (PSQRs) specifically designed for modeling longitudinal event data. By estimating the temporal relationships for all possible pairs of event types, TPSQRs can offer a holistic perspective about whether the occurrences of any given event type could excite or inhibit any other type. A TPSQR is learned by estimating a collection of interrelated PSQRs that share the same template parameterization. These PSQRs are estimated jointly in a pseudo-likelihood fashion, where Poisson pseudo-likelihood is used to approximate the original more computationally intensive pseudo-likelihood problem stemming from PSQRs. Theoretically, we demonstrate that under mild assumptions, the Poisson pseudolikelihood approximation is sparsistent for recovering the underlying PSQR. Empirically, we learn TPSQRs from a real-world large-scale electronic health record (EHR) with millions of drug prescription and condition diagnosis events, for adverse drug reaction (ADR) detection. Experimental results demonstrate that the learned TPSQRs can recover ADR signals from the EHR effectively and efficiently.

paragraphs: Longitudinal event records contain many event types whose occurrences may be related over time. Temporal Poisson square root graphical models extend an existing graphical-model family to represent these relationships. By considering every pair of event types, they offer a broad view of whether one type's occurrence could encourage or inhibit another.

The method learns a collection of linked Poisson square root models that share a common parameter template. Joint estimation uses a Poisson pseudo-likelihood approximation to avoid the more expensive original pseudo-likelihood computation. Under mild assumptions, the authors prove sparsistency: the approximation can recover the underlying pattern of present and absent relationships in the model.

The empirical application uses a large electronic health record containing millions of prescription and diagnosis events to detect adverse drug reaction signals. The learned models recover these signals effectively and efficiently in the reported experiments. This connects the computational approximation to a substantial event-data application, while the recovered signals provide evidence for detection rather than a claim that every modeled relationship establishes a causal drug effect.
summary.tldr: Temporal Poisson square root models efficiently estimate event relationships and recover adverse drug reaction signals from large electronic health records.

title: Temporal Poisson Square Root Graphical Models

abstract: The unfairness of a regressor is evaluated by measuring the correlation between the estimator and the sensitive attribute (e.g., race, gender, age), and the coefficient of determination (CoD) is a natural extension of the correlation coefficient when more than one sensitive attribute exists. As is well known, there is a trade-off between fairness and accuracy of a regressor, which implies a perfectly fair optimizer does not always yield a useful prediction. Taking this into consideration, we optimize the accuracy of the estimation subject to a user-defined level of fairness. However, a fairness level as a constraint induces a nonconvexity of the feasible region, which disables the use of an off-the-shelf convex optimizer. Despite such nonconvexity, we show an exact solution is available by using tools of global optimization theory. Furthermore, we propose a nonlinear extension of the method by kernel representation. Unlike most of existing fairness-aware machine learning methods, our method allows us to deal with numeric and multiple sensitive attributes.

paragraphs: The paper formulates regression fairness in terms of association between predictions and sensitive attributes, such as race, gender, or age. For multiple sensitive attributes, it uses the coefficient of determination as an extension of correlation. This gives a specific measurable fairness criterion with which to express a user's desired constraint.

Rather than requiring perfect fairness regardless of predictive usefulness, the method optimizes accuracy subject to a chosen fairness level. That constraint makes the feasible region nonconvex, preventing direct use of an ordinary convex optimizer. The authors nevertheless show that tools from global optimization yield an exact solution to the problem they formulate.

The paper also extends the method to nonlinear prediction through a kernel representation. It supports numerical sensitive attributes and multiple sensitive attributes, expanding the types of fairness constraints that can be handled. Its contribution is a tractable treatment of the accuracy–fairness trade-off under the stated association-based criterion, with an exact optimization result despite the constraint's nonconvexity.
summary.tldr: Global optimization yields an exact regression solution under a user-chosen correlation-based fairness constraint, with a kernel extension for nonlinear prediction.

title: Nonconvex Optimization for Regression with Fairness Constraints

abstract: In the recent literature the important role of depth in deep learning has been emphasized. In this paper we argue that sufficient width of a feedforward network is equally important by answering the simple question under which conditions the decision regions of a neural network are connected. It turns out that for a class of activation functions including leaky ReLU, neural networks having a pyramidal structure, that is no layer has more hidden units than the input dimension, produce necessarily connected decision regions. This implies that a sufficiently wide hidden layer is necessary to guarantee that the network can produce disconnected decision regions. We discuss the implications of this result for the construction of neural networks, in particular the relation to the problem of adversarial manipulation of classifiers.
originalAbstract: In the recent literature the important role of depth in deep learning has been emphasized. In this paper we argue that sufficient width of a feedforward network is equally important by answering the simple question under which conditions the decision regions of a neural network are connected. It turns out that for a class of activation functions including leaky ReLU, neural networks having a pyramidal structure, that is no layer has more hidden units than the input dimension, produce necessarily connected decision regions. This implies that a sufficiently wide hidden layer is necessary to guarantee that the network can produce disconnected decision regions. We discuss the implications of this result for the construction of neural networks, in particular the relation to the problem of adversarial manipulation of classifiers.

paragraphs: A classifier's decision region is the collection of inputs it assigns to a particular class. Such a region can be connected or can consist of separate pieces. This paper asks which network architectures can represent disconnected decision regions, using that question to examine the role of width alongside the often-emphasized role of depth.

The authors analyze a class of activation functions that includes leaky ReLU. For these activations, networks with the stated pyramidal structure, in which no layer has more hidden units than the input dimension, necessarily produce connected decision regions. Within the analyzed setting, this imposes a restriction on the shapes of classifications the architecture can express.

Consequently, a sufficiently wide hidden layer is necessary to guarantee the ability to produce disconnected regions. This is a representational requirement, not a claim that widening alone ensures successful training. The authors discuss implications for network construction and the relationship to adversarial manipulation of classifiers. The result makes width relevant to the topology of decisions, beyond simply adding more parameters.
summary.tldr: For the analyzed activations and architectures, insufficient width forces connected decision regions, restricting the classifications a network can represent.

title: Neural Networks Should Be Wide Enough to Learn Disconnected Decision Regions

abstract: Set functions predict a label from a permutation-invariant variable-size collection of feature vectors. We propose making set functions more understandable and regularized by capturing domain knowledge through shape constraints. We show how prior work in monotonic constraints can be adapted to set functions, and then propose two new shape constraints designed to generalize the conditioning role of weights in a weighted mean. We show how one can train standard functions and set functions that satisfy these shape constraints with a deep lattice network. We propose a nonlinear estimation strategy we call the semantic feature engine that uses set functions with the proposed shape constraints to estimate labels for compound sparse categorical features. Experiments on real-world data show the achieved accuracy is similar to deep sets or deep neural networks, but provides guarantees on the model behavior, which makes it easier to explain and debug.

paragraphs: Set functions predict from collections whose size can vary and whose ordering should not affect the result. This paper proposes using shape constraints to express domain knowledge about how such predictions should behave. These constraints are intended to regularize the model and make its responses easier to understand.

The authors adapt monotonic constraints to set functions and introduce two additional constraints that generalize the conditioning role of weights in a weighted mean. They show how deep lattice networks can train ordinary functions and set functions satisfying these requirements. They also propose a semantic feature engine, a nonlinear estimator that applies constrained set functions to compound sparse categorical features.

Experiments on real-world data achieve accuracy similar to deep sets or deep neural networks while providing guarantees about model behavior. The benefit is therefore the combination of competitive predictive performance and specified behavioral constraints. Those guarantees can make explanation and debugging easier because users have explicit expectations about how the model is allowed to respond.
summary.tldr: Shape-constrained set functions encode domain knowledge and provide behavioral guarantees while achieving accuracy similar to the tested neural alternatives.

title: Shape Constraints for Set Functions

abstract: Spherical convolutional networks have been introduced recently as tools to learn powerful feature representations of 3D shapes. Spherical CNNs are equivariant to 3D rotations making them ideally suited to applications where 3D data may be observed in arbitrary orientations. In this paper we learn 2D image embeddings with a similar equivariant structure: embedding the image of a 3D object should commute with rotations of the object. We introduce a cross-domain embedding from 2D images into a spherical CNN latent space. This embedding encodes images with 3D shape properties and is equivariant to 3D rotations of the observed object. The model is supervised only by target embeddings obtained from a spherical CNN pretrained for 3D shape classification. We show that learning a rich embedding for images with appropriate geometric structure is sufficient for tackling varied applications, such as relative pose estimation and novel view synthesis, without requiring additional task-specific supervision.

The model is supervised only by target embeddings obtained from a spherical CNN pretrained for 3D shape classification. We show that learning a rich embedding for images with appropriate geometric structure is sufficient for tackling varied applications, such as relative pose estimation and novel view synthesis, without requiring additional task-specific supervision.

paragraphs: A useful representation of an object should respond predictably when the object rotates. Spherical convolutional networks provide this property for three-dimensional shapes: a rotation produces a corresponding transformation in their representations. This paper transfers a similar geometric structure to embeddings computed from two-dimensional images of three-dimensional objects.

The method maps images into the latent space of a spherical CNN that has already been trained for shape classification. Its training targets are embeddings supplied by that network. This gives the image representation information about three-dimensional shape and a structured response to object rotations. Equivariance here means that rotating the observed object and embedding its image should agree with the corresponding rotation of the embedding.

The authors demonstrate applications to estimating relative pose and synthesizing new views without additional supervision specific to those tasks. The stated result is that a sufficiently rich image embedding with the appropriate geometry can support several applications. The method still uses supervision from the pretrained shape model; its reuse across tasks is the distinctive benefit.
summary.tldr: A pretrained spherical CNN supplies geometric supervision for image embeddings that support pose estimation and new-view synthesis without extra task-specific supervision.

title: Cross-Domain 3D Equivariant Image Embeddings

abstract: In most machine learning training paradigms a fixed, often handcrafted, loss function is assumed to be a good proxy for an underlying evaluation metric. In this work we assess this assumption by meta-learning an adaptive loss function to directly optimize the evaluation metric. We propose a sample efficient reinforcement learning approach for adapting the loss dynamically during training. We empirically show how this formulation improves performance by simultaneously optimizing the evaluation metric and smoothing the loss landscape. We verify our method in metric learning and classification scenarios, showing considerable improvements over the state-of-the-art on a diverse set of tasks. Importantly, our method is applicable to a wide range of loss functions and evaluation metrics. Furthermore, the learned policies are transferable across tasks and data, demonstrating the versatility of the method.
originalAbstract: In most machine learning training paradigms a fixed, often handcrafted, loss function is assumed to be a good proxy for an underlying evaluation metric. In this work we assess this assumption by meta-learning an adaptive loss function to directly optimize the evaluation metric. We propose a sample efficient reinforcement learning approach for adapting the loss dynamically during training. We empirically show how this formulation improves performance by simultaneously optimizing the evaluation metric and smoothing the loss landscape. We verify our method in metric learning and classification scenarios, showing considerable improvements over the state-of-the-art on a diverse set of tasks. Importantly, our method is applicable to a wide range of loss functions and evaluation metrics. Furthermore, the learned policies are transferable across tasks and data, demonstrating the versatility of the method.

paragraphs: A model is often trained using one objective but judged using another. The training loss is usually chosen in advance as a convenient proxy for the evaluation metric. This paper questions whether keeping that proxy fixed is the best way to obtain the performance that actually matters.

The proposed approach meta-learns a loss function that changes during training. A sample-efficient reinforcement learning method controls this adaptation, with the evaluation metric serving as the target of optimization. This makes the design of the training objective part of the learning process itself, rather than treating it as a settled choice made before training begins.

Experiments in classification and metric learning show considerable improvements over the state of the art across the evaluated tasks. The authors associate these gains with both better metric optimization and a smoother loss landscape. They also report that learned policies transfer across tasks and data, supporting the method’s usefulness across a broad range of losses and evaluation metrics.
summary.tldr: Adaptive Loss Alignment learns to change the training loss so that optimization better serves the evaluation metric.

title: Addressing the Loss-Metric Mismatch with Adaptive Loss Alignment

abstract: For SGD based distributed stochastic optimization, computation complexity, measured by the convergence rate in terms of the number of stochastic gradient calls, and communication complexity, measured by the number of inter-node communication rounds, are two most important performance metrics. The classical data-parallel implementation of SGD over N workers can achieve linear speedup of its convergence rate but incurs an inter-node communication round at each batch. We study the benefit of using dynamically increasing batch sizes in parallel SGD for stochastic non-convex optimization by charactering the attained convergence rate and the required number of communication rounds. We show that for stochastic non-convex optimization under the P-L condition, the classical data-parallel SGD with exponentially increasing batch sizes can achieve the fastest known $O(1/(NT))$ convergence with linear speedup using only $\log(T)$ communication rounds. For general stochastic non-convex optimization, we propose a Catalyst-like algorithm to achieve the fastest known $O(1/\sqrt{NT})$ convergence with only $O(\sqrt{NT}\log(\frac{T}{N}))$ communication rounds.

paragraphs: Parallel stochastic gradient descent has two distinct costs: computing stochastic gradients and exchanging information between workers. Classical data-parallel SGD can gain linear speedup from N workers, but it communicates after every batch. This paper studies whether increasing batch sizes during training can preserve strong convergence guarantees while reducing the number of communication rounds.

For stochastic nonconvex objectives satisfying the P-L condition, the authors analyze classical parallel SGD with exponentially increasing batches. They establish an O(1/(NT)) convergence rate with linear speedup and only log(T) communication rounds. The P-L condition is a substantive qualification: this stronger rate is tied to that particular class of optimization problems.

For general stochastic nonconvex optimization, the paper proposes a Catalyst-like algorithm with an O(1/√(NT)) convergence rate and O(√(NT) log(T/N)) communication rounds. Both convergence rates are described as the fastest known for their respective settings. The contribution shows how batch scheduling and algorithm design can reduce communication while retaining strong computational convergence guarantees.
summary.tldr: Increasing batch sizes enables parallel SGD methods to retain strong nonconvex convergence rates with substantially fewer communication rounds.

title: On the Computation and Communication Complexity of Parallel SGD with Dynamic Batch Sizes for Stochastic Non-Convex Optimization

abstract: In model-based reinforcement learning, planning with an imperfect model of the environment has the potential to harm learning progress. But even when a model is imperfect, it may still contain information that is useful for planning. In this paper, we investigate the idea of using an imperfect model selectively. The agent should plan in parts of the state space where the model would be helpful but refrain from using the model where it would be harmful. An effective selective planning mechanism requires estimating predictive uncertainty, which arises out of aleatoric uncertainty, parameter uncertainty, and model inadequacy, among other sources. Prior work has focused on parameter uncertainty for selective planning. In this work, we emphasize the importance of model inadequacy. We show that heteroscedastic regression can signal predictive uncertainty arising from model inadequacy that is complementary to that which is detected by methods designed for parameter uncertainty, indicating that considering both parameter uncertainty and model inadequacy may be a more promising direction for effective selective planning than either in isolation.

paragraphs: An imperfect environment model can still help a reinforcement learning agent, but planning with it can also damage learning. The paper investigates selective planning: using the model in regions where its predictions help and avoiding regions where they mislead. Making this distinction requires an informative estimate of predictive uncertainty.

The authors emphasize that uncertainty has multiple sources. Uncertain parameters are one source, but the model may also lack the capacity to represent the environment adequately. Prior selective-planning work has focused on parameter uncertainty. This study highlights model inadequacy as a separate concern that a useful uncertainty estimate should also be able to signal.

The paper shows that heteroscedastic regression, which allows predictive variability to differ across inputs, can signal uncertainty associated with model inadequacy. That signal complements uncertainty detected by methods focused on parameters. The conclusion is a qualified research direction: accounting for both sources may support more effective selective planning than considering either alone, because an imperfect model's usefulness can vary across the state space.
summary.tldr: Heteroscedastic regression can flag model inadequacy, complementing parameter uncertainty when deciding where an imperfect environment model is useful for planning.

title: Selective Dyna-Style Planning Under Limited Model Capacity

abstract: Shapley value is a classic notion from game theory, historically used to quantify the contributions of individuals within groups, and more recently applied to assign values to data points when training machine learning models. Despite its foundational role, a key limitation of the data Shapley framework is that it only provides valuations for points within a fixed data set. It does not account for statistical aspects of the data and does not give a way to reason about points outside the data set. To address these limitations, we propose a novel framework – distributional Shapley– where the value of a point is defined in the context of an underlying data distribution. We prove that distributional Shapley has several desirable statistical properties; for example, the values are stable under perturbations to the data points themselves and to the underlying data distribution. We leverage these properties to develop a new algorithm for estimating values from data, which comes with formal guarantees and runs two orders of magnitude faster than state-of-the-art algorithms for computing the (non distributional) data Shapley values. We apply distributional Shapley to diverse data sets and demonstrate its utility in a data market setting.

We prove that distributional Shapley has several desirable statistical properties; for example, the values are stable under perturbations to the data points themselves and to the underlying data distribution. paragraphs: Assigning a value to a training example requires deciding what its contribution should be measured against. Existing data Shapley methods answer this question within a fixed dataset. That makes the valuation tied to a particular collection and leaves no direct way to value a point outside it. This paper instead defines a point’s contribution relative to an underlying data distribution.

The resulting framework, distributional Shapley, brings statistical behavior into the definition of value. The authors prove properties including stability when either individual data points or the underlying distribution are perturbed. These results matter because a valuation should not depend excessively on small changes in the data used to establish it.

The authors use these properties to build an estimation algorithm with formal guarantees. They report that it runs two orders of magnitude faster than leading algorithms for conventional data Shapley, while computing the new distributional valuation. Applications across diverse datasets and a data market setting demonstrate the framework’s practical utility.
summary.tldr: Distributional Shapley values data relative to a population, enabling stable valuations and a fast estimation algorithm with formal guarantees.

title: A Distributional Framework For Data Valuation

abstract: Learning to control complex bodies and reuse learned behaviors is a longstanding challenge in continuous control. We study the problem of learning reusable humanoid skills by imitating motion capture data and joint training with complementary tasks. We show that it is possible to learn reusable skills through reinforcement learning on 50 times more motion capture data than prior work. We systematically compare a variety of different network architectures across different data regimes both in terms of imitation performance as well as transfer to challenging locomotion tasks. Finally we show that it is possible to interleave the motion capture tracking with training on complementary tasks, enriching the resulting skill space, and enabling the reuse of skills not well covered by the motion capture data such as getting up from the ground or catching a ball.

paragraphs: Controlling a humanoid requires coordinating a complex body, but useful control also means reusing learned movements in new situations. CoMic studies how to build reusable skills by combining imitation of motion capture recordings with reinforcement learning on complementary tasks. The goal is a collection of behaviors that supports more than accurate reproduction of recorded motion.

The authors show that reusable skills can be learned using 50 times as much motion capture data as prior work. They systematically compare several network architectures across different amounts of training data. These comparisons assess both imitation quality and transfer to challenging locomotion tasks, treating successful reuse as a separate concern from matching the original recordings.

The paper also shows that motion tracking can be interleaved with complementary task training. This enriches the learned skill space and enables reuse of behaviors poorly represented in the recordings, including getting up from the ground and catching a ball. The findings support combining recorded examples with task experience to extend the range of reusable humanoid behavior.
summary.tldr: CoMic combines large-scale motion imitation with complementary task training to learn humanoid skills that can be reused beyond the recorded motions.

title: CoMic: Complementary Task Learning & Mimicry for Reusable Skills

abstract: Increasing the scale of reinforcement learning experiments has allowed researchers to achieve unprecedented results in both training sophisticated agents for video games, and in sim-to-real transfer for robotics. Typically such experiments rely on large distributed systems and require expensive hardware setups, limiting wider access to this exciting area of research. In this work we aim to solve this problem by optimizing the efficiency and resource utilization of reinforcement learning algorithms instead of relying on distributed computation. We present the "Sample Factory", a high-throughput training system optimized for a single-machine setting. Our architecture combines a highly efficient, asynchronous, GPU-based sampler with off-policy correction techniques, allowing us to achieve throughput higher than $10^5$ environment frames/second on non-trivial control problems in 3D without sacrificing sample efficiency. We extend Sample Factory to support self-play and population-based training and apply these techniques to train highly capable agents for a multiplayer first-person shooter game. Github: https://github.com/alex-petrenko/sample-factory

Sample Factory addresses this access problem by improving efficiency and resource use within a single machine. Its goal is to make demanding training workloads faster through the design of the training system itself.

These pieces support rapid collection and use of experience while accounting for the off-policy aspect of training. On non-trivial three-dimensional control problems, the system achieves more than 100,000 environment frames per second without sacrificing sample efficiency. This separates processing experience quickly from needing more experience to learn.

The contribution therefore includes both a high-throughput single-machine architecture and support for more elaborate training setups. The stated results show how better use of available computation can expand the scale of reinforcement-learning experiments.
summary.tldr: Sample Factory exceeds 100,000 environment frames per second on 3D control tasks using efficient asynchronous reinforcement learning on a single machine.

title: Sample Factory: Egocentric 3D Control from Pixels at 100000 FPS with Asynchronous Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Recent research has shown that incorporating equivariance into neural network architectures is very helpful, and there have been some works investigating the equivariance of networks under group actions. However, as digital images and feature maps are on the discrete meshgrid, corresponding equivariance-preserving transformation groups are very limited. In this work, we deal with this issue from the connection between convolutions and partial differential operators (PDOs). In theory, assuming inputs to be smooth, we transform PDOs and propose a system which is equivariant to a much more general continuous group, the $n$-dimension Euclidean group. In implementation, we discretize the system using the numerical schemes of PDOs, deriving approximately equivariant convolutions (PDO-eConvs). Theoretically, the approximation error of PDO-eConvs is of the quadratic order. It is the first time that the error analysis is provided when the equivariance is approximate. Extensive experiments on rotated MNIST and natural image classification show that PDO-eConvs perform competitively yet use parameters much more efficiently. Particularly, compared with Wide ResNets, our methods result in better results using only 12.6% parameters.

paragraphs: Equivariance means that transforming an input produces a corresponding transformation in the network’s representation. Building that property into image networks is difficult because images and feature maps occupy discrete grids, which support only limited transformation groups exactly. This paper approaches the problem through the relationship between convolutions and partial differential operators.

Assuming smooth inputs, the authors construct a system equivariant to the continuous n-dimensional Euclidean group. They then discretize that system using numerical schemes for differential operators, producing PDO-eConvs. The implemented convolutions are approximately equivariant, and the paper provides an error analysis showing a quadratic-order approximation error. The findings support differential operators as a practical way to incorporate broader geometric structure into convolutional architectures while quantifying the approximation introduced by the grid.
summary.tldr: PDO-eConvs discretize a continuously equivariant differential-operator system into parameter-efficient convolutions with quantified approximate equivariance.

title: PDO-eConvs: Partial Differential Operator Based Equivariant Convolutions

abstract: Online recommender systems often face long delays in receiving feedback, especially when optimizing for some long-term metrics. While mitigating the effects of delays in learning is well-understood in stationary environments, the problem becomes much more challenging when the environment changes. In fact, if the timescale of the change is comparable to the delay, it is impossible to learn about the environment, since the available observations are already obsolete. However, the arising issues can be addressed if intermediate signals are available without delay, such that given those signals, the long-term behavior of the system is stationary. To model this situation, we introduce the problem of stochastic, non-stationary, delayed bandits with intermediate observations. We develop a computationally efficient algorithm based on UCRL, and prove sublinear regret guarantees for its performance. Experimental results demonstrate that our method is able to learn in non-stationary delayed environments where existing methods fail.

paragraphs: Learning from delayed outcomes becomes especially difficult when the environment changes before feedback arrives. For an online recommender optimizing long-term outcomes, observations may already describe an obsolete situation. The paper explains that learning can become impossible when environmental change occurs on a timescale comparable to the feedback delay.

The authors identify a condition under which immediate intermediate signals can help: after conditioning on those signals, the relationship to long-term behavior remains stationary. They formalize this setting as a stochastic bandit problem with environmental changes, delayed rewards, and intermediate observations. The signals provide a stable connection to eventual outcomes despite changes elsewhere in the system.

The paper develops an efficient algorithm based on UCRL and proves sublinear regret guarantees. Experiments show learning in changing, delayed environments where existing methods fail. The result depends on the stated stability condition for the intermediate signals. It demonstrates how appropriately informative early observations can make delayed learning possible in settings where the eventual feedback alone arrives too late.
summary.tldr: Immediate intermediate signals enable learning with delayed rewards in changing environments when long-term behavior is stationary conditional on those signals.

title: Non-Stationary Delayed Bandits with Intermediate Observations

abstract: We investigate the \textit{problem dependent regime} in the stochastic \emph{Thresholding Bandit problem} (\tbp) under several \emph{shape constraints}. In the \tbp the objective of the learner is to output, after interacting with the environment, the set of arms whose means are above a given threshold. The vanilla, unstructured, case is already well studied in the literature. Taking $K$ as the number of arms, we consider the case where (i) the sequence of arm’s means $(\mu_k){k=1}^K$ is monotonically increasing (\textit{MTBP}) and (ii) the case where $(\mu_k){k=1}^K$ is concave (\textit{CTBP}). We consider both cases in the \emph{problem dependent} regime and study the probability of error - i.e. the probability to mis-classify at least one arm. In the fixed budget setting, we provide nearly matching upper and lower bounds for the probability of error in both the concave and monotone settings, as well as associated algorithms. Of interest, is that for both the monotone and concave cases, optimal bounds on probability of error are of the same order as those for the two armed bandit problem.

This paper studies the probability of making at least one incorrect classification after a fixed sampling budget. Its analysis is problem dependent, focusing on the particular configuration of means rather than only a broad worst-case description.

The authors consider two forms of structure in the ordered sequence of arm means. In one, the means increase monotonically. In the other, they form a concave sequence. For each setting, they develop algorithms and nearly matching upper and lower bounds on error probability. The upper bounds describe achievable performance, while the lower bounds characterize the difficulty that algorithms must face.

A notable finding is that the optimal error bounds in both structured settings have the same order as those for a two-arm problem. This shows how strongly shape information can change the statistical difficulty of identifying above-threshold arms. The conclusion concerns the stated error-probability bounds under monotonicity or concavity and a fixed budget.
summary.tldr: Under monotone or concave arm means, thresholding bandits admit nearly matching error bounds of the same order as a two-arm problem.

title: Problem Dependent View on Structured Thresholding Bandit Problems

abstract: Attention mechanisms have shown promising results in sequence modeling tasks that require long-term memory. Recent work investigated mechanisms to reduce the computational cost of preserving and storing memories. However, not all content in the past is equally important to remember. We propose Expire-Span, a method that learns to retain the most important information and expire the irrelevant information. This forgetting of memories enables Transformers to scale to attend over tens of thousands of previous timesteps efficiently, as not all states from previous timesteps are preserved. We demonstrate that Expire-Span can help models identify and retain critical information and show it can achieve strong performance on reinforcement learning tasks specifically designed to challenge this functionality. Next, we show that Expire-Span can scale to memories that are tens of thousands in size, setting a new state of the art on incredibly long context tasks such as character-level language modeling and a frame-by-frame moving objects task. Finally, we analyze the efficiency of Expire-Span compared to existing approaches and demonstrate that it trains faster and uses less memory.

paragraphs: Attention-based sequence models can use distant history, but preserving and attending to many past states is computationally expensive. This paper starts from the observation that past information differs in importance. Expire-Span learns what to retain and what to let expire, allowing memory use to depend on the relevance of its contents.

By discarding information judged irrelevant, the method enables Transformers to attend across tens of thousands of previous time steps without preserving every state. The authors test whether models can identify and keep critical information on reinforcement-learning tasks designed to challenge that ability. They report strong performance, supporting the usefulness of learned forgetting for selective long-term memory.

The paper also reports state-of-the-art results on very long-context tasks, including character-level language modeling and a task involving moving objects presented frame by frame. Efficiency comparisons show faster training and lower memory use than existing approaches. These findings connect selective retention to both task performance and computational savings: a long usable history need not require keeping all previous representations.
summary.tldr: Expire-Span learns which memories to retain, enabling efficient attention over long histories with strong reported task performance.

title: Not All Memories are Created Equal: Learning to Forget by Expiring

abstract: This paper discusses the problem of weakly supervised classification, in which instances are given weak labels that are produced by some label-corruption process. The goal is to derive conditions under which loss functions for weak-label learning are proper and lower-bounded—two essential requirements for the losses used in class-probability estimation. To this end, we derive a representation theorem for proper losses in supervised learning, which dualizes the Savage representation. We use this theorem to characterize proper weak-label losses and find a condition for them to be lower-bounded. From these theoretical findings, we derive a novel regularization scheme called generalized logit squeezing, which makes any proper weak-label loss bounded from below, without losing properness. Furthermore, we experimentally demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed approach, as compared to improper or unbounded losses. The results highlight the importance of properness and lower-boundedness.

paragraphs: Weakly supervised classification uses labels produced by a corruption process, making the design of training losses especially important. The paper focuses on estimating class probabilities and asks when a loss has two desired properties: properness, which aligns the objective with probability estimation, and a lower bound, which prevents its value from decreasing without limit.

The authors first develop a representation theorem for proper losses in supervised learning that dualizes the Savage representation. They use this result to characterize proper losses for weak labels and identify a condition for lower-boundedness. This provides a theoretical basis for addressing both requirements together when designing a weak-label learning objective.

From the theory, they derive generalized logit squeezing, a regularization scheme that makes any proper weak-label loss bounded below while preserving properness. Experiments show the approach’s effectiveness compared with improper or unbounded losses. The result is both a characterization of suitable objectives and a constructive method for improving an existing proper weak-label loss.
summary.tldr: Generalized logit squeezing makes proper weak-label losses lower-bounded while preserving their suitability for class-probability estimation.

title: Lower-Bounded Proper Losses for Weakly Supervised Classification

abstract: We study the problem of reinforcement learning (RL) with low (policy) switching cost {—} a problem well-motivated by real-life RL applications in which deployments of new policies are costly and the number of policy updates must be low. In this paper, we propose a new algorithm based on stage-wise exploration and adaptive policy elimination that achieves a regret of $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{H^4S^2AT})$ while requiring a switching cost of $O(HSA \log\log T)$. This is an exponential improvement over the best-known switching cost $O(H^2SA\log T)$ among existing methods with $\widetilde{O}(\mathrm{poly}(H,S,A)\sqrt{T})$ regret. In the above, $S,A$ denotes the number of states and actions in an $H$-horizon episodic Markov Decision Process model with unknown transitions, and $T$ is the number of steps. As a byproduct of our new techniques, we also derive a reward-free exploration algorithm with a switching cost of $O(HSA)$. Furthermore, we prove a pair of information-theoretical lower bounds which say that (1) Any no-regret algorithm must have a switching cost of $\Omega(HSA)$; (2) Any $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$ regret algorithm must incur a switching cost of $\Omega(HSA\log\log T)$. Both our algorithms are thus optimal in their switching costs.

paragraphs: Deploying a new reinforcement learning policy can be costly, so learning efficiently may also require changing policies infrequently. This paper studies that tradeoff in episodic Markov decision processes with unknown transitions. The setting has S states, A actions, an episode horizon H, and T total interaction steps.

The proposed algorithm combines exploration in stages with adaptive elimination of policies. It achieves regret of order √(H⁴S²AT), up to logarithmic factors, with O(HSA log log T) policy switches. Relative to the cited methods with square-root dependence of regret on T, the switching dependence improves from log T to log log T, alongside a changed horizon factor. The techniques also yield reward-free exploration with O(HSA) switches.

Lower bounds establish the significance of these results. Any no-regret algorithm needs at least order HSA switches, while algorithms with square-root-T regret, up to logarithmic factors, need at least order HSA log log T switches. These bounds support the claimed optimal switching costs. The contribution is thus not simply fewer deployments, but fewer deployments while retaining the stated learning guarantees.
summary.tldr: Stage-wise exploration and policy elimination achieve square-root-T regret with optimal O(HSA log log T) switching cost in the studied episodic setting.

title: Sample-Efficient Reinforcement Learning with loglog(T) Switching Cost

abstract: We characterize the differential privacy guarantees of privacy mechanisms in the large-composition regime, i.e., when a privacy mechanism is sequentially applied a large number of times to sensitive data. Via exponentially tilting the privacy loss random variable, we derive a new formula for the privacy curve expressing it as a contour integral over an integration path that runs parallel to the imaginary axis with a free real-axis intercept. Then, using the method of steepest descent from mathematical physics, we demonstrate that the choice of saddle-point as the real-axis intercept yields closed-form accurate approximations of the desired contour integral. This procedure—dubbed the saddle-point accountant (SPA)—yields a constant-time accurate approximation of the privacy curve. Theoretically, our results can be viewed as a refinement of both Gaussian Differential Privacy and the moments accountant method found in Rényi Differential Privacy. In practice, we demonstrate through numerical experiments that the SPA provides a precise approximation of privacy guarantees competitive with purely numerical-based methods (such as FFT-based accountants), while enjoying closed-form mathematical expressions.

Its goal is an accurate approximation of the privacy curve that remains computationally inexpensive, using analytical expressions rather than relying entirely on numerical computation.

title: The Saddle-Point Method in Differential Privacy

abstract: Counterexample-guided repair aims at creating neural networks with mathematical safety guarantees, facilitating the application of neural networks in safety-critical domains. However, whether counterexample-guided repair is guaranteed to terminate remains an open question. We approach this question by showing that counterexample-guided repair can be viewed as a robust optimisation algorithm. While termination guarantees for neural network repair itself remain beyond our reach, we prove termination for more restrained machine learning models and disprove termination in a general setting. We empirically study the practical implications of our theoretical results, demonstrating the suitability of common verifiers and falsifiers for repair despite a disadvantageous theoretical result. Additionally, we use our theoretical insights to devise a novel algorithm for repairing linear regression models based on quadratic programming, surpassing existing approaches.

paragraphs: Counterexample-guided repair tries to fix a learned model by finding inputs that violate a desired safety property and using those failures to guide changes. Its appeal is the possibility of mathematical safety guarantees. But a basic question remains: will repeatedly finding and fixing failures eventually finish?

The paper studies this question by interpreting repair as robust optimisation. This connection supplies a mathematical framework for reasoning about the repair process. The authors prove termination for more restricted machine learning models and show that termination can fail in a general setting. They do not establish termination guarantees for neural network repair itself.

The practical results add nuance to these theoretical findings. Experiments indicate that common tools for verifying properties or finding violations can still be suitable for repair despite an unfavourable theoretical result. The analysis also leads to a quadratic-programming algorithm for repairing linear regression models that surpasses existing approaches. The contribution therefore combines a clearer account of termination with a concrete improvement for a restricted model class.
summary.tldr: Viewing model repair as robust optimisation yields conditional termination results and an improved linear-regression repair algorithm, while neural-network termination remains unresolved.

title: A Robust Optimisation Perspective on Counterexample-Guided Repair of Neural Networks

abstract: Stackelberg equilibria arise naturally in a range of popular learning problems, such as in security games or indirect mechanism design, and have received increasing attention in the reinforcement learning literature. We present a general framework for implementing Stackelberg equilibria search as a multi-agent RL problem, allowing a wide range of algorithmic design choices. We discuss how previous approaches can be seen as specific instantiations of this framework. As a key insight, we note that the design space allows for approaches not previously seen in the literature, for instance by leveraging multitask and meta-RL techniques for follower convergence. We propose one such approach using contextual policies, and evaluate it experimentally on both standard and novel benchmark domains, showing greatly improved sample efficiency compared to previous approaches. Finally, we explore the effect of adopting algorithm designs outside the borders of our framework.

paragraphs: Stackelberg problems involve a leader whose choices account for how a follower responds. They arise in settings such as security games and indirect mechanism design. This paper presents a general framework for expressing the search for Stackelberg equilibria as a multi-agent reinforcement learning problem, making different algorithmic choices easier to organize and compare.

The authors show how previous approaches fit within the framework as particular instances. They also identify additional possibilities, including using multitask learning and meta-reinforcement learning to help followers converge. This is useful because the follower's learning behavior is part of the equilibrium-search process, so its implementation affects the overall procedure.

The paper develops one such approach using contextual policies and evaluates it on both established and newly introduced benchmark domains. It reports greatly improved sample efficiency relative to previous approaches. The authors also explore designs outside their framework. Together, the framework and experiments offer a way to structure equilibrium-search algorithms and evidence that a contextual-policy design can reduce the experience needed in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: A general multi-agent RL framework enables a contextual-policy approach to Stackelberg equilibrium search with improved empirical sample efficiency.

title: Oracles & Followers: Stackelberg Equilibria in Deep Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We study reinforcement learning with function approximation for large-scale Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs) where the state space and observation space are large or even continuous. Particularly, we consider Hilbert space embeddings of POMDP where the feature of latent states and the feature of observations admit a conditional Hilbert space embedding of the observation emission process, and the latent state transition is deterministic. Under the function approximation setup where the optimal latent state-action $Q$-function is linear in the state feature, and the optimal $Q$-function has a gap in actions, we provide a computationally and statistically efficient algorithm for finding the exact optimal policy. We show our algorithm’s computational and statistical complexities scale polynomially with respect to the horizon and the intrinsic dimension of the feature on the observation space. Furthermore, we show both the deterministic latent transitions and gap assumptions are necessary to avoid statistical complexity exponential in horizon or dimension. Since our guarantee does not have an explicit dependence on the size of the state and observation spaces, our algorithm provably scales to large-scale POMDPs.

Large or continuous state and observation spaces make this especially difficult. This paper identifies a structured setting in which an algorithm can find the exact optimal policy with efficient computation and data use.

The result depends on several explicit assumptions. Hidden-state transitions must be deterministic. Features of hidden states and observations must be connected through a conditional Hilbert space embedding of the observation process. The optimal hidden-state action-value function must be linear in the state features, and its action values must have a gap. Together, these conditions provide the structure used by the algorithm.

The computational and statistical costs grow polynomially with the planning horizon and the intrinsic dimension of the observation features, without explicit dependence on the sizes of the underlying spaces. The authors also show that deterministic transitions and the action gap are necessary to avoid exponential statistical complexity in the horizon or dimension within their setting. The contribution therefore combines an efficiency guarantee with an explanation of why its structural assumptions matter.
summary.tldr: Under explicit embedding, determinism, linearity, and action-gap assumptions, the paper gives an efficient algorithm for exact optimal control in large POMDPs.

title: Computationally Efficient PAC RL in POMDPs with Latent Determinism and Conditional Embeddings

abstract: Language models (LMs) may lead their users to make suboptimal downstream decisions when they confidently hallucinate. This issue can be mitigated by having the LM verbally convey the probability that its claims are correct, but existing models cannot produce long-form text with calibrated confidence statements. Through the lens of decision-making, we define linguistic calibration for long-form generations: an LM is linguistically calibrated if its generations enable its users to make calibrated probabilistic predictions. This definition enables a training framework where a supervised finetuning step bootstraps an LM to emit long-form generations with confidence statements such as "I estimate a 30% chance of..." or "I am certain that...", followed by a reinforcement learning step which rewards generations that enable a user to provide calibrated answers to related questions. We linguistically calibrate Llama 2 7B and find in automated and human evaluations of long-form generations that it is significantly more calibrated than strong finetuned factuality baselines with comparable accuracy. These findings generalize under significant domain shifts to scientific and biomedical questions and to an entirely held-out person biography generation task. Our results demonstrate that long-form generations may be calibrated end-to-end by constructing an objective in the space of the predictions that users make in downstream decision-making.

The training procedure has two stages. Supervised fine-tuning first teaches the model to include confidence statements in extended answers. These findings support training uncertainty communication end to end through its effect on users’ predictions, rather than treating confidence wording as an isolated output feature.
summary.tldr: Training long-form answers around users’ downstream probability judgments improves linguistic calibration while maintaining accuracy comparable to factuality baselines.

title: Linguistic Calibration of Long-Form Generations

abstract: Generating long-form 44.1kHz stereo audio from text prompts can be computationally demanding. Further, most previous works do not tackle that music and sound effects naturally vary in their duration. Our research focuses on the efficient generation of long-form, variable-length stereo music and sounds at 44.1kHz using text prompts with a generative model. It is based on latent diffusion, with its latent defined by a fully-convolutional variational autoencoder. The generative model is conditioned on text prompts as well as timing embeddings, allowing for fine control over both the content and length of the generated music and sounds. It is capable of rendering stereo signals of up to 95 sec at 44.1kHz in 8 sec on an A100 GPU. Despite its compute efficiency and fast inference, the proposed model is one of the best in two public text-to-music and -audio benchmarks and, differently from state-of-the-art models, can generate music with structure and stereo sounds.

paragraphs: Text-guided audio generation must handle both content and duration: a sound effect and a musical passage naturally occupy different amounts of time. Producing long stereo signals at 44.1 kHz also creates a substantial computational burden. This paper addresses these requirements together with a timing-conditioned latent diffusion model.

A fully convolutional variational autoencoder defines the latent representation in which diffusion operates. The generator receives both a text prompt and timing embeddings, allowing control over what it produces and how long the output lasts. Duration is therefore an explicit conditioning input alongside the requested musical or acoustic content.

The model can generate up to 95 seconds of 44.1 kHz stereo audio in eight seconds on an A100 GPU. The authors also report that it ranks among the best models on two public text-to-music and text-to-audio benchmarks. Its demonstrated capabilities include structured music and stereo sounds. These results connect efficient generation with useful control over length and content, rather than measuring speed alone.
summary.tldr: Timing-conditioned latent diffusion generates controllable stereo audio, rendering up to 95 seconds in eight seconds on an A100 GPU.

title: Fast Timing-Conditioned Latent Audio Diffusion

abstract: Transformers have recently revolutionized many domains in modern machine learning and one salient discovery is their remarkable in-context learning capability, where models can solve an unseen task by utilizing task-specific prompts without further parameters fine-tuning. This also inspired recent theoretical studies aiming to understand the in-context learning mechanism of transformers, which however focused only on linear transformers. In this work, we take the first step toward studying the learning dynamics of a one-layer transformer with softmax attention trained via gradient descent in order to in-context learn linear function classes. We consider a structured data model, where each token is randomly sampled from a set of feature vectors in either balanced or imbalanced fashion. For data with balanced features, we establish the finite-time convergence guarantee with near-zero prediction error by navigating our analysis over two phases of the training dynamics of the attention map. More notably, for data with imbalanced features, we show that the learning dynamics take a stage-wise convergence process, where the transformer first converges to a near-zero prediction error for the query tokens of dominant features, and then converges later to a near-zero error for query tokens of under-represented features, via one and four training phases. Our proof features new techniques for analyzing the competing strengths of two types of attention weights, the change of which determines different training phases.

paragraphs: This paper studies how training gives a transformer the ability to learn linear functions from examples supplied in its prompt. The analysis concerns a one-layer transformer with softmax attention trained by gradient descent. It uses a structured data model in which tokens are sampled from a set of feature vectors with either balanced or imbalanced frequencies.

For balanced features, the authors prove finite-time convergence to near-zero prediction error. Their analysis separates attention learning into two phases. For imbalanced features, convergence happens in stages: prediction error becomes small for queries involving dominant features before it becomes small for queries involving underrepresented features.

The proof tracks competition between two types of attention weights, whose changing strengths determine the training phases. Dominant and underrepresented features follow one-phase and four-phase convergence descriptions, respectively. These results provide a theoretical account of how feature frequency can shape learning progress in the specified setting. They also extend convergence analysis beyond the linear-transformer models emphasized by earlier theoretical work to a model with softmax attention.
summary.tldr: A convergence analysis of a one-layer softmax transformer shows that imbalanced feature frequencies cause common features to be learned before underrepresented ones.

title: In-context Convergence of Transformers

abstract: Positive and Unlabeled (PU) learning refers to a special case of binary classification, and technically, it aims to induce a binary classifier from a few labeled positive training instances and loads of unlabeled instances. In this paper, we derive a theorem indicating that the probability boundary of the asymmetric disambiguation-free expected risk of PU learning is controlled by its asymmetric penalty, and we further empirically evaluated this theorem. Inspired by the theorem and its empirical evaluations, we propose an easy-to-implement two-stage PU learning method, namely Positive and Unlabeled Learning with Controlled Probability Boundary Fence (PULCPBF). In the first stage, we train a set of weak binary classifiers concerning different probability boundaries by minimizing the asymmetric disambiguation-free empirical risks with specific asymmetric penalty values. We can interpret these induced weak binary classifiers as a probability boundary fence. For each unlabeled instance, we can use the predictions to locate its class posterior probability and generate a stochastic label. In the second stage, we train a strong binary classifier over labeled positive training instances and all unlabeled instances with stochastic labels in a self-training manner. Extensive empirical results demonstrate that PULCPBF can achieve competitive performance compared with the existing PU learning baselines.

paragraphs: Positive and unlabeled learning builds a binary classifier from a small set of labeled positive examples and a larger unlabeled collection. The challenge is to extract useful supervision without already knowing which unlabeled examples are positive. This paper develops a two-stage approach grounded in a theorem connecting an asymmetric risk's probability boundary to its penalty.

The first stage trains several weak classifiers using different asymmetric penalties. Each classifier corresponds to a different probability boundary, and together they form a boundary fence. Their predictions help locate an unlabeled example's class posterior probability, which is then used to generate a stochastic label. Multiple boundaries therefore provide information beyond a single binary decision.

The second stage trains a stronger classifier using the original positive examples and the newly labeled collection in a self-training procedure. The authors empirically evaluate the motivating theorem and report competitive performance against existing positive-and-unlabeled learning baselines. The contribution links a controllable property of the training objective to a practical mechanism for constructing supervision from unlabeled examples.
summary.tldr: PULCPBF uses weak classifiers with controlled probability boundaries to generate stochastic labels and train a stronger positive-and-unlabeled classifier.

title: Positive and Unlabeled Learning with Controlled Probability Boundary Fence

abstract: Prompt-based learning has been demonstrated as a compelling paradigm contributing to large language models’ tremendous success (LLMs). Inspired by their success in language tasks, existing research has leveraged LLMs in embodied instruction following and task planning. In this work, we tackle the problem of training a robot to understand multimodal prompts, interleaving vision signals with text descriptions. This type of task poses a major challenge to robots’ capability to understand the interconnection and complementarity between vision and language signals. In this work, we introduce an effective framework that learns a policy to perform robot manipulation with multimodal prompts from multi-task expert trajectories. Our methods consist of a two-stage training pipeline that performs inverse dynamics pretraining and multi-task finetuning. To facilitate multimodal understanding, we design our multimodal prompt encoder by augmenting a pretrained LM with a residual connection to the visual input and model the dependencies among action dimensions. Empirically, we evaluate the efficacy of our method on the VIMA-BENCH and establish a new state-of-the-art (10% improvement in success rate). Moreover, we demonstrate that our model exhibits remarkable in-context learning ability.

paragraphs: This paper trains a robot manipulation policy to follow prompts that interleave text with visual information. Such prompts require the robot to understand how the two kinds of input complement each other. The framework learns from expert trajectories spanning multiple tasks, connecting multimodal instructions with the actions needed to perform manipulation.

Training proceeds through inverse dynamics pretraining followed by multi-task fine-tuning. The prompt encoder augments a pretrained language model with a residual connection to the visual input, providing a direct architectural connection for visual information. The method also models dependencies among action dimensions, addressing coordination in the policy's outputs alongside understanding of its inputs.
