These results support the combined training and architecture choices for learning manipulation from multimodal prompts, with evidence covering both task completion and the model's ability to use information provided in context.
summary.tldr: A two-stage training framework improves robot manipulation from interleaved visual and textual prompts, reporting a 10% success-rate improvement on VIMA-BENCH.

title: Mastering Robot Manipulation with Multimodal Prompts through Pretraining and Multi-task Fine-tuning

abstract: Large language models display remarkable capabilities in logical and mathematical reasoning, allowing them to solve complex tasks. Interestingly, these abilities emerge in networks trained on the simple task of next-token prediction. In this work, we present a theoretical framework for studying auto-regressive next-token predictors. We demonstrate that even simple models such as linear next-token predictors, trained on Chain-of-Thought (CoT) data, can approximate any function efficiently computed by a Turing machine. We introduce a new complexity measure—length complexity—which measures the number of intermediate tokens in a CoT sequence required to approximate some target function, and analyze the interplay between length complexity and other notions of complexity. Finally, we show experimentally that simple next-token predictors, such as linear networks and shallow Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs), display non-trivial performance on text generation and arithmetic tasks. Our results demonstrate that the power of today’s LLMs can be attributed, to a great extent, to the auto-regressive next-token training scheme, and not necessarily to a particular choice of architecture.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how training a model to predict the next token can support complex computation. It develops a theoretical framework for autoregressive predictors, focusing on the contribution of the prediction process itself. The motivation is that substantial reasoning abilities appear in language models despite their seemingly simple training objective.

The central result shows that even linear next-token predictors, when trained on chain-of-thought data, can approximate any function efficiently computed by a Turing machine. The chain of intermediate tokens is an essential part of this statement. To study its role, the authors introduce length complexity: the number of intermediate tokens needed to approximate a target function.

The paper analyzes how this measure interacts with other notions of computational complexity. Experiments also find nontrivial text-generation and arithmetic performance in linear networks and shallow multilayer perceptrons. These findings support the importance of autoregressive training as a source of capability. They do not require attributing all language-model performance to a particular architecture, or imply that intermediate computation comes without a token-length cost.
summary.tldr: Simple next-token predictors trained on chain-of-thought data can approximate efficiently computable functions, with intermediate-token length becoming a key complexity measure.

title: Auto-Regressive Next-Token Predictors are Universal Learners

abstract: A central approach to AI-safety research has been to generate aligned AI systems: i.e. systems that do not deceive users and yield actions or recommendations that humans might judge as consistent with their intentions and goals. Here we argue that truthful AIs aligned solely to human intent are insufficient and that preservation of long-term agency of humans may be a more robust standard that may need to be separated and explicitly optimized for. We discuss the science of intent and control and how human intent can be manipulated and we provide a formal definition of agency-preserving AI-human interactions focusing on forward-looking explicit agency evaluations. Our work points to a novel pathway for human harm in AI-human interactions and proposes solutions to this challenge.

paragraphs: This position paper examines whether truthful AI systems that follow human intentions provide a sufficient standard for safe interaction. The authors argue that alignment to intent alone is insufficient because human intentions can themselves be manipulated. An interaction can therefore appear consistent with a person’s goals while raising concerns about their longer-term agency.

The paper draws on the science of intent and control to develop this argument. It provides a formal definition of agency-preserving interactions between people and AI, emphasizing explicit evaluations that look ahead. This directs attention toward how an interaction affects a person’s future agency, extending evaluation beyond whether a current recommendation matches a stated intention.

The authors propose that preserving long-term human agency may be a more robust standard and may need its own explicit optimization objective. They identify a potential pathway to harm in human–AI interaction and propose responses to it. As a position contribution, the paper advances a conceptual and formal case for treating agency preservation as a distinct concern in alignment.
summary.tldr: The authors argue that truthful intent alignment is insufficient and propose explicitly evaluating and preserving people’s long-term agency.

title: Position: Intent-aligned AI Systems Must Optimize for Agency Preservation

abstract: Estimating high-dimensional covariance matrices is crucial in various domains. This work considers a scenario where two collaborating agents access disjoint dimensions of $m$ samples from a high–dimensional random vector, and they can only communicate a limited number of bits to a central server, which wants to accurately approximate the covariance matrix. We analyze the fundamental trade–off between communication cost, number of samples, and estimation accuracy. We prove a lower bound on the error achievable by any estimator, highlighting the impact of dimensions, number of samples, and communication budget. Furthermore, we present an algorithm that achieves this lower bound up to a logarithmic factor, demonstrating its near-optimality in practical settings.

paragraphs: A covariance matrix summarizes how different dimensions of data vary together. This paper considers estimating that matrix when the information is split between two collaborating agents. Each agent observes a separate set of dimensions from the same collection of samples, and both must send limited-bit messages to a central server that constructs the estimate.

The authors analyze how estimation accuracy depends jointly on the number of dimensions, the number of samples, and the communication budget. They prove a lower bound on the error achievable by any estimator in this setting. That bound identifies a fundamental restriction imposed by the available data and communication, rather than a shortcoming of one particular estimation method.

The paper then supplies an algorithm whose error matches the lower bound up to a logarithmic factor. Pairing an achievable result with an impossibility bound makes the near-optimality claim meaningful: the proposed procedure approaches the best accuracy permitted by the studied distributed setup. The contribution characterizes how communication constraints enter an otherwise statistical estimation problem.
summary.tldr: The paper bounds the best possible covariance-estimation accuracy under limited communication and gives an algorithm that approaches that bound.

title: Fundamental Limits of Distributed Covariance Matrix Estimation Under Communication Constraints

abstract: The performance of Markov chain Monte Carlo samplers strongly depends on the properties of the target distribution such as its covariance structure, the location of its probability mass and its tail behavior. We explore the use of bijective affine transformations of the sample space to improve the properties of the target distribution and thereby the performance of samplers running in the transformed space. In particular, we propose a flexible and user-friendly scheme for adaptively learning the affine transformation during sampling. Moreover, the combination of our scheme with Gibbsian polar slice sampling is shown to produce samples of high quality at comparatively low computational cost in several settings based on real-world data.

paragraphs: Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling can perform very differently depending on the target distribution's geometry. Relevant properties include correlations between variables, where probability mass lies, and tail behavior. This paper investigates improving sampling by changing the coordinates in which a sampler operates.

The method uses bijective affine transformations, combining a linear transformation with a shift while preserving a one-to-one correspondence between points. The sampler runs in the transformed space, whose target distribution can have more favorable properties. The authors propose a flexible scheme that learns the transformation adaptively during sampling, making the coordinate adjustment part of the procedure.

They combine this tuning approach with Gibbsian polar slice sampling and test it in several settings based on real-world data. The resulting method produces high-quality samples at comparatively low computational cost. These findings support adaptive coordinate transformations as a practical way to improve sampler performance, with the reported evidence specifically including the combination with Gibbsian polar slice sampling.
summary.tldr: Adaptively learned affine coordinate transformations improve MCMC sampling, with favorable results when paired with Gibbsian polar slice sampling.

title: Parallel Affine Transformation Tuning of Markov Chain Monte Carlo

abstract: The explosion of visual content available online underscores the requirement for an accurate machine assessor to robustly evaluate scores across diverse types of visual contents. While recent studies have demonstrated the exceptional potentials of large multi-modality models (LMMs) on a wide range of related fields, in this work, we explore how to teach them for visual rating aligning with human opinions. Observing that human raters only learn and judge discrete text-defined levels in subjective studies, we propose to emulate this subjective process and teach LMMs with text-defined rating levels instead of scores. The proposed Q-Align achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on image quality assessment (IQA), image aesthetic assessment (IAA), as well as video quality assessment (VQA) under the original LMM structure. With the syllabus, we further unify the three tasks into one model, termed the OneAlign. Our experiments demonstrate the advantage of discrete levels over direct scores on training, and that LMMs can learn beyond the discrete levels and provide effective finer-grained evaluations. Code and weights will be released.

paragraphs: A machine that rates images or videos should produce judgments aligned with human opinion. Q-Align studies how to teach that ability to large multimodal models. Its starting observation is that people in subjective rating studies learn and use discrete levels described in words, rather than learning to assign unrestricted numerical scores directly.

The method therefore trains models with text-defined rating levels. This changes how the task is taught while retaining the original multimodal model structure. The same teaching approach is also used to combine image quality assessment, image aesthetic assessment, and video quality assessment into a single model called OneAlign.

Experiments report state-of-the-art accuracy for Q-Align across all three assessment tasks and show an advantage for discrete-level training over direct-score training. The models can also provide effective evaluations finer than the levels used to teach them. This means a coarse verbal training scale need not force equally coarse output judgments, making the choice of supervision format central to the paper's contribution.
summary.tldr: Q-Align improves visual assessment by teaching multimodal models text-defined rating levels, while still enabling finer-grained evaluations.

title: Q-Align: Teaching LMMs for Visual Scoring via Discrete Text-Defined Levels

abstract: This paper studies the theoretical framework of the alignment process of generative models with Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF). We consider a standard mathematical formulation, the reverse-KL regularized contextual bandit for RLHF. Despite its widespread practical application, a rigorous theoretical analysis of this formulation remains open. We investigate its behavior in three distinct settings—offline, online, and hybrid—and propose efficient algorithms with finite-sample theoretical guarantees. Moving towards practical applications, our framework, with a robust approximation of the information-theoretical policy improvement oracle, naturally gives rise to several novel RLHF algorithms. This includes an iterative version of the Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) algorithm for online settings, and a multi-step rejection sampling strategy for offline scenarios. Our empirical evaluations on real-world alignment experiment of large language model demonstrate that these proposed methods significantly surpass existing strong baselines, such as DPO and Rejection Sampling Optimization (RSO), showcasing the connections between solid theoretical foundations and their potent practical implementations.

paragraphs: This paper studies the mathematical foundations of aligning generative models with human preferences. It uses a contextual-bandit formulation with reverse-KL regularization, which balances preference improvement against a penalty for changing the policy. The authors analyze this widely used formulation in offline, online, and hybrid learning settings.

They propose efficient algorithms with finite-sample guarantees, then connect the theory to practical procedures through a robust approximation of a policy-improvement oracle. Here, the oracle represents an idealized improvement operation that must be approximated to obtain a usable algorithm. This connection yields an iterative version of Direct Preference Optimization for online learning and a multistep rejection-sampling strategy for offline learning.

In the reported language-model alignment experiments, these methods significantly outperform strong baselines, including DPO and Rejection Sampling Optimization. The contribution is both analytical and practical: it establishes guarantees within the stated mathematical framework and uses that framework to derive algorithms that perform well empirically. The online and offline variants also show how a shared theoretical treatment can lead to different procedures depending on how feedback is available.
summary.tldr: A theoretical RLHF framework yields finite-sample guarantees and practical iterative preference-learning methods that outperform the reported strong baselines.

title: Iterative Preference Learning from Human Feedback: Bridging Theory and Practice for RLHF under KL-constraint

abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) have exhibited superb power in many graph related tasks. Existing GNNs can be categorized into spatial GNNs and spectral GNNs. The spatial GNNs primarily capture the local information around each node, while the spectral GNNs are able to operate on the frequency signals of the entire graph. However, most, if not all, existing spectral GNNs are faced with two limitations: (1) the polynomial limitation that for most spectral GNNs, the expressive power in the spectral domain is limited to polynomial filters; and (2) the transductive limitation that most spectral GNNs can only be applied to the transductive setting on relatively small-scale graphs. In this paper, we propose a novel spectral graph neural network named SLOG to solve the above two limitations. For the polynomial limitation, SLOG proposes a novel real-valued filter with geometric interpretability, mathematical feasibility and adaptive filtering ability to go beyond polynomial. For the transductive limitation, SLOG combines the subgraph sampling technique in spatial GNNs and the signal processing technique in spectral GNNs together to make itself tailored to the inductive setting on large-scale graphs. Extensive experimental results on 16 datasets demonstrate the superiority of SLOG in inductive homophilic and heterophilic node classification task.

The findings support the combination of more flexible spectral filters and scalable sampling. The contribution is an architecture that broadens how spectral methods can be used while demonstrating benefits across both tested types of graph structure.
summary.tldr: SLOG combines non-polynomial spectral filtering with subgraph sampling for inductive classification on large graphs.

title: SLOG: An Inductive Spectral Graph Neural Network Beyond Polynomial Filter

abstract: We present a novel perspective on temporal point processes (TPPs) by reformulating their intensity processes as solutions to stochastic differential equations (SDEs). In particular, we first prove the equivalent SDE formulations of several classical TPPs, including Poisson processes, Hawkes processes, and self-correcting processes. Based on these proofs, we introduce a unified TPP framework called Neural Jump-Diffusion Temporal Point Process (NJDTPP), whose intensity process is governed by a neural jump-diffusion SDE (NJDSDE) where the drift, diffusion, and jump coefficient functions are parameterized by neural networks. Compared to previous works, NJDTPP exhibits model flexibility in capturing intensity dynamics without relying on any specific functional form, and provides theoretical guarantees regarding the existence and uniqueness of the solution to the proposed NJDSDE. Experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that NJDTPP is capable of capturing the dynamics of intensity processes in different scenarios and significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art TPP models in prediction tasks.

paragraphs: Temporal point processes describe events occurring over time through an intensity that governs their occurrence. This paper reformulates that evolving intensity using stochastic differential equations. It first establishes equivalent formulations for several classical models, including Poisson, Hawkes, and self-correcting processes, creating a mathematical connection between familiar event models and this alternative representation.

The proposed Neural Jump-Diffusion Temporal Point Process builds on that connection. Its intensity follows an equation with drift, diffusion, and jump components, each parameterized by a neural network. These components allow the model to represent evolving intensity through continuous change, randomness, and jumps, without committing to a particular fixed functional form for those coefficient functions.

The paper provides theoretical guarantees for existence and uniqueness of the proposed equation’s solution. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show that the framework captures intensity dynamics across different scenarios and significantly outperforms state-of-the-art temporal point process models on the evaluated prediction tasks. The contribution combines flexible neural parameterization with a mathematically grounded description of how event intensity evolves.
summary.tldr: NJDTPP models event intensity with a neural jump-diffusion equation, combining flexible dynamics with existence and uniqueness guarantees.

title: Neural Jump-Diffusion Temporal Point Processes

abstract: Increasing experimental evidence suggests that the human hippocampus, evolutionarily shaped by spatial navigation tasks, also plays an important role in language comprehension, indicating a shared computational mechanism for both functions. However, the specific relationship between the hippocampal formation’s computational mechanism in spatial navigation and its role in language processing remains elusive. To investigate this question, we develop a prefrontal-hippocampal-entorhinal model (which called PHE-trinity) that features two key aspects: 1) the use of a modular continuous attractor neural network to represent syntactic structure, akin to the grid network in the entorhinal cortex; 2) the creation of two separate input streams, mirroring the factorized structure-content representation found in the hippocampal formation. We evaluate our model on language command parsing tasks, specifically using the SCAN dataset. Our findings include: 1) attractor dynamics can facilitate systematic generalization and efficient learning from limited data; 2) through visualization and reverse engineering, we unravel a potential dynamic mechanism for grid network representing syntactic structure. Our research takes an initial step in uncovering the dynamic mechanism shared by spatial navigation and language information processing.

paragraphs: Evidence linking the hippocampus to both spatial navigation and language comprehension motivates this paper's search for a shared computational mechanism. The authors build PHE-trinity, a model inspired by the prefrontal, hippocampal, and entorhinal systems. Its purpose is to investigate whether mechanisms associated with spatial representation can also support the structured processing needed for language commands.

The model has two central features. A modular continuous attractor neural network represents syntactic structure, drawing an analogy with entorhinal grid networks. Two separate input streams reflect the separation of structure and content described in the hippocampal formation. Together, these choices make the relationship between language structure and the network's dynamics part of the model's design.

Evaluations on the SCAN command-parsing dataset show that attractor dynamics can support systematic generalization and learning from limited data. Visualization and reverse engineering also reveal a possible dynamic mechanism through which a grid network could represent syntax. The work provides an initial computational account of a potential connection between navigation and language processing, with the biological interpretation presented as a possibility supported by the model.
summary.tldr: PHE-trinity uses navigation-inspired attractor dynamics to support language parsing, systematic generalization, and learning from limited data.

title: Leveraging Attractor Dynamics in Spatial Navigation for Better Language Parsing

abstract: Despite the constant development of new bias mitigation methods for machine learning, no method consistently succeeds, and a fundamental question remains unanswered: when and why do bias mitigation techniques fail? In this paper, we hypothesise that a key factor may be the often-overlooked but crucial step shared by many bias mitigation methods: the definition of subgroups. To investigate this, we conduct a comprehensive evaluation of state-of-the-art bias mitigation methods across multiple vision and language classification tasks, systematically varying subgroup definitions, including coarse, fine-grained, intersectional, and noisy subgroups. Our findings reveal that subgroup choice significantly impacts performance, with certain groupings paradoxically leading to worse outcomes than no mitigation at all. They suggest that observing a disparity between a set of subgroups is not a sufficient reason to use those subgroups for mitigation. Through theoretical analysis, we explain these phenomena and uncover a counter-intuitive insight that, in some cases, improving fairness with respect to a particular set of subgroups is best achieved by using a different set of subgroups for mitigation. Our work highlights the importance of careful subgroup definition in bias mitigation and presents it as an alternative lever for improving the robustness and fairness of machine learning models.

paragraphs: Bias-mitigation methods often operate on defined groups of examples, but the choice of groups can receive less attention than the method itself. This paper investigates whether subgroup definition helps explain why mitigation techniques sometimes fail. The authors systematically vary coarse, fine-grained, intersectional, and noisy groupings across vision and language classification tasks.

Their evaluation finds that subgroup choice substantially changes mitigation performance. Some definitions produce worse outcomes than applying no mitigation. This means that observing a disparity across a particular grouping is not, by itself, sufficient justification for using that same grouping to guide training. How a disparity is measured and how mitigation is organized can require different choices.

The authors provide theoretical analysis explaining these effects. In some cases, fairness for one set of subgroups improves most when mitigation uses another set. This makes subgroup definition a substantive part of the intervention, alongside the choice of algorithm. The findings support treating group construction as a way to improve both the robustness and fairness of mitigation.
summary.tldr: Subgroup definitions can determine whether bias mitigation helps or harms, and the best mitigation groups may differ from the groups used to measure fairness.

title: Subgroups Matter for Robust Bias Mitigation

abstract: Universal Domain Adaptation (UniDA) addresses unsupervised domain adaptation where target classes may differ arbitrarily from source ones, except for a shared subset. A widely used approach, partial domain matching (PDM), aligns only shared classes but struggles in extreme cases where many source classes are absent in the target domain, underperforming the most naive baseline that trains on only source data. In this work, we identify that the failure of PDM for extreme UniDA stems from dimensional collapse (DC) in target representations. To address target DC, we propose to jointly leverage the alignment and uniformity techniques in self-supervised learning on the unlabeled target data to preserve the intrinsic structure of the learned representations. Our experimental results confirm that SSL consistently advances PDM and delivers new state-of-the-art results across a broader benchmark of UniDA scenarios with different portions of shared classes, representing a crucial step toward truly comprehensive UniDA. Project page: https://dc-unida.github.io/

paragraphs: Universal domain adaptation handles cases where source and target datasets share some classes but may otherwise have very different class sets. Partial domain matching aligns the shared classes. The paper studies an extreme setting where many source classes are missing from the target, and this matching approach can perform worse than training on source data alone.

The authors identify dimensional collapse in target representations as the cause of this failure. In effect, the learned representation loses useful dimensions of the target data’s structure. Their remedy applies self-supervised learning to unlabeled target examples, combining alignment and uniformity techniques to preserve that structure while carrying out domain adaptation.

Experiments span a broader range of universal adaptation scenarios with different proportions of shared classes. The self-supervised approach consistently improves partial domain matching in those evaluations and achieves new state-of-the-art results. The findings explain why adaptation can fail severely when class overlap becomes small and show that maintaining the target representation’s structure helps matching work across a wider range of class-overlap conditions.
summary.tldr: Self-supervised alignment and uniformity counter dimensional collapse, improving universal domain adaptation across different levels of class overlap.

title: Tackling Dimensional Collapse toward Comprehensive Universal Domain Adaptation

abstract: Diffusion models have demonstrated remarkable performance in generating unimodal data across various tasks, including image, video, and text generation. On the contrary, the joint generation of multimodal data through diffusion models is still in the early stages of exploration. Existing approaches heavily rely on external preprocessing protocols, such as tokenizers and variational autoencoders, to harmonize varied data representations into a unified, unimodal format. This process heavily demands the high accuracy of encoders and decoders, which can be problematic for applications with limited data. To lift this restriction, we propose a novel framework for building multimodal diffusion models on arbitrary state spaces, enabling native generation of coupled data across different modalities. By introducing an innovative decoupled noise schedule for each modality, we enable both unconditional and modality-conditioned generation within a single model simultaneously. We empirically validate our approach for text-image generation and mixed-type tabular data synthesis, demonstrating that it achieves competitive performance. Code is available at https://github.com/KevinRojas1499/Diffuse-Everything.

paragraphs: Generating several kinds of data together requires a model to capture their relationships while handling their different representations. Existing multimodal diffusion approaches often use tokenizers or variational autoencoders to turn these representations into a common format. That makes generation depend heavily on encoder and decoder accuracy, which can be problematic when training data is limited.

This paper proposes a framework for constructing diffusion models on arbitrary state spaces, allowing coupled modalities to be generated in their native representations. A key component is a separate noise schedule for each modality. These decoupled schedules let one model support both unconditional generation and generation conditioned on a supplied modality.

The authors evaluate the framework on text-image generation and the synthesis of tabular data containing mixed data types, reporting competitive performance. These applications demonstrate the approach across two different forms of heterogeneous data. Its contribution is a route to joint generation that reduces dependence on external conversion into a single representational format while accommodating multiple generation modes.
summary.tldr: A multimodal diffusion framework uses modality-specific noise schedules to generate coupled data natively and support conditional and unconditional generation.

title: Diffuse Everything: Multimodal Diffusion Models on Arbitrary State Spaces

abstract: Imposing input-output constraints in multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) plays a pivotal role in many real world applications. Monotonicity in particular is a common requirement in applications that need transparent and robust machine learning models. Conventional techniques for imposing monotonicity in MLPs by construction involve the use of non-negative weight constraints and bounded activation functions, which poses well known optimization challenges. In this work, we generalize previous theoretical results, showing that MLPs with non-negative weight constraint and activations that saturate on alternating sides are universal approximators for monotonic functions. Additionally, we show an equivalence between saturation side in the activations and sign of the weight constraint. This connection allows us to prove that MLPs with convex monotone activations and non-positive constrained weights also qualify as universal approximators, in contrast to their non-negative constrained counterparts. This results provide theoretical grounding to the empirical effectiveness observed in previous works, while leading to possible architectural simplification. Moreover, to further alleviate the optimization difficulties, we propose an alternative formulation that allows the network to adjust its activations according to the sign of the weights. This eliminates the requirement for weight reparameterization, easing initialization and improving training stability. Experimental evaluation reinforce the validity of the theoretical results, showing that our novel approach compares favorably to traditional monotonic architectures.

Building this monotonicity into a neural network can make the constraint reliable, but conventional constructions combine non-negative weights with bounded activation functions, creating optimization difficulties. This paper expands the theoretical options for constructing networks that can approximate monotonic functions.

title: Advancing Constrained Monotonic Neural Networks: Achieving Universal Approximation Beyond Bounded Activations

abstract: Pipeline parallelism (PP) is widely used for training large language models (LLMs), yet its scalability is often constrained by high activation memory consumption as the number of in-flight microbatches grows with the degree of PP. In this paper, we focus on addressing this challenge by leveraging the under-explored memory offload strategy in PP. With empirical study, we discover that in the majority of standard configurations, at least half, and potentially all, of the activations can be offloaded with negligible overhead. In the cases where full overload is not possible, we introduce a novel selective offload strategy that decreases peak activation memory in a better-than-linear manner. Furthermore, we integrate memory offload with other techniques to jointly consider overall throughput and memory limitation. Our experiments proves that the per-device activation memory effectively reduces with the total number of stages, making PP a stronger alternative than TP, offering up to a 19% acceleration with even lower memory consumption.

paragraphs: Pipeline parallelism distributes large-model training across stages, but storing activations can limit its scalability. As the pipeline grows, more microbatches remain in flight, increasing the associated memory demand. This paper studies memory offloading as a way to reduce that pressure while preserving useful training throughput.

An empirical study finds that, in most standard configurations examined, at least half of the activations—and potentially all of them—can be offloaded with negligible overhead. In the experiments, activation memory per device decreases as the total number of stages increases. The resulting pipeline approach offers acceleration of up to 19% over tensor parallelism while using less memory. These results show how managing activation storage can change the practical scaling behavior of pipeline training, with the extent of inexpensive offloading dependent on the configuration.
summary.tldr: PipeOffload reduces pipeline-training activation memory through offloading, achieving up to 19% acceleration over tensor parallelism in the experiments.

title: PipeOffload: Improving Scalability of Pipeline Parallelism with Memory Optimization

abstract: Many important phenomena in scientific fields like climate, neuroscience, and epidemiology are naturally represented as spatiotemporal gridded data with complex interactions. Inferring causal relationships from these data is a challenging problem compounded by the high dimensionality of such data and the correlations between spatially proximate points. We present SPACY (SPAtiotemporal Causal discoverY), a novel framework based on variational inference, designed to model latent time series and their causal relationships from spatiotemporal data. SPACY alleviates the high-dimensional challenge by discovering causal structures in the latent space. To aggregate spatially proximate, correlated grid points, we use spatial factors, parametrized by spatial kernel functions, to map observational time series to latent representations. Theoretically, we generalize the problem to a continuous spatial domain and establish identifiability when the observations arise from a nonlinear, invertible function of the product of latent series and spatial factors. Using this approach, we avoid assumptions that are often unverifiable, including those about instantaneous effects or sufficient variability. Empirically, SPACY outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on synthetic data, even in challenging settings where existing methods struggle, while remaining scalable for large grids. SPACY also identifies key known phenomena from real-world climate data. An implementation of SPACY is available at https://github.com/Rose-STL-Lab/SPACY/

The framework discovers latent time series and studies causal connections among them, reducing the dimensionality of the causal discovery problem.

title: Discovering Latent Causal Graphs from Spatiotemporal Data

abstract: One of the key technologies for the success of Large Language Models (LLMs) is preference alignment. However, a notable side effect of preference alignment is poor calibration: while the pre-trained models are typically well-calibrated, LLMs tend to become poorly calibrated after alignment with human preferences. In this paper, we investigate why preference alignment affects calibration and how to address this issue. For the first question, we observe that the preference collapse issue in alignment undesirably generalizes to the calibration scenario, causing LLMs to exhibit overconfidence and poor calibration. To address this, we demonstrate the importance of fine-tuning with domain-specific knowledge to alleviate the overconfidence issue. To further analyze whether this affects the model’s performance, we categorize models into two regimes: calibratable and non-calibratable, defined by bounds of Expected Calibration Error (ECE). In the calibratable regime, we propose a calibration-aware fine-tuning approach to achieve proper calibration without compromising LLMs’ performance. However, as models are further fine-tuned for better performance, they enter the non-calibratable regime. For this case, we develop an EM-algorithm-based ECE regularization for the fine-tuning loss to maintain low calibration error. Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of the proposed methods.

paragraphs: A calibrated language model’s confidence should reflect how often its answers are correct. This paper examines why preference alignment can disrupt that relationship. The authors observe that preference collapse extends into calibration, producing overconfidence, even though pretrained models are typically well calibrated before alignment.

They show that fine-tuning with domain-specific knowledge is important for reducing overconfidence. To understand when calibration can improve without harming performance, they distinguish calibratable and non-calibratable regimes using bounds on Expected Calibration Error. Within the calibratable regime, their calibration-aware fine-tuning approach achieves proper calibration while preserving model performance.

Experiments validate the proposed methods. The distinction between regimes matters because it changes the intervention: ordinary calibration-aware adaptation is supplemented by explicit error regularization as performance-oriented training progresses.
summary.tldr: Calibration-aware fine-tuning and an EM-based regularizer address overconfidence introduced by preference alignment across two calibration regimes.

title: Restoring Calibration for Aligned Large Language Models: A Calibration-Aware Fine-Tuning Approach

abstract: Diffusion models have recently emerged as a powerful tool for planning. However, unlike Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS)—whose performance naturally improves with inference-time computation scaling—standard diffusion-based planners offer only limited avenues for the scalability. In this paper, we introduce Monte Carlo Tree Diffusion (MCTD), a novel framework that integrates the generative strength of diffusion models with the adaptive search capabilities of MCTS. Our method reconceptualizes denoising as a tree-structured process, allowing partially denoised plans to be iteratively evaluated, pruned, and refined. By selectively expanding promising trajectories while retaining the flexibility to revisit and improve suboptimal branches, MCTD achieves the benefits of MCTS such as controlling exploration-exploitation trade-offs within the diffusion framework. originalAbstract: Diffusion models have recently emerged as a powerful tool for planning. However, unlike Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS)—whose performance naturally improves with inference-time computation scaling—standard diffusion-based planners offer only limited avenues for the scalability. In this paper, we introduce Monte Carlo Tree Diffusion (MCTD), a novel framework that integrates the generative strength of diffusion models with the adaptive search capabilities of MCTS. Our method reconceptualizes denoising as a tree-structured process, allowing partially denoised plans to be iteratively evaluated, pruned, and refined. By selectively expanding promising trajectories while retaining the flexibility to revisit and improve suboptimal branches, MCTD achieves the benefits of MCTS such as controlling exploration-exploitation trade-offs within the diffusion framework. paragraphs: Diffusion models can generate plans, but standard diffusion planners have limited ways to turn additional inference computation into better solutions. Monte Carlo Tree Diffusion, or MCTD, addresses this by combining diffusion generation with Monte Carlo Tree Search. The aim is to make planning more deliberative as additional computation becomes available.

MCTD treats denoising as a branching search process. Partially denoised plans can be evaluated, pruned, and refined, allowing the search to allocate more effort to promising trajectories. It can also revisit and improve less successful branches. This gives the planner a way to balance exploring alternatives against developing candidates that already look useful.

On challenging long-horizon tasks, the authors report that MCTD outperforms diffusion baselines and produces better solutions as inference-time computation increases. The results support the value of organizing generation as adaptive search. Additional computation can then be directed toward evaluating and refining alternative plans within the diffusion process, rather than leaving the planner with only limited scaling options.
summary.tldr: MCTD turns diffusion denoising into adaptive tree search, improving long-horizon plans as inference computation increases in experiments.

title: Monte Carlo Tree Diffusion for System 2 Planning

abstract: Recent advancements in video generation have enabled models to synthesize high-quality, minute-long videos. However, generating even longer videos with temporal coherence remains a major challenge and existing length extrapolation methods lead to temporal repetition or motion deceleration. In this work, we systematically analyze the role of frequency components in positional embeddings and identify an intrinsic frequency that primarily governs extrapolation behavior. Based on this insight, we propose RIFLEx, a minimal yet effective approach that reduces the intrinsic frequency to suppress repetition while preserving motion consistency, without requiring any additional modifications. RIFLEx offers a true free lunch—achieving high-quality $2\times$ extrapolation on state-of-the-art video diffusion transformers in a completely training-free manner. Moreover, it enhances quality and enables $3\times$ extrapolation by minimal fine-tuning without long videos.

paragraphs: Generating a video beyond a model’s usual length can introduce repeated temporal patterns or unnaturally slow motion. This paper investigates those problems through the frequency components of positional embeddings, which provide information about positions in the sequence. The authors identify an intrinsic frequency that primarily governs the model’s behavior when extending video length.

RIFLEx reduces that intrinsic frequency to suppress repetition while maintaining motion consistency. The intervention is deliberately small and requires no additional modifications. Its significance is the connection between a specific part of the positional representation and the temporal failures observed during extrapolation, providing a targeted way to change long-video behavior.

The authors report high-quality generation at twice the original length on state-of-the-art video diffusion transformers without training. With minimal fine-tuning, the approach improves quality and supports threefold extrapolation without using long videos for that fine-tuning. These are two distinct operating conditions: the twofold result is training-free, while the threefold result uses additional learning. Both support the usefulness of adjusting the identified frequency.
summary.tldr: RIFLEx adjusts an intrinsic positional frequency to enable training-free twofold video-length extrapolation and threefold extrapolation with minimal fine-tuning.

title: RIFLEx: A Free Lunch for Length Extrapolation in Video Diffusion Transformers

abstract: Preference optimization is widely used to align large language models (LLMs) with human preferences. However, many margin-based methods also suppress the chosen response when they try to suppress the rejected one, and there is no general way to prevent this across different objectives. We address this issue with a unified incentive-score decomposition of preference optimization, revealing that different objectives share the same local update directions and differ only in their scalar weights. This decomposition provides a common framework for analyzing objectives that were previously studied in separate settings. Building on this decomposition, by analyzing the dynamics of the chosen/rejected likelihoods, we identify the disentanglement band (DB), a simple, testable condition that tells us when training can follow the desired path: suppress the loser while preserving the winner, possibly after an early stage. Using the DB, we propose reward calibration (RC), a plug-and-play method that adaptively rebalances the updates for chosen and rejected likelihoods to satisfy the DB, without redesigning the base objective. Empirical results show that RC leads to more disentangled dynamics, with better downstream performance observed across several settings. Our code is available at https://github.com/IceyWuu/DisentangledPreferenceOptimization.

summary.tldr: Reward calibration rebalances preference updates to help suppress rejected responses while preserving chosen ones under a testable condition.

title: Towards Disentangled Preference Optimization Dynamics: Suppress the Loser, Preserve the Winner

abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems are vulnerable to attacks that inject poisoned passages into the retrieved context, even at low corruption rates. We show that existing attacks are not designed to be stealthy, allowing reliable detection and mitigation. We formalize a distinguishability-based security game to quantify stealth for such attacks. If a few poisoned passages control the response, they must bias the inference process more than the benign ones, inherently compromising stealth. This motivates analyzing intermediate signals of LLMs, such as attention weights, to approximate the influence of different passages on the response. Leveraging attention weights, we introduce the Normalized Passage Attention Score (NPAS) and a lightweight Attention-Variance Filter (AV Filter) that flags anomalous passages. Our method improves robustness, yielding up to 20% higher accuracy than baseline defenses. We also develop adaptive attacks that attempt to conceal such anomalies, achieving up to 35% success rate and underscoring the challenges of achieving true stealth in poisoning RAG systems.

paragraphs: Retrieval-augmented generation can be manipulated by poisoned passages inserted into the retrieved context, even when relatively few passages are corrupted. This paper examines whether those attacks can also remain inconspicuous. It formalizes stealth through a distinguishability-based security game and argues that a few passages controlling the response must exert disproportionate influence on inference.

The defense looks for that influence in the language model's intermediate attention signals. The authors introduce a Normalized Passage Attention Score and a lightweight Attention-Variance Filter that flags anomalous passages. Attention weights serve as an approximation of how strongly different passages affect the response, translating the stealth analysis into a practical detection mechanism.

The authors also construct adaptive attacks designed to conceal the anomalies, reaching success rates of up to 35%. These attacks show that the defense does not eliminate poisoning, while the combined results expose a useful tension between controlling a response and hiding the influence used to control it.
summary.tldr: Attention-based passage scoring detects influential RAG poisoning and improves robustness, though adaptive attacks retain reported success.

title: Through the Stealth Lens: Attention-Aware Defenses Against Poisoning in RAG

abstract: We introduce ELECTRAFI, a fast, end-to-end differentiable model for predicting periodic charge densities in crystalline materials. ELECTRAFI constructs anisotropic Gaussians in real space and exploits their closed-form Fourier transforms to analytically evaluate plane-wave coefficients via the Poisson summation formula. This formulation delegates non-local and periodic behavior to analytic transforms, enabling reconstruction of the full periodic charge density with a single inverse FFT. By avoiding explicit real-space grid probing, periodic image summation, and spherical harmonic expansions, ELECTRAFI matches or exceeds state-of-the-art accuracy across periodic benchmarks while being up to $633\times$ faster than the strongest competing method, reconstructing crystal charge densities in a fraction of a second. When used to initialize DFT calculations, ELECTRAFI reduces total DFT compute cost by up to $\sim$20 %, whereas slower charge density models negate savings due to high inference times. Our results show that accuracy and inference cost jointly determine end-to-end DFT speedups, and motivate our focus on efficiency.

paragraphs: ELECTRAFI predicts how electrical charge is distributed throughout a repeating crystal. Its central design connects a local representation to the full periodic density: the model constructs anisotropic Gaussians in real space, then uses their analytically available Fourier transforms to obtain plane-wave coefficients through the Poisson summation formula.

This shifts the handling of periodicity and non-local behavior into analytic transformations. A single inverse fast Fourier transform reconstructs the density, avoiding explicit probing of a real-space grid, summing periodic images, and spherical harmonic expansions. The whole model remains differentiable from end to end, while the reconstruction procedure keeps inference inexpensive.

Used to initialize density functional theory calculations, it reduces total compute cost by up to roughly 20 percent. Slower predictors can consume the savings they create, so the practical finding concerns combined prediction accuracy and inference cost, not accuracy alone.
summary.tldr: ELECTRAFI uses analytic Fourier transforms of local Gaussians to predict crystal charge densities quickly enough to reduce total DFT compute cost.

title: Global Plane Waves from Local Gaussians: Periodic Charge Densities in a Blink

abstract: Integrating language models (LMs) in healthcare systems holds great promise for improving medical workflows and decision-making. However, a critical barrier to their global adoption is the lack of reliable evaluation of their trustworthiness in multilingual healthcare settings. Existing LMs are predominantly trained in high-resource languages, making them ill-equipped to handle the complexity and diversity of healthcare queries in mid- and low-resource languages, which poses significant challenges for deployment in global healthcare contexts where linguistic diversity is essential. In this work, we present CLINIC, a Comprehensive Multilingual Benchmark to evaluate the trustworthiness of language models in healthcare. CLINIC systematically benchmarks LMs across five key dimensions of trustworthiness: truthfulness, fairness, safety, robustness, and privacy, operationalized through 18 diverse tasks spanning 15 languages and covering a wide range of critical healthcare topics. Our extensive evaluation reveals that LMs struggle with factual correctness, demonstrate bias across demographic and linguistic groups, and remain susceptible to privacy breaches and adversarial attacks. By highlighting these shortcomings, CLINIC lays the foundation for enhancing the global reach and safety of LMs in healthcare across diverse languages.

paragraphs: A language model's usefulness in healthcare depends on more than its ability to produce fluent answers. It must also handle factual questions, demographic differences, sensitive information, and adversarial inputs across languages. The paper addresses a gap in evaluating these properties when healthcare users speak languages with differing amounts of training data.

CLINIC is a multilingual benchmark covering truthfulness, fairness, safety, robustness, and privacy. It turns these five dimensions into 18 tasks across 15 languages and a range of healthcare topics. This structure makes trustworthiness a collection of assessable capabilities, allowing evaluation to consider both language coverage and different kinds of failure.

The reported evaluation finds problems with factual correctness, bias across demographic and linguistic groups, vulnerability to privacy breaches, and susceptibility to adversarial attacks. These findings identify obstacles to broader healthcare deployment among the evaluated models. The benchmark provides a framework for studying those shortcomings across languages, so progress can be assessed beyond performance in the high-resource languages that dominate model training.
summary.tldr: CLINIC evaluates healthcare language models across 15 languages and reveals weaknesses in factuality, fairness, privacy, and resistance to attacks.

title: CLINIC : Evaluating Multilingual Trustworthiness in Language Models for Healthcare

abstract: We study the implicit bias of momentum-based optimizers on smooth homogeneous models. We show that momentum steepest descent algorithms like Muon (spectral norm), MomentumGD ($\ell_2$ norm), and Signum ($\ell_\infty$ norm) are approximate steepest descent trajectories under a decaying learning rate schedule, proving that these algorithms have a bias towards KKT points of the corresponding margin maximization problem. We extend the analysis to Adam (without the stability constant), which maximizes the $\ell_\infty$ margin, and to Muon-Signum and Muon-Adam, which maximize a hybrid norm. Our experiments corroborate the theory and show that the identity of the margin maximized depends on the choice of optimizer. Overall, our results extend earlier lines of work on steepest descent in homogeneous models and momentum-based optimizers in linear models.

We show that momentum steepest descent algorithms like Muon (spectral norm), MomentumGD ($\ell_2$ norm), and Signum ($\ell_\infty$ norm) are approximate steepest descent trajectories under a decaying learning rate schedule, proving that these algorithms have a bias towards KKT points of the corresponding margin maximization problem. We extend the analysis to Adam (without the stability constant), which maximizes the $\ell_\infty$ margin, and to Muon-Signum and Muon-Adam, which maximize a hybrid norm. Our experiments corroborate the theory and show that the identity of the margin maximized depends on the choice of optimizer. Overall, our results extend earlier lines of work on steepest descent in homogeneous models and momentum-based optimizers in linear models.

paragraphs: An optimizer can influence which solution a neural network favors, beyond simply reducing its training objective. This paper studies that implicit bias for momentum-based optimization in smooth homogeneous models. It connects the optimizer's update geometry to a margin-maximization problem, showing that the notion of margin favored by training depends on the optimizer.

Under a decaying learning-rate schedule, momentum steepest-descent methods approximately follow steepest-descent trajectories. The analysis covers Muon with the spectral norm, MomentumGD with the Euclidean norm, and Signum with the infinity norm. It establishes a bias toward KKT points of their corresponding margin problems, which are constrained optimality points rather than an unconditional guarantee of finding a global optimum.

The authors extend the analysis to Adam without its stability constant, associating it with the infinity-norm margin, and to Muon-Signum and Muon-Adam with hybrid norms. Experiments corroborate the theory and the dependence of the maximized margin on optimizer choice. The result expands earlier analyses to connect momentum, model homogeneity, and several optimizer geometries within a shared account.
summary.tldr: For smooth homogeneous models under the studied conditions, momentum optimizers favor margin solutions determined by their update geometry.

title: The Implicit Bias of Adam and Muon on Smooth Homogeneous Neural Networks

abstract: Large-scale medical biobanks provide imaging data complemented by extensive tabular information, such as clinical measurements or demographics. However, this abundance of tabular attributes does not reflect real-world datasets, where only a subset of attributes may be available. This discrepancy calls for methods that remain robust to missing values at inference. To address this challenge, we propose RoVTL (Robust Vision-Tabular Learning), a framework designed to handle any level of tabular data availability, from 0% to 100%. RoVTL comprises two key stages: contrastive pretraining, where we introduce tabular attribute missingness as data augmentation to promote robustness, and downstream task tuning, where tabular missingness is complemented by a novel Tabular More vs. Fewer loss that ranks performance based on the amount of available tabular data. Combined with gated-cross attention fusion module, our tuning approach enables consistent performance across all tabular data completeness scenarios. We evaluate RoVTL on cardiac MRI scans from the UK Biobank, demonstrating superior robustness to missing tabular data compared to prior methods. Furthermore, RoVTL successfully generalizes to an external cardiac MRI dataset for multimodal disease classification, and extends to the natural images domain, achieving robust performance on a car advertisements dataset. The model weights and code are available at https://github.com/marteczkah/RoVTL.

RoVTL addresses this mismatch for systems combining images with tabular information. It is designed to operate across the full range of tabular availability, including cases where all tabular attributes are missing but the image remains available.

During downstream tuning, it combines further missingness with a Tabular More vs. Fewer loss that ranks performance according to the amount of available tabular data. The model also generalizes to an external cardiac MRI dataset for multimodal disease classification and extends to a car advertisements dataset. These findings support training explicitly across availability levels so that useful multimodal behavior persists as the amount of tabular information changes.
summary.tldr: RoVTL trains image-and-table models across missing-data levels, improving reported robustness from complete tabular information to none.

title: No Data? No Problem: Robust Vision-Tabular Learning with Missing Values

abstract: Modern deep learning for asset allocation typically separates forecasting from optimization. We argue this creates a fundamental mismatch where minimizing prediction errors fails to yield robust portfolios. We propose the Signature Informed Transformer to address this by unifying feature extraction and decision making into a single policy. Our model employs path signatures to encode complex path dependencies and introduces a specialized attention mechanism that targets geometric asset relationships. By directly minimizing the Conditional Value at Risk we ensure the training objective aligns with financial goals. We prove that our attention module rigorously amplifies signature derived signals. Experiments across diverse equity universes show our approach significantly outperforms both traditional strategies and advanced forecasting baselines. The code is available at: https://github.com/Yoontae6719/Signature-Informed-Transformer-For-Asset-Allocation

The authors argue that this separation creates a mismatch: reducing forecast error does not necessarily produce a robust portfolio. Their Signature-Informed Transformer combines feature extraction and allocation decisions within a single policy.

The model uses path signatures to encode dependencies in how asset trajectories evolve. A specialized attention mechanism targets geometric relationships among assets, and training directly minimizes Conditional Value at Risk, a measure focused on unfavorable outcomes. This makes the optimization objective explicitly reflect portfolio risk instead of relying on forecasting accuracy as an intermediate target.

The authors prove that their attention module amplifies signature-derived signals. Experiments across diverse equity universes show significant improvements over traditional strategies and advanced forecasting baselines. The contribution therefore connects a trajectory representation, a tailored attention mechanism, and a risk-aligned learning objective. Its empirical findings support the proposed integration of representation learning and portfolio decisions in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: A transformer combines path-signature features with direct portfolio-risk optimization, outperforming the evaluated traditional and forecasting-based allocation methods.

title: Signature-Informed Transformer for Asset Allocation

abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have shown remarkable capabilities in learning from graph-structured data with various applications such as social analysis and bioinformatics. However, the presence of label noise in real scenarios poses a significant challenge in learning robust GNNs, and their effectiveness can be severely impacted when dealing with noisy labels on graphs, often stemming from annotation errors or inconsistencies. To address this, in this paper we propose a novel approach called ICGNN that harnesses the structure information of the graph to effectively alleviate the challenges posed by noisy labels. Specifically, we first design a novel noise indicator that measures the influence contradiction score (ICS) based on the graph diffusion matrix to quantify the credibility of nodes with clean labels, such that nodes with higher ICS values are more likely to be detected as having noisy labels. Then we leverage the Gaussian mixture model to precisely detect whether the label of a node is noisy or not. Additionally, we develop a soft strategy to combine the predictions from neighboring nodes on the graph to correct the detected noisy labels. At last, pseudo-labeling for abundant unlabeled nodes is incorporated to provide auxiliary supervision signals and guide the model optimization. Experiments on benchmark datasets show the superiority of our approach over competitive baselines in noisy label scenarios. The source code is available at: https://github.com/wayc04/ICGNN.

paragraphs: Incorrect labels can undermine a graph neural network even when the graph contains useful structural information. ICGNN uses that structure to identify suspicious labels and improve the supervision used for training. Its approach combines detection, correction, and additional learning signals from nodes that initially have no labels.

The first step computes an influence contradiction score from the graph diffusion matrix. This score captures a form of inconsistency in graph influence, with higher scores indicating a greater likelihood of label noise. A Gaussian mixture model then uses the indicator to distinguish potentially noisy labels from clean ones.

For labels identified as noisy, ICGNN combines neighboring nodes’ predictions through a soft correction strategy. It also assigns pseudo-labels to unlabeled nodes, supplying auxiliary supervision during optimization. Benchmark experiments show better performance than competitive baselines in noisy-label settings. The overall contribution is a coordinated training approach that uses graph relationships to assess label credibility and repair supervision, rather than simply training through the annotation errors.
summary.tldr: ICGNN uses graph-based contradiction scores to detect noisy labels, correct them with neighboring predictions, and improve training.

title: Identifying and Correcting Label Noise for Robust GNNs via Influence Contradiction

abstract: We propose a modular, data-driven framework for jointly learning unknown functional mappings and discovering the underlying one-parameter symmetry subgroup governing the data. Unlike conventional geometric deep learning methods that assume known symmetries, our approach identifies the relevant continuous subgroup directly from data. Our framework focuses on three primary geometric components of one-parameter subgroup actions: elliptic, hyperbolic, and parabolic regimes. For the given regime, our framework instantiates a corresponding symmetry discovery architecture with invariant and equivariant representation layers structured according to the Lie algebra of the subgroup, and learns the exact generator parameters end-to-end from data. This yields models whose invariance or equivariance is guaranteed by construction and admits formal proofs, enabling symmetry to be explicitly traced to identifiable components of the architecture. The approach is applicable to one-parameter subgroups of a wide range of matrix Lie groups, including $SO(n)$, $SL(n)$, and the Lorentz group. Experiments on synthetic and real-world systems, including moment of inertia prediction, double-pendulum dynamics, and high-energy Top Quark Tagging, demonstrate accurate subgroup recovery and strong predictive performance across both compact and non-compact regimes.

paragraphs: Symmetry-aware models often begin with a known transformation rule that their predictions should respect. This paper develops a framework that learns an unknown functional mapping together with the continuous one-parameter symmetry subgroup governing the data. The discovered symmetry is tied to identifiable architectural components.

The framework covers elliptic, hyperbolic, and parabolic regimes. For a given regime, it builds invariant and equivariant representation layers using the subgroup’s Lie algebra, then learns the generator parameters end to end. Invariance means that a representation remains unchanged under the transformation; equivariance means that it changes in the prescribed way. These properties are guaranteed by the architecture and admit formal proofs.

The approach applies to one-parameter subgroups within several matrix Lie groups, including rotation, special linear, and Lorentz groups. Experiments include moment-of-inertia prediction, double-pendulum dynamics, and top-quark tagging, with accurate subgroup recovery and strong predictive performance across compact and non-compact settings. The contribution combines data-driven identification of symmetry parameters with explicit structural guarantees, given the selected geometric regime.
summary.tldr: Given a geometric regime, the framework learns continuous symmetry generators while guaranteeing architectural invariance or equivariance.

title: Interpretable Discovery of One-parameter Subgroups: A Modular Framework for Elliptical, Hyperbolic, and Parabolic Symmetries

abstract: Diffusion-based large language models (dLLMs) support parallel text generation via iterative denoising, yet inference remains latency-heavy because many steps are spent on redundant refinement and repeated remasking of tokens whose final values are already determined. Prior acceleration methods mainly depend on step-local confidence heuristics or fixed schedules, which are sensitive to prompt and task variation and ignore strong positional effects within a sequence. We cast diffusion decoding as a dynamic control problem and show that token-wise denoising trajectories provide the key signal for reliable control. We propose a trace-aware decoding framework with two components. First, Temporal-Spatial Parallel Decoding (TSPD) uses a lightweight temporal-spatial correctness sensor that consumes per-token trajectory features, including confidence, entropy, and momentum, together with token position, to decide when a token has converged and can be safely fixed. Second, we introduce ]Confidence Extrapolation (CE)], a training-free state-space module that forecasts future logit trends with uncertainty to support proactive decisions, including safe look-ahead and targeted stabilization when trajectories are oscillatory or underconfident. Together, TSPD and CE reduce unnecessary denoising iterations while preserving output quality, and they compose cleanly with system optimizations such as KV caching.

paragraphs: Diffusion language models generate text through repeated denoising, allowing multiple tokens to be processed in parallel. However, repeated refinement can waste time on tokens whose final values are already settled. This paper treats decoding as a control problem, using the history of each token’s evolution to decide when further work is useful.

Temporal-Spatial Parallel Decoding uses a lightweight correctness sensor that considers confidence, entropy, momentum, and token position. It determines when a token has converged and can be fixed. Confidence Extrapolation adds a training-free state-space component that predicts future logit trends together with uncertainty. These forecasts support looking ahead and selectively stabilizing tokens whose trajectories oscillate or remain uncertain.

The authors state that combining these components reduces unnecessary denoising iterations while preserving output quality. The framework also composes with system optimizations such as KV caching. Its contribution is to use temporal evidence and position together, making decoding decisions sensitive to how individual tokens develop rather than relying solely on their current confidence.
summary.tldr: TSPD and Confidence Extrapolation accelerate diffusion language-model decoding by tracking token histories and forecasting when further refinement is unnecessary.

title: Efficient Diffusion LLMs via Temporal-Spatial Parallel Decoding and Confidence Extrapolation

abstract: Computer-using agents (CUAs) enable task completion through natural interaction with operating systems and software interfaces. While script-based verifiers are widely adopted for evaluation, they suffer from limited scalability and inability to provide step-wise assessment. Reward models offer promising alternatives, but their effectiveness on CUA evaluation remains largely underexplored. To address this gap, we present CUARewardBench, comprising four key contributions: (1) First-ever Comprehensive CUA Reward Benchmark: We introduce the first benchmark for evaluating both outcome reward models (ORM) and process reward models (PRM) on CUA tasks, enabling systematic assessment across trajectory-level and step-level evaluation. (2) Diverse, Practical and Reliable Dataset: CUARewardBench encompasses trajectories from 10 software categories and 7 agent architectures with varying performance levels (25.9%-50.8% success rates). All trajectories are expertly annotated through carefully designed protocols, with rigorous quality control to ensure reliability and practical applicability. (3) Comprehensive Analysis and Insights: Through extensive experiments across 7 vision-language models and 3 prompt templates, we reveal critical limitations of current CUA RMs, including insufficient visual reasoning capabilities, knowledge deficiencies, and the superiority of general VLMs over specialized CUA models for reward evaluation. (4) Unanimous Prompt Ensemble (UPE): Based on the insights from our comprehensive analysis, we propose UPE, a novel ensemble method that significantly enhances reward model reliability through strict unanimous voting and strategic prompt-template configurations. UPE achieves 88.0% precision and 95.3% NPV for ORM, and 83.1% precision and 86.2% NPV for PRM, substantially outperforming single VLMs and traditional ensemble approaches. In a short, this work introduces both a comprehensive benchmark and a novel ensemble method that substantially enhances CUA reward model reliability.

paragraphs: CUARewardBench tests whether reward models can reliably assess agents that operate software interfaces. It covers both judging an entire task attempt and evaluating individual steps. This distinction matters because script-based verifiers have limited scalability and cannot provide the stepwise assessments needed to understand how an agent's behavior progresses.

The benchmark contains expert-annotated trajectories spanning ten software categories and seven agent architectures, with annotation protocols and quality controls. Experiments compare seven vision-language models and three prompt templates. They identify weaknesses in visual reasoning and relevant knowledge, and find that general vision-language models outperform specialized computer-using models as reward evaluators in the studied setting.

The authors also propose Unanimous Prompt Ensemble, which combines strategically configured prompts through strict unanimous voting. It reaches 88.0% precision and 95.3% negative predictive value for outcome evaluation, and 83.1% and 86.2% respectively for process evaluation. These findings show that evaluator design can improve the reliability of both positive and negative judgments, beyond choosing a single model.
summary.tldr: CUARewardBench evaluates whole-task and stepwise reward judgments for computer-using agents and introduces unanimous prompt voting to improve reliability.

title: CUARewardBench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Reward Models for Computer-Using Agents

abstract: While music generation models have evolved to handle complex multimodal inputs mixing text, lyrics, and reference audio, evaluation mechanisms have lagged behind, remaining fragmented and narrowly focused. In this paper, we bridge this critical gap by establishing a comprehensive ecosystem for Compositional Music Instruction (CMI) reward modeling, where the generated music may be conditioned on text descriptions, lyrics, and/or audio prompts. We first introduce CMIPref-Pseudo, a large-scale preference dataset comprising 110k pseudo-labeled samples, and CMI-Pref, a high-quality, human-annotated corpus tailored for fine-grained alignment tasks. To unify the evaluation landscape, we propose CMIRewardBench, a unified benchmark that evaluates music reward models on heterogeneous samples across musicality, text–music alignment, and compositional instruction alignment. Leveraging these resources, we develop CMI reward models (CMI-RMs), a parameter-efficient reward model family capable of processing heterogeneous inputs. We evaluate their correlation with human judgments scores on Music Arena and CMI-Pref test set, as well as preference agreement on Music Arena and CMI-Pref. Additional analyses examine performance variation across factors such as annotators, annotation timing and confidence, music generation models, and audio length. Experiments demonstrate that CMI-RM not only correlates strongly with human judgments, but also enables effective inference-time scaling via topk filtering. Our work provides the necessary data, benchmarks, and models to advance aligned music generation.

paragraphs: Music generators can accept combinations of descriptions, lyrics, and reference audio, but evaluating whether their outputs satisfy those combinations requires more than a narrow quality score. This paper develops data, evaluation tools, and reward models for Compositional Music Instruction, bringing these different input types into a shared evaluation setting.

The resources include CMIPref-Pseudo, with 110,000 pseudo-labeled samples, and CMI-Pref, a human-annotated corpus for detailed alignment assessment. CMIRewardBench evaluates musicality, alignment between text and music, and compliance with compositional instructions. Further analyses examine variation associated with annotators, annotation timing and confidence, generators, and audio length. summary.tldr: CMI-RewardBench combines datasets, evaluation criteria, and reward models for music generated from text, lyrics, and audio instructions.

title: CMI-RewardBench: Evaluating Music Reward Models with Compositional Multimodal Instruction

abstract: In critical domains like clinical reporting, legal analysis, and policy drafting, large language models (LLMs) are increasingly expected to produce extended, fact-rich narratives rather than isolated sentences. Reliable uncertainty quantification in such long-form outputs is crucial. Existing techniques either assign a single confidence score to an entire paragraph or evaluate factual consistency by comparing extracted atomic facts across multiple generations. Some recent approaches represent fact–paragraph relationships using bipartite entailment graphs and derive uncertainty from fact centrality. However, these methods ignore the explicit dependencies among facts within a paragraph and the structural and semantic variation across multiple LLM outputs for the same prompt, missing a key source of uncertainty specific to long-form generation. We propose GAUSS (Graph-Assisted Uncertainty Quantification using Structure and Semantics), a principled framework that models each generated paragraph as a semantic graph of atomic facts and their relations. We posit that uncertainty arises from structural and semantic discrepancies among these graphs across different samples. GAUSS quantifies uncertainty as the expected alignment cost between the semantic graph of an anchor paragraph and those of alternative generations. By capturing both semantic content and structural coherence, GAUSS offers a more interpretable and theoretically grounded measure of uncertainty than coarse, sentence-level scores.
