paragraphs: A long generated answer contains facts whose relationships matter alongside their individual content. This paper argues that uncertainty measures can miss that structure when they assign one confidence score to a paragraph or compare extracted facts without explicitly modeling their dependencies. Different answers to the same prompt may vary in both what they say and how their claims connect.

GAUSS represents each generated paragraph as a semantic graph. Atomic facts form the content of the graph, and relations capture connections among them. The framework treats structural and semantic discrepancies between graphs from different generations as a source of uncertainty specific to extended outputs.

Its uncertainty measure is the expected cost of aligning an anchor paragraph's graph with graphs from alternative generations. This makes disagreement about relationships part of the score, alongside disagreement about factual content. The proposed framework offers an interpretable account of uncertainty grounded in graph comparisons, making the organization of a narrative an explicit part of what is assessed.
summary.tldr: GAUSS measures uncertainty in long answers by comparing both facts and their relationships across semantic graphs of alternative generations.

title: GAUSS: Graph-Assisted Uncertainty Quantification using Structure and Semantics for Long-Form Generation in LLMs

abstract: Human episodic memory supports the retrieval of experiences that unfold over extended timescales, yet the computational mechanisms underlying this ability remain debated due to the limited mechanistic accessibility in long-term memory experiments in humans. Long-context LLMs may offer promising ways to reveal plausible computational mechanisms that drive this type of retrieval. Here, we investigate whether and how LLMs capture the core behavioral signatures of episodic memory via a temporal order memory task. Using a new dataset of human behavior based on memory of a full-length novel, we show that models exhibit the same characteristic distance effect observed in humans on this task. We next apply long-context mechanistic interpretability analyses to uncover how models solve this task, and find that model performance relies on a one-dimensional temporal code that is reinstated during retrieval by a single time-reinstatement attention head. These findings support temporal context reinstatement as an important mechanism for episodic-like temporal-order memory in LLMs, offering new insights into how temporal aspects of long-term episodic memory may be instantiated in both artificial and biological systems.

summary.tldr: Long-context models retrieve narrative order using a reinstated temporal code and exhibit a distance effect also observed in humans.

title: Temporal Context Reinstatement Drives Episodic-Like Order Memory in Long-Context Language Models

abstract: While prior studies have successfully compressed vision Transformers (ViTs) through various pruning techniques, most have concentrated on width pruning to achieve significant reductions in model size. Depth pruning, which removes entire layers from a ViT, is notoriously difficult for accuracy recovery despite its potential to deliver higher speedups, limiting the acceleration achieved by existing joint width-and-depth pruning methods. In this work, we reveal that the failure of existing depth pruning methods lies in their neglect of heterogeneity between different layers, and we introduce HetDPT, a heterogeneity-aware depth pruning method that avoids dimension mismatch. Comprehensive experiments on ImageNet-1K, CIFAR-100, COCO, and ADE20K validate our method: HetDPT achieves a 1.58$\times$ speedup for DeiT-B while maintaining accuracy and a 1.39$\times$ speedup for DeiT-S with nearly no accuracy degradation. Furthermore, when combined with width pruning, HetDPT+ sets a new state-of-the-art record in extreme ViT pruning, enhancing the acceleration ratio from 4.24$\times$ to 5.19$\times$ for the Isomorphic-Pruning-2.6G configuration while maintaining near-lossless accuracy; our code is available at https://github.com/Efficient-AI-for-All/HetDPT.

paragraphs: Removing whole layers from a vision Transformer can offer substantial speedups, but recovering accuracy afterward is difficult. Consequently, much pruning work focuses on reducing width instead. This paper attributes failures in existing depth-pruning methods to their neglect of differences between layers and introduces HetDPT to account for that heterogeneity.

HetDPT is designed to avoid dimension mismatch when pruning depth. The underlying point is that layers cannot always be treated as interchangeable parts when deciding how to shorten the network. The authors also combine their method with width pruning in HetDPT+, bringing the layer-aware approach into more aggressive compression settings.

These findings show that accounting for layer differences can make depth pruning a more effective contributor to model acceleration.
summary.tldr: HetDPT accounts for differences between Transformer layers to remove depth with strong speedups and little or no reported accuracy loss.

title: Rethinking Depth Pruning for Vision Transformers: A Heterogeneity-Aware Perspective

abstract: Neural acoustic fields often model time-domain impulse responses, which struggle to capture the frequency-selective wave behaviors that dominate confined, resonant environments. To address this, we propose INFER (Implicit Neural Frequency Response fields), a framework that directly learns continuous, complex-valued frequency response fields. Unlike prior time-domain methods, our frequency-first approach enables three key innovations: (1) end-to-end learning of frequency-specific attenuation and phase delay in 3D space; (2) a physics-based Kramers–Kronig consistency constraint that causally regularizes attenuation and phase delay; and (3) perceptual and hardware-aware spectral supervision that prioritizes critical auditory bands. We evaluate INFER across diverse settings, ranging from standard room-scale benchmarks (MeshRIR, RAF) to challenging, highly reverberant environments like real car cabins. Our approach significantly outperforms time- and hybrid-domain baselines, reducing average magnitude and phase reconstruction errors by over 39% and 51%, respectively, demonstrating state-of-the-art accuracy in modeling complex acoustic spaces.

paragraphs: Confined acoustic spaces can affect different sound frequencies very differently, especially when resonance and reverberation are strong. INFER models those effects directly through a continuous, complex-valued frequency response field. This places frequency-dependent behavior at the center of learning, addressing difficulties encountered by acoustic fields based on time-domain impulse responses.

The framework jointly learns how attenuation and phase delay vary with frequency and position in three-dimensional space. A physics-based Kramers–Kronig consistency constraint links those quantities to regularize the model according to causality. Its spectral supervision also accounts for perception and hardware, placing emphasis on auditory bands identified as especially important.

The authors evaluate INFER on room-scale benchmarks and highly reverberant environments, including real car cabins. They report reductions of over 39% in average magnitude reconstruction error and over 51% in average phase reconstruction error against time-domain and hybrid-domain baselines. These findings support direct frequency-response learning as an effective approach for representing the frequency-selective behavior of the evaluated acoustic environments.
summary.tldr: INFER directly learns spatial frequency responses with physical consistency constraints, substantially improving reported acoustic magnitude and phase reconstruction.

title: INFER: Learning Implicit Neural Frequency Response Fields for Confined Acoustic Environments

abstract: Recent advances in Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) demonstrate remarkable performance improvements by iteratively reflecting, exploring, and executing complex tasks, yet suffer from inefficiencies due to redundant reasoning, known as “overthinking”. Existing methods to mitigate this issue either rely on static difficulty estimates or require task-specific training, and thus fail to adapt to the dynamic complexity during reasoning. In this work, we empirically show that the problem difficulty evolves dynamically throughout the reasoning process and is linearly encoded in the LRM’s step-level embeddings. Building on this insight, we propose DyCon, a training-free framework that leverages latent step-level representations to explicitly model the evolving task difficulty, enabling the dynamic control of reasoning depth to mitigate the overthinking issue. Extensive experiments conducted on four models ranging from 4B to 32B, and across twelve benchmarks in math reasoning, general question answering, and coding tasks demonstrate that DyCon significantly enhances reasoning efficiency by reducing redundant steps without sacrificing accuracy or generalization. Project page and code are available at https://github.com/yu-lin-li/DyCon.

paragraphs: Reasoning models can spend computation on additional reflection after it stops being useful. DyCon addresses this overthinking by treating difficulty as something that changes during a solution. A problem’s initial difficulty estimate may become outdated as the model makes progress, which motivates monitoring the reasoning process itself.

The authors empirically find that evolving difficulty is linearly encoded in representations associated with individual reasoning steps. DyCon uses these latent representations to model difficulty as reasoning unfolds and dynamically control reasoning depth. The framework is training-free, avoiding the task-specific training required by some existing approaches while responding to information available during the current solution.

Experiments span four models from 4 billion to 32 billion parameters and twelve benchmarks covering mathematics, general question answering, and coding. The authors report fewer redundant reasoning steps without sacrificing accuracy or generalization in these evaluations. The result supports using internal, step-level signals to allocate reasoning effort according to the model’s changing progress rather than relying only on a fixed assessment made before reasoning begins.
summary.tldr: DyCon uses evolving difficulty signals inside reasoning models to reduce redundant steps without reported accuracy or generalization loss.

title: DyCon: Dynamic Reasoning Control via Evolving Difficulty Modeling

abstract: Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents employ external and internal memory systems to handle complex, goal-oriented tasks, yet this exposes them to severe extraction attacks, and corresponding defenses are currently lacking. In this paper, we propose MemPot, the first theoretically verified defense framework against memory extraction attacks by injecting optimized honeypots into the memory. Through a two-stage optimization process, MemPot generates trap documents that maximize the retrieval probability for attackers while remaining inconspicuous to benign users. We model the detection process as Wald’s Sequential Probability Ratio Test (SPRT) and theoretically prove that MemPot achieves a lower average number of sampling rounds compared to optimal static detectors. Empirically, MemPot significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving a 50% improvement in detection AUROC and an 80% increase in True Positive Rate under low False Positive Rate constraints. Furthermore, our experiments confirm that MemPot incurs zero online inference latency and preserves the agent’s utility on standard tasks, verifying its superiority in safety, harmlessness and efficiency.

paragraphs: Memory helps language-model agents handle complex tasks, but it also creates material that attackers may try to extract. MemPot defends these memory systems by inserting optimized honeypots: trap documents designed to be retrieved by attackers while remaining inconspicuous during benign use. The defense uses interactions with these documents as evidence for detecting extraction attempts.

A two-stage optimization process shapes the trap documents toward those competing goals. The authors model detection using Wald’s Sequential Probability Ratio Test, which accumulates evidence across sampling rounds. Under this formulation, they prove that MemPot requires fewer sampling rounds on average than optimal static detectors, connecting the defense design to an explicit sequential detection result.

The authors also report zero online inference latency and preserved agent utility on standard tasks. These findings support the proposed combination of selective trap retrieval and sequential detection as an effective defense in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: MemPot uses optimized memory honeypots and sequential evidence gathering to detect extraction attacks while preserving tested agent utility.

title: MemPot: Defending Against Memory Extraction Attack with Optimized Honeypots

abstract: Foundation models are often used as fixed black-box predictors for downstream tasks with limited labeled data, but their predictions may be biased and unsafe to trust blindly. We study this setting through black-box assisted nonparametric regression: a learner observes labeled samples and can query a fixed predictor $f_0$, while the target $f^*$ is close to $f_0$ in $L_2(P_X)$ up to an unknown radius $\delta$. We give a finite-sample minimax characterization showing a phase transition at $\delta_c(n)\asymp n^{-\beta/(2\beta+d)}$, with leading risk $\min{\delta^2, n^{-2\beta/(2\beta+d)}}$. We then analyze a Safe Residual Estimator: it learns a correction around $f_0$, initializes the residual head at zero so the initial predictor equals $f_0$, and uses holdout selection to revert to $f_0$ when the learned correction is not supported by validation data. Here, “safe” means avoiding negative transfer, i.e., performing worse than the black-box predictor alone. The estimator matches the leading minimax term up to an additive validation-selection cost. Synthetic regression experiments verify the predicted phase transition, while CIFAR-100 with CLIP and AG News with Qwen3-8B provide practice-facing evidence that the same residual-correction tradeoff is useful beyond the formal squared-loss regression setting.
originalAbstract: Foundation models are often used as fixed black-box predictors for downstream tasks with limited labeled data, but their predictions may be biased and unsafe to trust blindly. We study this setting through black-box assisted nonparametric regression: a learner observes labeled samples and can query a fixed predictor $f_0$, while the target $f^*$ is close to $f_0$ in $L_2(P_X)$ up to an unknown radius $\delta$. We give a finite-sample minimax characterization showing a phase transition at $\delta_c(n)\asymp n^{-\beta/(2\beta+d)}$, with leading risk $\min{\delta^2, n^{-2\beta/(2\beta+d)}}$. We then analyze a Safe Residual Estimator: it learns a correction around $f_0$, initializes the residual head at zero so the initial predictor equals $f_0$, and uses holdout selection to revert to $f_0$ when the learned correction is not supported by validation data. Here, “safe” means avoiding negative transfer, i.e., performing worse than the black-box predictor alone. The estimator matches the leading minimax term up to an additive validation-selection cost. Synthetic regression experiments verify the predicted phase transition, while CIFAR-100 with CLIP and AG News with Qwen3-8B provide practice-facing evidence that the same residual-correction tradeoff is useful beyond the formal squared-loss regression setting.

paragraphs: This paper asks when limited labeled data should be used to correct a fixed black-box predictor. Its formal setting assumes that the target function lies within an unknown distance δ of that predictor, measured using the input distribution. The challenge is to exploit a useful starting point without making predictions worse through an unreliable correction.

The analysis characterizes the best achievable worst-case error with finite data. It finds a transition at δ of order n raised to −β/(2β+d), with leading risk given by the smaller of δ squared and n raised to −2β/(2β+d). This distinguishes regimes where proximity to the existing predictor or learning from labeled samples determines the leading error.

The Safe Residual Estimator starts with a zero correction and uses held-out data to decide whether to retain a learned adjustment or revert to the original predictor. It matches the leading theoretical rate plus a validation-selection cost. Synthetic experiments confirm the transition; image and text experiments provide additional practical evidence beyond the formal squared-loss regression setting.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes when correcting a black-box predictor helps and proposes validation-based residual learning to avoid negative transfer.

title: Black-Box Assisted Regression: Phase Transitions and Minimax Optimality

abstract: Offline-to-online reinforcement learning (O2O RL) faces a central challenge between retaining offline conservatism and adapting to online feedback under distribution shift. This challenge arises because data behavior evolves during fine-tuning, rendering data origin a misleading basis for constraint handling and thereby leading to objective–data mismatch. We therefore propose Dynamic Alignment for RElaxation (DARE), a distribution-aware framework for sample-level constraint relaxation based on the behavioral consistency with a behavior model. To our knowledge, DARE is the first to condition constraint relaxation on behavioral consistency via a posterior-induced exchange mechanism, moving beyond a binary offline/online data distinction. Importantly, DARE requires only per-sample behavioral alignment, enabling instantiation on top of many offline algorithms with flexible choices of behavior models and fine-tuning objectives. We provide a theoretical analysis showing that behavior-based sample exchange consistently improves the distinction between offline-like and online-like subsets. Experiments on D4RL demonstrate that DARE consistently improves fine-tuning stability and achieves superior final performance over strong offline-to-online baselines. (The code is publicly available at https://github.com/lpzu/DARE.)

paragraphs: Offline-to-online reinforcement learning starts with existing data and then adapts through fresh interaction. Constraints that encourage caution during offline learning can become poorly matched to changing behavior during fine-tuning. This paper argues that deciding how to handle a sample solely from whether it came from offline or online collection can therefore be misleading.

DARE adjusts constraints according to each sample’s behavioral consistency with a behavior model. A posterior-based exchange mechanism reorganizes samples into offline-like and online-like subsets using that consistency. Because the framework needs only a per-sample alignment measure, it can be built on many offline algorithms with different behavior models and fine-tuning objectives.

The theoretical analysis shows that behavior-based exchange consistently improves the distinction between those subsets. On D4RL experiments, DARE improves fine-tuning stability and final performance over strong offline-to-online baselines. The contribution is a distribution-aware basis for relaxing constraints as behavior evolves, connecting the training objective more closely to what individual samples represent during adaptation.
summary.tldr: DARE relaxes reinforcement-learning constraints using each sample’s behavioral alignment, improving offline-to-online fine-tuning in reported experiments.

title: From Static Constraints to Dynamic Adaptation: Sample-Level Constraint Relaxation for Offline-to-Online Reinforcement Learning
Explanation-Based Acceleration of Similarity-Based Learning
Knowledge Base Refinement as Improving an Incorrect, Inconsistent and Incomplete Domain Theory

abstract: We present an examination of the state-of-the-art for using value iteration to solve large-scale discrete Markov Decision Processes. We introduce an architecture which combines three independent performance enhancements (the intelligent prioritization of computation, state partitioning, and massively parallel processing) into a single algorithm. We show that each idea improves performance in a different way, meaning that algorithm designers do not have to trade one improvement for another. We give special attention to parallelization issues, discussing how to efficiently partition states, distribute partitions to processors, minimize message passing and ensure high scalability. We present experimental results which demonstrate that this approach solves large problems in reasonable time.

paragraphs: P3VI addresses the computational cost of using value iteration to solve large discrete Markov decision processes. The paper examines existing performance techniques and introduces an architecture that combines three of them: prioritizing computation intelligently, dividing states into partitions, and distributing work across many processors.

The authors show that these enhancements improve performance in different ways, so their architecture can combine them without requiring a choice of one improvement at the expense of another. Prioritization, partitioning, and parallel execution are treated as complementary parts of the same algorithm. This is the paper's central design argument for improving value iteration at scale.

Much of the discussion concerns making the parallel system efficient: how to partition states, assign partitions to processors, reduce message passing, and achieve scalability. These details connect the algorithmic design to the cost of coordinating distributed computation. Experimental results show that the combined approach solves large problems in reasonable time, supporting the practical value of bringing the three enhancements together.
summary.tldr: P3VI combines prioritization, state partitioning, and massive parallelism to make value iteration practical for large discrete decision problems.

title: P3VI: a partitioned, prioritized, parallel value iterator

abstract: Neighbor search is a fundamental task in machine learning, especially in classiﬁcation and retrieval. Eﬃcient nearest neighbor search methods have been widely studied, with their emphasis on data structures but most of them did not consider the underlying global geometry of a data set. Recent graph-based semi-supervised learning methods capture the global geometry, but suﬀer from scalability and parameter tuning problems. In this paper we present a (nearest) neighbor search method where the underlying global geometry is incorporated and the parameter tuning is not required. To this end, we introduce deterministic walks as a deterministic counterpart of Markov random walks, leading us to use the minimax distance as a global dissimilarity measure. Then we develop a message passing algorithm for eﬃcient minimax distance calculation, which scales linearly in both time and space. Empirical study reveals the useful behavior of the method in image retrieval and semi-supervised learning.

paragraphs: Neighbor search supports tasks such as classification and retrieval, but efficient search structures do not necessarily account for the overall geometry of the dataset. Graph-based semi-supervised methods can capture that geometry, yet the paper identifies scalability and parameter tuning as obstacles. It proposes a neighbor-search method that incorporates global geometry without requiring parameter tuning.

The authors introduce deterministic walks as a counterpart to Markov random walks. This leads to using minimax distance as the measure of dissimilarity. The important shift is that neighbor relationships reflect the dataset's global structure, rather than relying only on a search procedure that overlooks that structure.

To make the distance useful computationally, the paper develops a message-passing algorithm with linear time and space scaling. Empirical studies in image retrieval and semi-supervised learning show useful behavior. The contribution thus joins a geometrically informed definition of neighbors with an efficient calculation procedure, addressing the practical cost of bringing global structure into neighbor search.
summary.tldr: A parameter-free neighbor-search method incorporates global geometry through minimax distance computed by a message-passing algorithm with linear time and space scaling.

title: Neighbor search with global geometry: a minimax message passing algorithm

abstract: Positive definite kernels on probability measures have been recently applied in structured data classification problems. Some of these kernels are related to classic information theoretic quantities, such as mutual information and the Jensen-Shannon divergence. Meanwhile, driven by recent advances in Tsallis statistics, nonextensive generalizations of Shannon�s information theory have been proposed. This paper bridges these two trends. We introduce the Jensen-Tsallis q-difference, a generalization of the Jensen-Shannon divergence. We then define a new family of nonextensive mutual information kernels, which allow weights to be assigned to their arguments, and which includes the Boolean, Jensen-Shannon, and linear kernels as particular cases. We illustrate the performance of these kernels on text categorization tasks.

paragraphs: The paper connects kernels on probability measures with nonextensive generalizations of information theory. Such kernels had been used for structured data classification, with some linked to quantities such as mutual information and Jensen-Shannon divergence. The authors bring this line of work together with ideas motivated by Tsallis statistics.

They introduce the Jensen-Tsallis q-difference as a generalization of Jensen-Shannon divergence. Using this development, they define a family of nonextensive mutual information kernels. The family allows weights to be attached to its arguments, making weighting part of the kernel construction rather than treating all arguments identically.

Boolean, Jensen-Shannon, and linear kernels appear as particular cases within the proposed family. This places several familiar constructions inside a common framework and shows how the new formulation connects to existing kernels. The authors illustrate the kernels on text categorization tasks. The stated empirical contribution is a performance illustration, while the main mathematical contribution is the generalized information quantity and the weighted kernel family built from it.
summary.tldr: A generalized information-theoretic quantity produces a weighted kernel family that includes Boolean, Jensen-Shannon, and linear kernels.

title: Nonextensive entropic kernels

abstract: Compressive sensing (CS) is an emerging field that, under appropriate conditions, can significantly reduce the number of measurements required for a given signal. In many applications, one is interested in multiple signals that may be measured in multiple CS-type measurements, where here each signal corresponds to a sensing "task". In this paper we propose a novel multi-task compressive sensing framework based on a Bayesian formalism, where a Dirichlet process (DP) prior is employed, yielding a principled means of simultaneously inferring the appropriate sharing mechanisms as well as CS inversion for each task. A variational Bayesian (VB) inference algorithm is employed to estimate the full posterior on the model parameters.
originalAbstract: Compressive sensing (CS) is an emerging field that, under appropriate conditions, can significantly reduce the number of measurements required for a given signal. In many applications, one is interested in multiple signals that may be measured in multiple CS-type measurements, where here each signal corresponds to a sensing "task". In this paper we propose a novel multi-task compressive sensing framework based on a Bayesian formalism, where a Dirichlet process (DP) prior is employed, yielding a principled means of simultaneously inferring the appropriate sharing mechanisms as well as CS inversion for each task. A variational Bayesian (VB) inference algorithm is employed to estimate the full posterior on the model parameters.

paragraphs: Compressive sensing can reduce the measurements needed to recover a signal when appropriate conditions hold. This paper considers applications involving several signals, each associated with its own sensing task. The central question is how to reconstruct those signals while also deciding what information should be shared across their tasks.

The authors propose a Bayesian framework with a Dirichlet process prior. This prior supplies a principled mechanism for inferring the sharing relationships at the same time as performing each task’s compressive sensing inversion. The sharing arrangement is therefore itself part of the inference problem, connecting decisions about relationships among tasks with the recovery of their signals.

A variational Bayesian algorithm estimates the posterior distribution over the model parameters. This treatment represents uncertainty across the modeled quantities while fitting the coupled tasks. The main contribution is the unified formulation: signal reconstruction and the determination of appropriate sharing are handled together, providing a framework for multiple sensing problems whose relationships need to be inferred.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian compressive sensing framework jointly reconstructs multiple signals and infers how their sensing tasks should share information.

title: Multi-task compressive sensing with Dirichlet process priors

abstract: Low-rank matrix approximation is an effective tool in alleviating the memory and computational burdens of kernel methods and sampling, as the mainstream of such algorithms, has drawn considerable attention in both theory and practice. This paper presents detailed studies on the Nystrom sampling scheme and in particular, an error analysis that directly relates the Nystrom approximation quality with the encoding powers of the landmark points in summarizing the data. The resultant error bound suggests a simple and efficient sampling scheme, the k -means clustering algorithm, for Nystrom low-rank approximation. We compare it with state-of-the-art approaches that range from greedy schemes to probabilistic sampling. Our algorithm achieves significant performance gains in a number of supervised/unsupervised learning tasks including kernel PCA and least squares SVM.

The resultant error bound suggests a simple and efficient sampling scheme, the k -means clustering algorithm, for Nystrom low-rank approximation. We compare it with state-of-the-art approaches that range from greedy schemes to probabilistic sampling. paragraphs: Kernel methods can require substantial memory and computation, making low-rank matrix approximations useful. The Nyström approach builds such an approximation using selected landmark points. This paper examines how the choice of those landmarks affects approximation quality, connecting the computational shortcut to how well the selected points summarize the data.

The authors derive an error analysis that directly relates approximation quality to the landmarks' ability to encode the dataset. The resulting bound suggests using k-means clustering as a simple, efficient way to obtain landmarks. This gives the selection procedure a theoretical motivation: a useful summary of the data can also support a useful approximation of the kernel matrix.

The proposed method is compared with leading alternatives, including greedy selection and probabilistic sampling. It achieves significant performance gains across several supervised and unsupervised tasks, including kernel PCA and least squares SVM. Together, the error analysis and experiments support paying attention to the representational quality of landmarks when reducing the cost of kernel-based learning.
summary.tldr: An error bound motivates k-means landmark selection for Nyström approximation, with significant gains in several learning tasks.

title: Improved Nyström low-rank approximation and error analysis

abstract: We present the first polynomial algorithm for learning a class of inversion transduction grammars (ITGs) that implement context free transducers -- functions from strings to strings. The class of transductions that we can learn properly includes all subsequential transductions. These algorithms are based on a generalisation of distributional learning; we prove correctness of our algorithm under an identification in the limit model.
originalAbstract: We present the first polynomial algorithm for learning a class of inversion transduction grammars (ITGs) that implement context free transducers -- functions from strings to strings. The class of transductions that we can learn properly includes all subsequential transductions. These algorithms are based on a generalisation of distributional learning; we prove correctness of our algorithm under an identification in the limit model.

paragraphs: The paper studies learning functions that transform one string into another. Its representations are a class of inversion transduction grammars implementing context-free transducers. The central contribution is a polynomial algorithm for learning this class, presented as the first such result. The claim concerns a specified learnable class of grammars rather than every possible string transformation.

The learnable transductions strictly include all subsequential transductions. In other words, the class covers that entire existing family and extends beyond it. This inclusion describes the expressive reach of the learning result: its significance rests on both the algorithm’s polynomial computation and the range of string-to-string functions that it can learn.

The algorithms build on a generalization of distributional learning. Their correctness is proved under an identification-in-the-limit model, so the guarantee is tied to that formal account of learning. The paper’s stated contribution is theoretical: it establishes a computational learning method and proves correctness for the designated class within the specified learning model.
summary.tldr: The paper gives a polynomial learning algorithm for a class of inversion transduction grammars, with correctness under identification in the limit.

title: Inference of Inversion Transduction Grammars
Scientific Theory Formation Through Analogical Inference
